News.title: Russell Brand latest: Rapist's 'humiliation' moments after arriving at HMP Wandsworth
News.content:
Russell Brand remains caged inside HMP Wandsworth in South London as the disgraced star awaits his sentencing for rape and sexual assault on Monday

Russell Brand is said to have faced a "humiliating" first day in HMP Wandsworth.

Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday, and is due to be sentenced on Monday.

The judge told the 51-year-old that he faces a lengthy prison term. He also denied Brand's lawyer's plea to grant him bail so he could say goodbye to his children, instead remanding the rapist in custody.

It has been claimed that prisoners at HMP Wandsworth - where he is being held - have been warned not to speak to him. One source, who had just visited her son inside the jail, told the Mirror: "My son said Brand is downstairs from him. He said no one is allowed to see or speak to him."

Brand was reportedly made to "strip off in reception" when he first arrived at the lock-up in South London. A source told The Sun: "The first night for anyone in a jail is really daunting – and Brand was petrified... All prisoners have to strip off in reception, which is humiliating and a real wake-up call.

News.title: BBC Weather issues verdict on where snow may fall in the UK in November
News.content:
BBC Weather issues verdict on where snow may fall in the UK in November

BBC Weather forecasters say conditions will likely turn chilly towards the end of next week, and showers could turn wintry in some parts of the UK

UK weather: Met Office forecasts brighter conditions as fog lifts

Wintry showers and snow could be on the cards in some parts of the UK this month.

‌



‌



Weather forecasting models have already started showing some snow falling in the latter half of November, with chilly temperatures expected too. The ECMWF weather model suggests daytime temperatures could plunge to -4C in some areas on Friday.

‌



The Met Office has said we could see the earliest major stratospheric warming event in history over the coming days. The weather phenomenon, caused by temperatures rising well above the Earth’s surface, means cold air rushes downwards and often leads to cold snaps in the UK.

‌



View 2 Images Weather models suggest daytime temperatures could plunge to -4C in some areas on Friday (Image: WXCHARTS)

Met Office issues flight cancellation warning in 85 areas for 17 hours – list READ MORE :

BBC Weather forecast for next week

BBC Weather forecasters say the first half of next week will be “dominated by a relatively weak high pressure system” centred over Scotland, leading to “dry weather” but with “extensive banks of cloud”. This should also lead to “chillier” conditions.

Much of England and Wales will likely “turn wet, milder and breezier at times” from Wednesday, the BBC forecast adds, while Scotland and Northern Ireland “could be drier and brighter for a day or so”.

‌



However, “a colder north to north-westerly flow of winds is likely to develop” before the weekend. Despite this leading to “drier and sunnier conditions spreading southwards”, there will still be some showers “blowing across windward areas”.

View 2 Images Some showers could turn wintry next week, BBC Weather says (stock) (Image: PA)

‌



BBC Weather says these showers “could be wintry” over higher ground in Scotland and northern England.

BBC Weather forecast for November 16 to 22

For the subsequent week, BBC Weather says “periods of wet and windy weather” are on the cards, “interspersed with brighter but showery interludes”.

Article continues below

“It should be a relatively mild seven days, with temperatures more likely to be above normal than below for the week,” the forecast states.

“However, there will be day-to-day variability, with some transient chillier conditions in between weather systems, especially across the northern UK, where there could be some fleeting wintriness in showers over higher ground.”

News.title: Closer ties with EU will come with 'costs as well as benefits', Lisa Nandy says
News.content:
Closer ties with EU will come with 'costs as well as benefits', Lisa Nandy says

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has acknowledged there will be 'costs as well as benefits' for Britain as it seeks to get closer to the European Union again

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has reignited the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU (Image: NEIL HALL/EPA/Shutterstock)

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has acknowledged there will be trade-offs for Britain as it seeks to get closer to the European Union again.

‌



‌



The Cabinet minister admitted there are “costs as well as benefits” to a closer relationship with the bloc as she was asked about the possibility of thousands of young people from the EU entering Britain.

‌



Andy Burnham has reignited the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU since entering Downing Street this summer. The Prime Minister has said Brexit had done more harm than good and that a better relationship with the bloc could boost economic growth and help tackle illegal immigration.

‌



The issue will remain high on the agenda this month as the PM heads to the European Political Community (EPC) Summit this week and major UK-EU summit in Brussels on November 20.

A youth mobility scheme - that would allow young people in EU members to live and work in the UK - is among deals under negotiation ahead of the crunch summit. The UK is said to be pushing for a cap of about 50,000 people arriving a year but the EU wants the limit to be more like 150,000.

View 2 Images Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has acknowledged there will be trade-offs for Britain (Image: Jeff Overs/BBC/Press Association)

‌



Asked if the 150,000 figure was true, and whether it would be acceptable to her constituents, Ms Nandy said: “Well, we’ll have those conversations with our European counterparts, but we’ll also have those conversations too with the British people, because it is right to say that there are costs as well as benefits to a closer relationship with the European Union.

"There are trade-offs to be made, and we can’t cut people out of that conversation.” Ms Nandy, who represents the leave-voting Wigan constituency, suggested she is not in favour of rejoining the trade bloc.

‌



She told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg: “The only thing that I think the British people are absolutely united on right now is that we left the European Union a decade ago with the promise of a close Brexit deal and the promise of benefits from that deal, and most of those have not been realised. It’s not working for people across this country, and we’ve got to do better.”

Brussels’ former chief Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier told the BBC Britain cannot rejoin without having freedom of movement between the UK and the EU.

‌



Mr Barnier said: “There is no cherry picking. There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms (of good, movement of people, services and capital) are clearly the four conditions to be inside the single market.”

Andy Burnham told the Sunday Mirror any deals made at an upcoming UK-EU summit are "not the end of our ambition" in improving the relationship with the bloc.

‌



The Prime Minister said: “It pays to have a good relationship with your neighbours, and the practical deals we are agreeing with Europe will pay off for families across the UK.

“Cutting red tape on food coming in and out of the country will ease pressure on prices at the supermarket, while making life easier for farmers and food producers. This summit will show what we can achieve when we work together, but it doesn’t need to be the end of our ambition.

Article continues below

“Working more closely with Europe could drive growth, make our country safer and give us more tools to tackle illegal migration. That’s a conversation worth having.”

Elsewhere, Ms Nandy rejected allegations that celebrating the UK rejoining Erasmus+ by linking it to Remembrance Sunday was inappropriate. The Tories suggested she was using the national civic occasion to “try to make an EU membership pitch”. She told Sky News: “I strongly, strongly disagree, and it’s Remembrance Sunday, it’s not a time for politicking."

News.title: Mum demands school attendance rewards end after her kids were denied cake and hot chocolate
News.content:
Mum demands school attendance rewards end after her kids were denied cake and hot chocolate

Danielle Hand has launched a petition to have school attendance rewards ended after her son and daughter did not get sweet treats in class after missing some days of school

View 4 Images Danielle Hand said her son and daughter were left in tears at school (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

A furious mum said school attendance rewards should be scrapped after her kids were left bawling when they were denied hot chocolate and cake because they did not have 100 per cent attendance.

‌



‌



Danielle Hand, 30, claimed her two young kids were singled out in their class and were not given any sweet treats at their primary school, after missing a few days this school year. Michael-James Kendall, five, and Brooklyn-Harper Bond, seven, told their mum they had to sit and watch their friends eat their cake or cookie and drink a hot chocolate or milkshake.

‌



Brooklyn-Harper had missed six days of school and Michael-James missed five, which included an unauthorised four-day holiday.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images The mum has set up a petition to ban school attendance rewards (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

Danielle, from Doncaster, said she could only afford to go away out of the summer holiday period. She took the kids to Tattershall, Lincolnshire, in September to cheer them up after losing several family members over the past year.

‌



The mum-of-three said she found out about the incident on October 22, the last day of school ahead of the October half-term, while putting her children to bed.

Pupils in the class were given a reward, to eat and drink while doing their work, if they had 100 per cent from the start of the school year in September.

‌



View 4 Images The mum said the kids were denied a sweet treat in class because of the attendance record (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

She said: "When I put them to bed, I get them a drink of their choice. Brooklyn asked me why she couldn't have a hot chocolate. I hadn't made them yet, so I asked what she meant, and she said at school. I thought I might not have paid for something, so I asked her what happened.

‌



"That was when she explained the attendance issues, and that she and a couple of other children in her class had to watch their friends eat cake in front of them while doing Maths. Brooklyn is currently being tested for autism, and she was really upset about it.

"I asked Michael if the same thing had happened to him, and he said so, but he wasn't given a cookie and milkshake, I'm assuming because he was in a lower key stage.

‌



"But what broke my heart was that he is only a toddler still and is being punished for something he doesn't understand. I later found out four other children in his class weren't given treats. I felt sick to my stomach, I was furious."

View 4 Images Brooklyn-Harper Bond and Michael-James Kendall (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

‌



Danielle said she was not made aware of any rewards scheme for attendance by the school but suggested there had been similar instances in the past.

The mum has now launched a petition against attendance rewards and put in a formal complaint to the school, which she said has a good Ofsted rating.

‌



The school has since opened an internal investigation and has agreed to meet with Danielle to discuss what happened. The mum also contacted Ofsted and her local MP, Ed Miliband.

He has since sent a letter to Danielle stating that he has "noted her concerns" and "encouraged" her to raise the issues with the school. Mr Miliband also said he wishes her concerns were given "full consideration" and to find a "constructive resolution".

Article continues below

A spokesperson for Outwood Grange Academies Trust said: "As this matter is currently under review by the school principal in accordance with our complaints procedure, we will not be issuing a comment at this time."

Attendance rewards are often used in schools as an incentive to encourage pupils to come in to school and on time.

News.title: Pharmacist ‘speak to your GP’ alert if they get ‘serious’ atorvastatin side effect
News.content:
Pharmacist ‘speak to your GP’ alert if they get ‘serious’ atorvastatin side effect

People taking the cholesterol-lowering drug are being urged not to ignore one thing

View 3 Images Atorvastatin may cause some issues (Image: Getty Images)

People taking a widely prescribed cholesterol-lowering medication have been urged to speak to their GP if they notice changes in their memory. Atorvastatin is used to lower cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes, but memory problems have previously been listed among possible side effects of statin medicines.

‌



‌



Dr Naheed Ali, MD, PhD, a physician and Senior Contributor at Vera Clinic, said people should not stop taking the medication simply because they are worried about their memory. Speaking exclusively to the Daily Mirror, he said: "The Oxford trial data cited here is reassuring, and it's why I wouldn't advise a patient to stop atorvastatin over memory concerns alone.

‌



"That said, someone noticing real changes in recall shouldn't brush them off either, since the cause could be sleep, stress, another medication or something unrelated entirely. The right move is exactly what this piece points to: raise it with a GP rather than quietly stopping a medicine that's protecting the heart."

‌



View 3 Images Millions of people take statins across the UK (Image: Getty Images)

His advice comes after research led by Oxford Population Health, published in The Lancet in February, examined potential side effects associated with statins. Researchers analysed 23 large-scale randomised trials involving more than 150,000 participants and found no meaningful excess of memory impairment among people taking statins compared with those given a placebo.

‌



The findings are reassuring for patients who worry that statins could affect their memory, but they do not mean that new symptoms should be ignored. The researchers found that memory or cognitive problems were reported at a similar annual rate of 0.2 per cent among people taking statins and those receiving a dummy treatment.

Atorvastatin is part of the statin family, which works by reducing the amount of cholesterol made by the liver. Lowering cholesterol can help prevent fatty deposits building up in the arteries, reducing the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.

‌



View 3 Images Millions of people take atorvastatin (Image: Getty)

The NHS advises patients to keep taking atorvastatin unless their doctor tells them to stop, as cholesterol levels can rise again after treatment is discontinued. Anyone concerned about side effects should speak to a doctor or pharmacist rather than changing their dose or abandoning treatment without advice.

Article continues below

Although memory loss has appeared in statin safety information, the latest research found no good evidence that statins cause the problem at a population level. If someone notices persistent or concerning changes in their recall, a GP can help assess possible explanations, including other medicines, sleep difficulties or unrelated health conditions.

News.title: Remembrance Sunday live: Kate’s moving tribute to fallen as she joins King in leading nation in silence
News.content:
The King and other members of the Royal Family, including the Princess of Wales gathered at the Cenotaph this morning for the annual Remembrance Sunday service

Remembrance Sunday live: Kate’s moving tribute to fallen as she joins King in leading nation in silence

The Princess of Wales bowed her head in reflection as she joined the King as he led the nation in falling silent for the war dead in a moving service at the Cenotaph with the rest of the Royal Family today.

They were joined by former Prime Ministers, senior politicians, religious leaders and 10,000 veterans, who marched past the War Memorial, for the annual Remembrance Sunday service this morning.

Charles, who recently returned from his Caribbean tour, and Prince William laid wreaths in memory of the fallen alongside Princess Anne and Prince Edward.

Kate, who wore three poppies and her HMS Glasgow brooch, watched on from the balcony of the Foreign Office alongside Queen Camilla. On another balcony were the Duchess of Edinburgh, the Duke and Duchess of Gloucester and the Duke of Kent , who also watched proceedings.

It came hours after the King and Queen led the royal family in applauding Britain’s servicemen and women during a evening of remembrance at London’s Royal Albert Hall.

Prince Harry and Meghan were not at the service today and are marking Remembrance Sunday privately.

News.title: Woman dies as air ambulance scrambled to Tesco and shoppers evacuated
News.content:
Woman dies as air ambulance scrambled to Tesco and shoppers evacuated

A woman in her 50s has tragically died after emergency services were scrambled to a Tesco store in Rochdale - the shop was evacuated during the incident

View 2 Images An air ambulance landed at the Tesco store yesterday (Image: Mcroutlaws Facebook)

A woman has sadly died after emergency services were scrambled to a Tesco store.

‌



‌



The incident took place on Saturday afternoon at the supermarket's branch on Silk Street in Rochdale, on the outskirts of the town centre.

‌



Police received a report of a concern for welfare for a woman inside the store, a Greater Manchester Police (GMP) spokesperson said.

‌



Shoppers described the women being treated first by staff and then paramedics when they arrived, Manchester Evening News reports.

Others said they were told to leave the store and vacate the car park to allow the emergency services to deal with the incident.

‌



View 2 Images Shoppers were evacuated from the supermarket (Image: Google Maps)

Ambulances called to Russell Brand's prison HMP Wandsworth as rapist awaits sentencing READ MORE :

It is understood staff and managers at the store were supporting the emergency services while the incident unfolded.

‌



Footage posted on social media showed an air ambulance landing on the supermarket's car park.

Sadly the woman, who was in her 50s, could not be saved and died, the GMP spokesperson confirmed this afternoon.

Article continues below

Her next of kin have been informed.

News.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor under fresh pressure in the US as Democrats pledge to "get creative" in investigation
News.content:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor under fresh pressure in the US as Democrats pledge to "get creative" in investigation

Democrats issue new vow to “get creative” in helping British police investigate former Prince Andrew over his friendship with the late convicted paedophile Jeffrey Epstein

View 6 Images Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew facing fresh pressure in the US (Image: AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth)

Former Prince Andrew is now under increased pressure in the United States following the Democrats stunning political victories last week.

‌



‌



They have vowed to “get creative” in helping British police investigate Mountbatten-Windsor. And - after taking control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives - the Democrats pledged to renew their demand that the explosive unredacted Jeffrey Epstein files are handed over to the Metropolitan Police - in full.

‌



Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley made a high profile visit to the US in March. Suhas Subramanyam, who sits on the powerful House Oversight Committee, said they will have to think differently on how they approach the case.

‌



The former prince has so far ignored a request from the committee to testify - as a foreign national, he cannot be forced to. Mountbatten-Windsor has always firmly denied all allegations against him.

View 6 Images Former Prince Andrew, Virginia Giuffre, and Ghislaine Maxwell (Image: US District Court - Southern Dis)

Sarah Ferguson seen in public for first time with Beatrice and Eugenie after fleeing UK over Epstein scandal READ MORE :

But Mr Subramanyam said this decision has been taken as a sign he has “something to hide”.

‌



He added: “We're going to continue to push for information, and if they are in newly released files or testimony we will find out.

“It's in Andrew's best interests to co-operate. If you're not willing to co-operate with an investigation into the sexual assault and trafficking of underage girls, that is very questionable in my mind. Staff, secretaries, other people around Epstein. We'll have to get creative.”

‌



View 6 Images Former Prince Andrew and Jeffrey Epstein (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

At the time of his visit Sir Mark said: "Of course, there's a big body of that evidence... in the United States in all those files and at some stage we're going to need the unredacted evidence.

‌



"We need the original copy, and where it came from, and that's going to be necessary if we get to the stage of court cases."

In 2022 Mountbatten-Windsor paid a reported £12million to Virginia Giuffre, who claimed that Epstein trafficked her to have sex with the former prince three times in 2001 when she was 17. Ms Giuffre took her own life last year.

‌



View 6 Images Former Prince Andrew and Jeffrey Epstein (Image: POOL/New York State Sex Offender Registry/AFP via Getty Images)

The Democrats' victory in the midterm elections will give them control of Congress from January for the next two years.

‌



Mr Subramanyam said they will also 'keep pushing' the DoJ to hand over the unredacted Epstein files needed by Scotland Yard to continue its stalled probe into Lord Mandelson, sacked as Britain's ambassador to the US last year as the full extent of his relationship with the disgraced financier became clear.

Mr Subramanyam added: “We cannot compel the DoJ to release information to UK police. We're going to keep pushing on that.'

‌



View 6 Images Virginia Roberts Giuffre, with a photo of herself as a teen, when she says she was abused by Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell and Prince Andrew, among others. (Image: Emily Michot/TNS via ZUMA Press Wire/REX/Shutterstock)

If the DoJ still refuse, he said they will then use their powers to 'find information from other sources'. Earlier this year the Mirror revealed that Mountbatten-Windsor’s ex-wife Sarah Ferguson made it clear she would not be returning to the US fearing being questioned.

‌



An insider told the Mirror: “Sarah has made it clear to those around her she will never set foot in America again. She is deeply worried about the reaction she would face, whether from Epstein’s victims or scrutiny from Congress.

View 6 Images Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew facing fresh pressure in the US (Image: AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth)

Article continues below

"She feels it would be unbearable and does not want to be put in a position under oath where she would be asked not only about Epstein but also about Andrew. It has not been a difficult decision despite how deeply entrenched in America she once was.” As a non-US citizen, Ferguson, 66, is not compelled to appear before Congress or respond to the request.

News.title: King leads solemn Remembrance service at Cenotaph
News.content:
King Charles led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who have died in conflict.

On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph, Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.

That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".

But the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham was attending for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.

News.title: Watch: Royals and veterans reflect at Remembrance ceremony
News.content:
King Charles has led the annual Remembrance Sunday commemorations at the Cenotaph, laying a wreath on Whitehall in central London.

With autumn leaves falling, he was joined by other members of the Royal Family, senior politicians and veterans.

Read the BBC's live coverage of Remembrance Day across the UK.

News.title: 'Time is up': Minister warns media industry to take abuse seriously in wake of Brand case
News.content:
Abuse in the media industry is probably still happening as organisations are not doing enough to protect women, the culture secretary has warned in the wake of Russell Brand's conviction.

Lisa Nandy told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "Time is up, it really is time for the media industry to take this seriously."

She added that since entering government, "many people" from within the industry had reached out to her "to allege that things have happened to them".

Brand was found guilty of rape and sexual assault after a four-week trial, following allegations from multiple women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.

Nandy was asked whether she believed there was still exploitation and abuse within the media industry, following the Brand trial and cancellation of Channel 4 reality show Married at First Sight after the BBC revealed rape allegations.

She said: "I do not see that much has changed in terms of the way that institutions in the media industry and across public life, including politics, deal with women who very bravely come forward to allege abuse."

Nandy added that there was often no protection and a "very heavy cost" for women who speak up in industries such as media and politics, pointing to power imbalances and short-term contracts some staff members are given.

"Hand on heart, I can't say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is."

She said many had come forward from within the industry, including from the BBC.

But she added that the BBC had been an "exemplar" in signing up to the industry body to protect whistleblowers - the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority - and urged other organisations to follow suit.

A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster "has made a significant commitment to improve its culture, processes and standards".

"Last year, following an independent culture review, we set out the behavioural expectations for everyone who works with or for the BBC and we were clear action would be taken if these were not met," the spokesperson added.

News.title: Government 'looking seriously' at banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay
News.content:
Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.

Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "to keep children safe".

The UK's social media ban for under-16s is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted has not responded to requests for comment.

Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."

It came after the Sunday Times reported, external that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the popular second-hand online marketplaces.

The move was due to fears that messaging functions on the platforms allowed strangers to groom children, according to the newspaper. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.

Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".

Vinted also says its users need to be at least 18 years old. The site, on which users mostly buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly recently to reach 17 million UK users.

An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers".

"While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added in a statement.

News.title: My parents chose to die together and I was left to grieve alone
News.content:
Some people might find this article upsetting.

Early one morning in June 2024, Bas pulled up next to his parents' campervan, parked on a sunny marina in the north of the Netherlands.

His father and mother, Jan and Els, had spent most of their married life on water. Now in their 70s, they could no longer manage a houseboat. Their campervan, positioned close to the yachts and dinghies, was the next best thing.

Jan and Els got into their son's car. Bas started the engine. This would be the final time he drove his parents anywhere. For Jan and Els, this journey - to the local hospice - would be their last.

At 10:30 that morning they would be administered lethal medication by doctors and die together in what is known in the Netherlands as duo-euthanasia. It's legal and it's rare, but every year more Dutch people choose to end their lives this way.

News.title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
News.content:
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.

The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.

But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.

The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".

Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.

"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.

The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.

It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.

News.title: He spent $50,000 on Labubus but now the craze is dying
News.content:
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.

Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (Â£11) or more.

Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.

The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.

Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (Â£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".

He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.

But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."

Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.

It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.

Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.

The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.

News.title: Ambika Mod wants to change how South Asian women are seen on-screen
News.content:
She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles.

Fans have questioned why she hasn't gone on to appear in as many roles as her One Day co-star Leo Woodall, who's since appeared in major films including Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy and A24's Anthony Bourdain biopic, Tony.

Addressing this remark, Mod tells Newsbeat she thinks "there's definitely an issue in this industry with systemic racism".

"I think it is really hard for South Asian actors to really push through.

"I feel like the glass ceiling is always getting higher and higher and higher."

A report from the Creative Diversity Network, external suggested that representation of minority ethnic groups on and off-screen dropped slightly last year, after a few years of improvement.

And similar research from media watchdog Ofcom , externalfound people from certain backgrounds are less well-represented across the UK broadcasting industry.

It said "people from minority ethnic groups (across the industry as a whole) only account for 11% of those in senior management roles".

It also found under-representation in creative, production and on-screen roles.

Mod says she doesn't know if on-screen representation is changing, but says she "won't engage" with a role if she thinks its tokenistic or stereotypical.

"I've been very, very lucky in my career so far from very early on to play really complex, meaty roles and to have changed the narrative in many ways," she says.

"And I'm not looking to regress."

And when it comes to considering what to take on next, she says she tries to follow advice Dame Emma Thompson once gave her: "There's no such thing as a career, there's only what you do next."

"I'm always just trying to focus on what the new challenging thing is going to be, or cool people that I want to work with," she says.

"And also what's going to be fun, as well."

News.title: Briton among six killed in 'far-right' shooting in Krakow
News.content:
A gunman believed to have been inspired by far-right ideology has killed six people and injured more than a dozen others in an attack in the busy centre of Poland's second largest city.

Police said the attacker drove on to Main Market Square in Krakow, a popular tourist attraction, on Saturday afternoon and fired randomly at people.

Four women and two men were killed. Three were Polish, one was British and two have not been identified.

Among the 16 injured are five foreign nationals from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and Britain.

Another three bodies were found when counter-terrorism police searched the suspect's home around 125 miles (200km) away, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.

A massive armed police presence was deployed across Krakow on Saturday evening, as security measures were ramped up in the capital Warsaw and elsewhere.

A period of mourning has been declared in Krakow until 11 November.

Two police officers are also among those injured, one critically.

The suspect, who was equipped with military-style weapons and attire, is a 25-year-old Polish man - described by a minister as "ultra-nationalist".

Police shot and arrested him and he remains in hospital having undergone surgery.

Tusk said there were "strong indications" the two women and one man found dead at the suspect's home in Ostrowiec ÅwiÄtokrzyski were his immediate family members.

He said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism... that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "I'm shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in KrakÃ³w today."

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.

The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in the historic centre of Krakow, an ornate square which has long been a draw for tourists.

Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.

The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.

Images from the scene show overturned tables and scattered belongings left behind as people ran for their lives.

Armed police officers pursued the attacker's car until it crashed, at which point they engaged him in a firefight.

Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify captured the moment a police officer confronted the suspect as he lay on the ground.

The officer, who is visibly injured, can then be seen falling to the ground.

News.title: Nandy rejects claims of politicising Remembrance Sunday after Erasmus row
News.content:
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has rejected accusations of politicising Remembrance Sunday after being criticised for linking the event to the UK rejoining the European Union's Erasmus scheme.

Her department announced on Saturday night that "as we mark Remembrance Sunday, Erasmus+ will give a new generation the chance to build connections across Europe".

That sparked a backlash from the Conservatives, who said "veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme" and accused her of making an "EU membership pitch".

Nandy said she was "horrified" by the Tory response and insisted that the expanded EU scheme for study and work would help young Britons recognise wartime sacrifice.

The UK is rejoining the scheme in January, six years after leaving it as part of the Brexit deal.

On Saturday, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport drew comparisons between that scheme and events on Sunday to commemorate veterans who had died in conflict.

Referring to the scheme, Nandy said in her department's press release: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."

Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake described her comments as "tone deaf and frankly shameful" and called on Nandy to apologise.

He said the bonds that veterans forged "run far deeper" than Erasmus.

"It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," he added.

Reform leader Nigel Farage told the BBC: "For Lisa Nandy to use Remembrance Sunday to announce this and say it's all about peace, it's all about the war - I find that very, very poor taste."

Peter Sharples, chief executive of the Veterans Institute, told the Telegraph that people should "just honour the fallen" on Remembrance Sunday rather than discussing "party political matters".

Asked about the criticism on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Nandy stood by her initial remarks.

"It was Winston Churchill after the Second World War who talked about extending the hand of friendship across Europe and making sure that we honoured the legacy of that generation," she said.

She said that after Brexit "we closed off opportunities for young people from this country to understand not just the impact that generation made here in the UK, but the way in which they went off and fought for the freedom of people across Europe".

Asked to respond to accusations she had chosen Remembrance Sunday to "promote part of the new deal the government has done with the EU", Nandy said she was "not choosing today or any day actually to promote a deal with the EU".

Pressed about linking the day to what the government believes are the cultural benefits of the scheme, Nandy said: "There was a time where that wouldn't have even raised an eyebrow as somehow political, it was just common sense - and it is common sense."

News.title: We face paying £9,000 tax even though our second home is in a war zone
News.content:
A Ukrainian woman who fled to Scotland after Russia invaded her homeland has been told she could face a Â£9,000 property tax charge because she still owns a flat in Kyiv.

Kateryna Stepanovych, 38, discovered the potential charge when she tried to buy a house in North Ayrshire with her Scottish partner Mattias Lindgren.

The couple were told the Additional Dwelling Supplement (ADS) charge would apply because she already owned a property overseas.

Kateryna bought the small flat in 2018, before Russia's invasion. She fled the war zone in 2023, leaving the property behind.

News.title: I won't let my daughter's killer live in my head, says Sarah Payne's mum
News.content:
The mother of murdered schoolgirl Sarah Payne says she wants to change how people see victims of crime.

Sara Payne's daughter was abducted while playing with her siblings and murdered in July 2000, aged just eight.

Roy Whiting - a convicted sex offender - was jailed for life in December 2001 for her killing.

Sara told BBC South East there were many reasons behind how people behaved, but they "still have choices".

"You have to choose which path you're going to take," she said.

"I chose not to allow him [Whiting] to live in my head.

"It had to be her - so I keep Sarah."

Sarah's body was found 17 days after she went missing from a field near her grandparents' house in West Sussex.

Her disappearance prompted one of the most heavily publicised searches in UK history and led to landmark legal changes.

"I don't have anger. I don't have aggression. I don't want to bring back hanging or any of those things," Sara continued.

"I just want to go forward in a humane way and be human."

News.title: Veterans shouldn't sleep rough this Christmas, Burnham says
News.content:
No one who served in the UK armed forces should have to sleep on the streets this Christmas, Andy Burnham has said.

Downing Street said the PM would personally write to councils across England on Armistice Day (11 November) to urge them to draw up plans to offer accommodation for veterans sleeping rough ahead of the festive period.

He will say that national and local government should work under the "simple principle" that "no one who has served our country should ever be left to sleep rough on our streets".

The Conservatives have meanwhile criticised Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy for linking participation in an EU scheme for young people with the armed forces' sacrifices on Remembrance Sunday.

Burnham will ask local authorities to use part of the additional Â£874m already announced to tackle homelessness specifically for housing veterans.

"People who stepped forward prepared to put their lives on the line for the rest of us should never lack a roof over their head," Burnham said in a statement issued on Saturday.

"When they need help, the country owes them more than warm words. It owes them a bed every night, a proper plan and someone in their corner from day one."

The PM will ask councils to work with local organisations and charities to tackle homelessness amongst veterans.

Downing Street said an additional Â£8.7m in funding would be allocated to eight organisations across the UK to help housing providers offer assistance to veterans with complex needs, including those with health or addiction problems.

Among them are Veteran Housing Scotland, Launchpad and SSAFA, the Armed Forces Charity.

News.title: Two seriously hurt in 30-vehicle crash on the M20 in Kent
News.content:
More than 30 vehicles were involved in a crash which left two people seriously injured on the M20 in Kent on Saturday evening.

The crash happened in foggy conditions just after 18:40 GMT on the London-bound carriageway between junctions eight (Maidstone) and nine (Ashford).

Paramedics attended to 11 people, and two were taken to hospital, Kent Fire and Rescue Service said.

The road was shut in both directions early on Sunday, but has since reopened.

An air ambulance crew, three fire engines and a "technical rescue unit" were sent to the scene, where National Highways said "thick fog" had been confirmed.

Kent Police said one of the two people seriously injured had been taken to a hospital locally, and the other to a London hospital.

"Other drivers have sustained injuries not believed to be serious," it said in a statement.

The force has asked anyone with information about the incident or dashcam footage to come forward.

News.title: Two arrests and police officers hurt after brawl outside bare-knuckle fighting event
News.content:
Two men have been arrested and three police officers injured during a street disturbance outside a bare-knuckle fighting championship in Glasgow.

Footage circulating on social media shows a group of men trading punches in the street outside the Ovo Hydro where the event was held on Saturday evening.

More than 20 police vehicles and a police helicopter converged on the area. Three officers were hurt, two of them requiring medical treatment, as they responded to the disorder.

Police Scotland said two men, aged 32 and 27, had been arrested and charged with offences including assault, obstructing police and threatening and abusive behaviour.

News.title: School Street fines at one location exceed £1m
News.content:
A London council has issued more than Â£1m worth of penalty charge notices (PCNs) to drivers under a School Street scheme in less than two years.

Brent Council issued PCNs totalling Â£1.15m after introducing the scheme outside Manor School in Kensal Rise in November 2024, saying it would improve road safety and the environment.

Ward councillor Barbara Want raised concerns about the scheme and claimed that the signs were "too high and not properly visible".

Brent Council said the signs in place complied with Department for Transport guidelines, but that it had decided to install extra lower-level signs and gateway features to give more clarity to drivers.

In the 21 months the scheme has been in place, the north-west London council has collected Â£54,799 on average per month, with the scheme only in place during term time.

School Streets are being trialled across the borough to enforce road closures during drop-off and pick-up times, policed by CCTV cameras and mobile enforcement teams. Those caught face a PCN of Â£160, reduced to Â£80 if paid within 14 days.

Previously, it was reported that 70,000 PCNs were issued in 12 months, at a rate of 384 per school day.

In July 2025, the two cameras enforcing the scheme outside Manor School raised more than Â£107,000 in a single month, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

Want said: "For months I have been highlighting the huge volume of PCNs issued to drivers on the Manor School Street. The fact that it has raked in more than Â£1m in two years should have told them something wasn't right.

"It is failing children's safety if drivers are still using the road. I fear the scheme is more about revenue generation than improving road safety or air quality."

Promise Knight, the council's cabinet member for cleaner streets, transport and public realm, said School Streets existed in the borough "to make the journey to and from school safer for children and families".

"The purpose of the scheme is to protect children by reducing congestion and improving air quality.

"We will continue to review the scheme and make practical improvements where they can help drivers comply."
