World.title: Africa: CANEX Opens Doors for Gambian Fashion Entrepreneurs Seeking Global Recognition
World.content:
For Gambian fashion entrepreneur Ndey Bassin Faye, building an internationally recognised brand begins with empowering women, celebrating local culture, and embracing African-made textiles. At CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos, she and fellow entrepreneurs are looking beyond borders to build connections that could help transform their businesses and the continent's fashion industry.

When Ndey Bassin Faye discusses her fashion brand's global expansion, she also refers to promoting Gambian culture internationally.

The founder of Bassin's Couture, established in 2016, is one of three Gambian fashion and tailoring entrepreneurs, Mariama Jallow, Ndey Bassin, and Ida, attending the Creative Africa Nexus Weekend (CANEX WKND) 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria.Their attendance is sponsored by the Andandorr programme, with support from EU YEP – Tourism and Creative Industries.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

For entrepreneurs, the four-day gathering is more than an opportunity to showcase their work. It is a chance to meet potential partners, connect with suppliers, learn from industry experts, and explore new markets for their businesses.

At the heart of Faye's work is a commitment to women and girls. Through Bassin's Couture, she uses fashion not only as a business opportunity but also as a means of empowering women to pursue entrepreneurship while promoting Gambian culture through design.

Like many African fashion entrepreneurs, she faces challenges that extend beyond creativity and craftsmanship. One of the biggest obstacles is accessing materials.

"One of the challenges we face is the difficulty of sourcing diverse fabrics, particularly those outside of Gambian culture," says Faye.

She highlights the challenges of sourcing materials from other African countries, noting that, in some instances, it is easier to access supplies from Europe and China than from within the continent.

While the continent is home to rich textile traditions, cotton-producing countries, and a growing community of designers, connecting the different parts of the value chain remains difficult.

For Faye and her partners, CANEX offers an opportunity to help bridge some of those gaps. She hopes to use the gathering to establish relationships with suppliers, meet fellow designers, and explore collaborations that could strengthen her business and expand its reach.

"I want us to go international. I want our brand to be seen and to be known internationally," she says.

She also wishes to see more African materials incorporated into African fashion.

The Gambia has a tradition of handweaving, and Faye is proud to work with locally grown cotton. By incorporating hand-woven fabrics into her designs, she is taking practical steps towards building a fashion business that promotes local resources while celebrating the country's cultural identity.

Building a fashion industry that supports African designers

The challenges facing entrepreneurs such as Faye are part of the bigger conversations at CANEX, particularly during different masterclasses offered by experts in the textile industry. In a masterclass about how African fashion businesses could strengthen their marketing management and expand into global markets, luxury brand consultant Anita Ehui highlighted the structural difficulties that continue to affect African fashion businesses, particularly in manufacturing, textiles, sourcing, quality control, and pricing.

"I think we have a big manufacturing problem, whether in textiles or production itself, and that makes things difficult," Ehui said.

She explained that while many designers aspire to manufacture their products entirely on the continent, achieving this can be challenging due to limitations in material availability, production capacity, and quality.

Designers are often forced to make compromises, whether on quality, pricing, or design, because the necessary resources and infrastructure are not always readily available. Ehui encouraged entrepreneurs to prioritise African sourcing and production wherever possible, arguing that increasing demand for locally manufactured products could help strengthen the continent's manufacturing ecosystem.

However, she also cautioned against some common mistakes made by emerging fashion businesses.

One common mistake is overcomplicating business decisions, such as designing and selling products based solely on personal preferences rather than genuine customer demand.

For African fashion businesses aiming for growth, identifying the correct market is crucial. Instead of trying to appeal to everyone, entrepreneurs should understand their target customers, their desires, and the most effective ways to communicate the value of their products.

She highlighted how CANEX provides an important platform for designers to connect with potential customers and fosters conversations that can lead to partnerships and new ideas.

"CANEX is giving fashion designers a platform. It is also connecting some of the brands with customers," she stated.

She added that gatherings like CANEX create opportunities for collaboration, knowledge-sharing, and has potential to expose creators to new perspectives.

"When we gather at CANEX, there is always a conversation that can spark a collaboration or even open your mind to something new," she said.

Close 

From Local to Global Markets

For the three Gambian entrepreneurs, these conversations are particularly important as they plan the next phase of their businesses. Access to industry experts through masterclasses, exposure to other African brands and suppliers, and opportunities to engage with potential business partners offer valuable insights into building sustainable fashion enterprises.

Organised by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) and hosted by the Federal Government of Nigeria, CANEX WKND brings together leading African and diaspora creatives, investors, and policymakers from various sectors including music, film, fashion, sport, publishing, gastronomy, and visual arts.

The four-day event is designed to facilitate partnerships, encourage investment, and expand access to international markets for Africa's creative industries.

For Faye, the journey towards that future is already underway. The vision is to reach international markets without losing the local identity that makes the brand distinctive. Faye and Ehui agree that African fashion can compete globally, but the continent must first make it easier for African creatives to work, source, produce, and grow together.

World.title: Africa: CANEX WKND 2026 Showcases Africa's Creative Brilliance in a Night of Fashion and Awards
World.content:
Glitz, glamour and a vibrant celebration of African creativity took centre stage at the CANEX WKND 2026 fashion show in Lagos, Nigeria.

Designers from across the continent brought their unique interpretations of African fashion to the runway.

Held under the theme “One People, United in Culture, Creating for the World,” the evening celebrated the richness and diversity of Africa’s creative industries. It showcased an impressive blend of contemporary designs, traditional craftsmanship, cultural heritage and innovative fashion.

The runway featured collections reflecting Africa’s evolving fashion identity, with designers demonstrating the continent’s growing influence in global style and the creative economy.

From music performances accompanying the models to bold silhouettes, intricate detailing and contemporary interpretations of traditional African textiles, the presentation highlighted the talent, originality and entrepreneurial spirit driving the continent’s fashion industry.

Canex Nigeria's Federal Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment (FMITI), Dr Jumoke Oduwole at the CANEX WKND fashion show.

The event was attended by Nigeria’s Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr Jumoke Oduwole. Her presence underscored the importance of the creative economy in advancing Africa’s industrial development, trade and economic diversification.

Canex A night of celebrations at the CANEX WKND fashion show and awards ceremony.

Beyond fashion, the evening brought together Africa’s wider creative community, with awards recognising outstanding contributions across the film, publishing and gastronomy industries. The celebrations highlighted the interconnectedness of Africa’s cultural sectors and their growing potential to create employment, stimulate investment and strengthen the continent’s presence in international markets.

The showcase also reflected the broader vision of the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX), an initiative established by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) to support and scale the continent’s creative and cultural industries.

Canex African designers showcased some of their colourful pieces during CANEX WKND in Lagos, Nigeria.

Afreximbank has committed US$2 billion in financing between 2024 and 2027, quadrupling its original US$500 million commitment announced in 2020. The bank expanded its financing in response to growing demand for investment across Africa’s creative ecosystem, spanning music, film, fashion, sport, publishing and gastronomy. The 2024 edition of CANEX WKND, held in Algiers, attracted participants from 81 countries.

Through its investment in creative enterprises, market access and international partnerships, CANEX seeks to transform Africa’s cultural wealth into sustainable economic opportunities, while enabling local creators to compete on the global stage.

World.title: Africa: A Just Energy Transition Cannot Leave Water Behind
World.content:
guest column

As Africa weighs how to power its industries and expand electricity access, water must be part of the equation. Ahead of COP31, Dr Jonty Cogger and Paul Wani Lado draw on South Africa’s experience to argue that a just energy transition must test proposed fossil fuel investments against their water demands—and protect the communities whose supplies could come under pressure.

South Africa's energy debate often focuses on electricity supply, energy security and economic growth. Oil and gas infrastructure is increasingly presented as part of the answer to these challenges. This framing hides a key test for any proposed development: whether its promised benefits justify the strain it will put on scarce water, and whether affected communities will carry an unfair share of the costs.

South Africa is a water-scarce country. Local communities increasingly struggle with unreliable water services, crumbling infrastructure and growing demand for water. Given this, plans to expand fossil fuel infrastructure need far closer scrutiny than they usually get.

Climate change makes matters worse by bringing more heat, more drought and less predictable rainfall. Writing for the Endangered Wildlife Trust, Dr Ian Little warns that a strong El Niño during the 2026/2027 summer season could bring below-average rainfall, higher temperatures, lower river flows and less water reaching dams. It could also cut crop yields, strain livestock farming and increase the demand for irrigation. In a country where water and food systems are already under pressure, this combination of risks shows why water security, food security and climate policy must shape any decision to expand fossil fuels further.



Oil and gas are not just a matter of energy policy. Expanding them affects the environment, the climate, water security and the rights of local communities. Yet debates about new gas infrastructure tend to focus on the promise of energy and industrial growth, rather than taking a hard look at the environmental costs and the local communities that may pay them.

Calling gas part of a just energy transition does not make it just. More electricity or investment does not, on its own, tell us who benefits, who pays the environmental, social and economic costs, and whether those costs can be avoided. Nor does calling gas a transitional fuel solve the problems of building fossil fuel infrastructure that will last for decades.

The risk is that South Africa repeats an old development model under the banner of a new transition where powerful economic interests reap the benefits of resource-hungry industry and local communities are left to deal with the environmental costs.

Water makes this contradiction especially clear because it links national energy choices to direct local effects. A project sold as improving energy security may make others less secure if it competes with households, farmers and nature for a limited and increasingly unreliable supply of water.

Putting water at the centre of the just transition means treating it as a firm limit on development, not just one factor to consider after energy and investment decisions have been made. Government should assess from the outset how proposed fossil fuel and industrial projects would affect how much water is available, its quality, and the ability of communities and ecosystems to cope as the climate worsens.

As government considers expanding gas infrastructure and attracting energy-intensive industries, it must account for how much water these developments will need. The critical question is whether the combined demand from multiple developments, together with existing uses and worsening climate pressures, can be met without harming communities' access to water, the health of ecosystems or the needs of other lawful water users.

This scrutiny must be based on evidence that is public and can be independently checked. Decision-makers should disclose how much water proposed projects need, where that water would come from, the condition and capacity of the water systems involved, what would happen in a drought, and the combined demands of existing and likely future developments.

The same scrutiny must apply to the infrastructure needed to support these developments, including pipelines, power stations and related industrial facilities. Decisions about these projects cannot ignore the water systems and communities they depend on.

Close 

Local communities should not have to face less reliable water supply so that fossil fuel expansion and industrial growth can go ahead. If government is serious about a just energy transition, it must require open water assessments that account for climate change and the combined impact of all projects before approving new developments, and it must show that communities will continue to have enough reliable water. Economic benefits should not be assumed to outweigh environmental and social costs; they must be weighed against them.

Dr Jonty Cogger is a public interest attorney at the Centre for Environmental Rights whose work focuses on using legal strategies to challenge pollution and climate change.

Paul Wani Lado is an attorney at the Centre for Environmental Rights where his work focuses on the extractives industry, particularly mining and upstream oil and gas projects.

World.title: Africa: CANEX Aims to Empower African Creatives to Compete in Global Markets and Drive Economic Growth
World.content:
CANEX WKND 2026 opens in Lagos, Nigeria, an initiative of the Afreximbank aimed at boosting creatives from across the African continent.

Creatives from across the continent are gathering in Lagos, Nigeria, for the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX). This initiative brings together Africa's creative talent, investors, policymakers, and industry leaders to unlock the economic potential of the continent's cultural industries.

Dubbed CANEX WKND, the four-day event attracted more than 15,000 registrations from across the global creative community, under the theme "One People, United in Culture, Creating for the World."

Hosted by the Federal Government of Nigeria and organised by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) through its Creative Africa Nexus programme, the event runs from 5 to 8 November. It aims to transform Africa's growing cultural influence into sustainable businesses, increased trade, investment, and employment opportunities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"CANEX was established to offer a comprehensive suite of solutions aimed at developing the capacity of Africa's creators and enhancing the value retained within the continent, through CANEX finance," said Dr George Elombi, President and Chairman of the Board of Directors of Afreximbank.

From film and television to music, fashion, publishing, sport, gastronomy, and visual arts, CANEX WKND is positioning the creative economy as an increasingly important contributor to Africa's economic transformation.

For a continent with the world's youngest population, the creative industries offer significant opportunities to harness the talents, innovation, and entrepreneurial ambitions of young people. However, translating this potential into sustainable livelihoods requires more than talent and international recognition. It requires access to finance, skills development, markets, technology, and the commercial infrastructure necessary to build viable businesses.

This is the gap Afreximbank's CANEX initiative seeks to address.

The bank recognises that financing is not the industry's only challenge; a holistic approach is needed for the industry to thrive.

"We can put financing skills into music and movie productions, yet the value we derive could still be low. We must, therefore, focus on building the creative ecosystem, focusing not just on idea generation, creation, and production, but particularly on value capture from those activities that we now know attract the greatest value. These include vending and production, and CANEX was created for that purpose," said Elombi.

He noted that the budget has increased significantly since CANEX started to meet the needs and demands.

"When CANEX began, we had a budget of U. S$500 million for the creative economy. We soon found out that it was too small, so we raised it to U.S. $ 1 billion, and that was also too small. In 2024, we raised it to U.S.$2 billion," he noted.

One of the key discussions of this event is to encourage creatives and provide a platform for practical discussions on financing creative enterprises, commercialising intellectual property, and strengthening the continent's position in global creative markets.

"Africa already has its cultural influence; our challenge is to build economic power. Look at Afrobeats, Nollywood, our fashion, literature, and visual arts: our creativity is thriving more than ever before. However, recognition is not the same thing as ownership, and global popularity does not automatically translate into prosperity," noted legendary Nigerian actor Richard Mofe-Damijo.

Mofe-Damijo emphasised the need for access to better finance, stronger protection for intellectual property, reliable institutions that work, and businesses that can grow beyond success stories.

Financing will also take centre stage at the Creative Economy Finance Summit, presented by Afreximbank in partnership with the Creative Economy Practice at Co-Creation Hub. The summit will bring together financial institutions and investors to examine how creative-economy transactions can be structured, financed and de-risked.

Among many topics, discussions will also explore one of the world's most compelling topics, artificial intelligence, examining how African creatives can leverage digital technologies to develop products capable of competing internationally.

Close 

On the list of prominent figures from across the continent and diaspora are Nobel Laureate and writer Professor Wole Soyinka, Emmy Award-winning actor Uzo Aduba, filmmaker and actor Funke Akindele, actors Richard Mofe-Damijo and Thuso Mbedu, and former professional footballers Didier Drogba and Jay-Jay Okocha, musicians Davido, Fally Ipupa, Flavour, Libianca and Charlotte Dipanda.

Cultural ministers from across the continent are also in attendance, including from Côte d'Ivoire, South Africa, and Rwanda, alongside representatives from the International Finance Corporation and Afreximbank.

Speakers highlighted that strengthening access to financing, protecting intellectual property, and improving distribution channels are essential for African creatives to compete internationally and retain a greater share of the value they generate. For Afreximbank, supporting the creative industries is also part of a wider strategy to diversify African economies, promote intra-African trade, and strengthen the continent's participation in global markets.

World.title: Africa: Deadly Viruses Know No Borders, Nor Should Our Resolve to Stop Them
World.content:
Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland.

guest column

In this guest column for AllAfrica, the Dutch Trade and Development Minister and the head of the World Health Organization stress that addressing viral health crises anywhere protects everyone everywhere. The government of the Netherlands is committing funding both for the current Ebola crisis and flexible funding to quickly respond to new or emerging global threats.

COVID-19 may feel like a distant memory to many. But the virus claimed millions of lives around the world, including approximately 50,000 in the Netherlands. The lesson is clear: preparedness is not optional.

Preventing health crises abroad is in the interest of all countries, including the Netherlands.

Governments everywhere face competing priorities and constrained budgets. But infectious diseases do not respect national borders. In an interconnected world, health threats that emerge in one place can quickly become risks for all of us. No country can safeguard its health security alone.

That lesson is evident today in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where a major Ebola outbreak is unfolding in a region already affected by insecurity, displacement and limited access to health services.

Already the outbreak has crossed national boundaries, underlining how quickly a health threat in one country can become a shared international concern.

Responding effectively requires rapid action, strong local leadership and international solidarity. Under the DRC Government's leadership, the World Health Organization (WHO) is working closely with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, local authorities, communities and partners to contain the outbreak in the DRC and save lives.

Mystic Stock Photography / Shutterstock.com The MV Hondius, a cruise ship owned by the Dutch company Oceanwide Expeditions experienced a Hantavirus outbreak last year. The Netherlands and the World Health Organized collaborated to safely evacuate passengers and crew.

To support these efforts, the Netherlands is providing €7 million to WHO for the Ebola response. But responding to outbreaks requires more than emergency funding alone. It requires flexible, predictable financing that can be directed rapidly to where needs are greatest. That is why the Netherlands is also providing a new €10 million flexible contribution to WHO for future emergencies, enabling the WHO to rapidly respond to health threats while helping countries strengthen preparedness and prevent future outbreaks whenever possible. This is additional to the existing €9.6 million yearly core funding to the WHO.

No country can safeguard its health security alone.

Some may ask why the Netherlands, or any country, should invest in health emergencies far from its own borders when domestic health systems also face challenges. The answer is simple: diseases do not stop at borders. Supporting countries to detect and contain outbreaks early is not only the right thing to do. It protects local populations while reducing the risk of wider international spread. Investing in health security abroad is also an investment in health security at home.

Outbreaks are most effectively controlled at their source. Local leadership is essential. National authorities understand their communities, their health systems and the challenges they face. WHO's role is to support those efforts, coordinate international expertise and ensure that countries have access to the tools, funding and technical assistance they need.

International cooperation remains the foundation of effective health security. This year, for example, a hantavirus outbreak on a Dutch-flagged cruise ship was swiftly contained through rapid collaboration among countries and partners coordinated through WHO. During an earlier outbreak caused by the "Sudan virus" species of Ebola in Uganda, investments that helped advance an Ebola vaccine developed by the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) and Batavia Biosciences contributed to global preparedness efforts. These examples demonstrate that cooperation works.

Dany Bitita/WHO Two new candidate vaccines to join Ebola trial as treatment research advances.

Yet this progress cannot be taken for granted. The international health system is under growing strain, even as health threats continue to increase. Climate change is altering the distribution of infectious diseases. Europe has already seen growing concern from vector-borne diseases, including West Nile virus, while other diseases such as dengue and malaria are expanding into new regions. At the same time, funding for global health, including for WHO, is declining.

Diseases spreading to new areas amid decreased global health funding is dangerous.

This is a dangerous combination. The need for cooperation, preparedness and rapid response is growing, just as the resources required to sustain them are coming under pressure.

We therefore call on European governments to strengthen their support for global health security by increasing flexible and unearmarked contributions to WHO. Such investments enable outbreaks to be detected earlier, contained more rapidly and addressed where they begin, before they become larger regional or global crises.

No one can rule out the possibility of another pandemic. . But we can ensure that we are better prepared for the next one. Strong health systems in the DRC, and in countries everywhere, are not only vital for the local communities. They are an investment in a safer, healthier and more secure future for us all.

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma is the Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation. Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Cult Leader Paul Mackenzie Sentenced to 200 Years
World.content:
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in October of the murder of 190 children.

A court in Kenya has sentenced Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and an adult. He told them to starve themselves to death as part of his apocalyptic religious cult.

Kenyan religious sect leader Paul Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Friday, at the culmination of a trial following the discovery of hundreds of corpses in the woods.

A self-proclaimed pastor and longstanding leader of a new age Christian apocalyptic cult called the Good News International Church, Mackenzie was convicted in October of 191 counts of murder in the deaths of one adult and 190 children.

Justice Diana Kavedza said the sentence was comprised of 100 years for 183 counts of murder by starvation and another 100 years for eight counts of murder by direct homicide.

He could have faced the death penalty, which is still technically on the books in Kenya.

However, like several countries that have kept capital punishment in their legal code but stopped actually using it, Kenya has not executed anybody since 1987.

While the charges against Mackenzie pertained to 191 deaths, some 400 people were found dead in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre." Mackenzie's so-called church had been operating since 2003, based in the coastal town of Malindi.

Mackenzie had denied the charges, saying that he did not force the cult followers to starve.

A total of 28 accomplices were given various prison sentences for their roles in the deaths.

World.title: Tanzania: Tanzania Opposition Leader Lissu Cleared of Treason but Jailed for Incitement
World.content:
A Tanzanian court on Friday sentenced opposition leader Tundu Lissu to four years in jail for inciting unrest, after earlier in the day clearing him of treason - meaning he avoided a possible death sentence. The verdict follows a disputed presidential election and a deadly crackdown on protesters, in a case that has drawn international condemnation and raised concerns about political freedom in the country.

A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania's commercial capital, convicted the 58-year-old leader of the country's main opposition party, Chadema, over remarks he made calling for electoral reforms.

"We are satisfied that through his statements, the accused intended to disrupt elections and instigate violence," a judge told a courtroom packed with supporters, French news agency AFP reported.



Lissu has been detained since April 2025. He has denied any wrongdoing, arguing that his campaign was lawful and the charges against him politically motivated.

Facing heavy security, Tanzania protesters fear repeat of election violence

Campaign in the dock

His arrest came six months before the October 2025 vote, shortly after he launched a drive for changes to Tanzania's electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".

Prosecutors argued that his statements were intended to disrupt the vote and threaten the government, amounting to treason.

Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments had been taken out of context and that he had committed no crime.

"My hope is that you will carry that heavy historical burden without bias, with courage and with the dignity carried by your judicial oaths," he told the panel in his closing arguments.

Tanzania's Hassan makes historic Russia visit amid frayed ties with West

Criticism abroad

The trial drew criticism from British and European Union lawmakers, who described it as politically driven and called for Lissu's immediate release.

"The use of capital punishment against a political opponent risks turning the justice system into an instrument of political repression," they wrote in a letter to President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

Security was tightened across Dar es Salaam and around the courthouse ahead of Friday's verdict, as Lissu's supporters gathered for the hearing.

Groups were mobilising to travel to the city, police said on Wednesday, warning against "those who want to stage a coup".

Elections, coups and crackdowns: Africa's mixed democratic record in 2025

Close 

Death toll in dispute

Lissu's arrest, Chadema's disqualification and alleged abductions of government critics helped fuel protests during last year's presidential election.

Hassan won with 98 percent of the vote after her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded. The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy.

A government-appointed commission put the death toll at at least 518, blaming protesters for the violence. Opposition groups and human rights organisations say the authorities killed thousands.

Accusations that security forces used excessive force have been rejected by the government. The election was fair and transparent, Hassan has insisted, blaming foreigners for the unrest.

(with newswires)

World.title: Namibia: Distance No Longer a Death Sentence
World.content:
Namibia's air ambulance is expected to reduce some journeys that take hours by road to minutes or a few short hours by air, depending on the distance and emergency.

A 12-year-old boy who needed urgent medical attention died while waiting to be transferred from Katima Mulilo to Windhoek, a tragedy that has now become one of the reasons behind Namibia's first State-owned air ambulance service.

The boy's death, followed by the loss of patients who could not be transported quickly enough after a road accident along the Otjiwarongo road, exposed the cost of delays in Namibia's emergency healthcare system.

Health minister Esperance Luvindao recounted the painful experiences on Wednesday as the country officially launched its first State-owned air ambulance service,

a move expected to reduce the time critically ill and injured patients spend travelling to specialised hospitals.



"Unfortunately, in the early hours of the next morning, I got a call that this 12-year-old boy had passed away," Luvindao said, recalling the incident involving the patient from Katima Mulilo.

"This was heartbreaking. Because I knew that a young life had just been lost," she narrated. The minister said another emergency occurred in April 2026 when a road accident along the Otjiwarongo road left patients needing urgent transportation to Windhoek. "Unfortunately, this was not possible and lives were lost," she said.

The experiences, she said, forced the health ministry to look for solutions that could save lives while the government continues with plans to build more hospitals.

The launch, officiated by Vice President Lucia Witbooi in Windhoek, marks a major change in how the country intends to respond to medical emergencies, particularly in remote areas where patients face long journeys to reach referral hospitals.

For patients who need urgent specialist care, the difference between reaching a hospital in time and waiting hours could determine whether they survive.

Witbooi said the service was intended to ensure that a person's chances of survival were not determined by where they live.

"No Namibian should lose their life simply because they live far from a hospital," she said.

She added that the country's vast geographical size and the distance between remote communities and referral hospitals had long created challenges for emergency medical care.

The air ambulance is expected to reduce some journeys that take hours by road to minutes or a few short hours by air, depending on the distance and emergency.

The service includes a Learjet air ambulance equipped with medical equipment to provide critical care during flights.

Government Air Transport Services will provide aircraft and pilots in collaboration with the ministries of health and works and transport. It will also use helicopter evacuation services through cooperation with the Namibian Police and the Namibian Defence forces to respond to emergencies in areas where helicopters are needed.

Specialised medical personnel will accompany patients requiring urgent care, while emergency service centres at national referral hospitals will help ensure patients receive treatment immediately after landing.

Luvindao said the service was developed as a practical response to the country's healthcare challenges, rather than waiting for the construction of more referral hospitals.

"While we build those hospitals, Namibians want service. While we build those hospitals, there is another 12-year-old boy that might have severe head injuries and need urgent transportation. And so it is our role to make a plan, not just for the future, but for now," she said. She said the government was working towards constructing four hospitals in the coming years, but acknowledged that such projects require substantial financial resources and time.

Close 

The air ambulance, she said, would complement existing ground ambulance services and provide an additional option for patients whose conditions require urgent specialist intervention.

The ministry has also activated an emergency callcentre to coordinate requests, verify referrals and dispatch the service.

Luvindao said the centre would serve as a single point of coordination to ensure that patients with justified medical needs are transferred promptly.

The service will prioritise patients who require urgent specialist treatment, including those with serious trauma, neurological, cardiac and obstetric emergencies, as well as patients whose conditions make road transport unsafe or too slow.

The initiative requires cooperation between the health sector, aviation authorities, emergency responders and security institutions. - [email protected]

World.title: Cowboys star Brandon Aubrey details journey from soccer player to software engineer to Pro Bowl kicker
World.content:
Brandon Aubrey has become one of the best kickers in the NFL with the Dallas Cowboys, but his road to stardom has been far from linear.

Aubrey, 31, first played professional soccer in Major League Soccer (MLS) and then the United Soccer League (USL) before hanging up the spikes.

"I wasn't ready to retire from soccer, but when I looked around at the environment, I didn't perform as well as I needed to stick on a roster and I got cut a couple of times. And at that point, there wasn't a whole lot of money in soccer at the second tier. So, I slipped from the MLS into the USL," Aubrey told OutKick in a recent interview.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I had to really take a long, hard look at it, see if it was worth pursuing, and I could make triple the money I was making in that league as a software engineer, which my degree was in."

Aubrey said he had just gotten married to his wife, Jenn, and didn’t want to set his family back , so into software engineering he went. However, working as a software engineer wasn’t very fun for Aubrey.

Aubrey said that Jenn had a good, stable job and pushed him to pursue a career as an NFL kicker.

"With that support and a lot of hard work and commitment we were able to shift over towards being a kicker, and got a job in the USFL and eventually got noticed at the NFL level and was able to get a job here," Aubrey said.

Aubrey is in his fourth season with the Cowboys and has made the Pro Bowl in each of his first three seasons. He has made 127 of his 146 field-goal attempts with a long of 65 yards, while nailing 146 of 151 extra points.

One of his 127 made field goals stands out more than the rest.

The New York Giants had gone up 37-34 in Week 2 of the 2025 season with just 25 seconds left in the game. It looked like the Cowboys were going to go 0-2 to start the year.

"They just put the dagger in us where they scored a long touchdown. to Nabers and he did the night-night celebration," Aubrey said. "We had like 12 seconds to go get 10 yards, got it and then we were in field-goal position and that's still a pretty coin-flippy field goal, maybe even less than a coin flip for historical statistics."

While a 64-yard field goal to tie the game might seem like less than a coin flip for Aubrey, he made it look easy. He nailed the kick to force overtime.

"To be able to go and hit that one through the uprights was awesome," Aubrey said.

However, his day wasn’t done there. Aubrey made a 46-yard field goal as the clock expired in overtime to give the Cowboys a thrilling 40-37 win.

"If you smile, I think that shows a lot of your personality. And for me, I put a lot of time and effort into my smile as a as a young kid. I guess I could say my parents put that time and effort into it and it was in a good spot and then shift happens. I didn't take good enough care of it as a college athlete and a young adult and my smile shifted as well. World.title: ELAINE PARKER: Democrat win is a wake-up call for Republicans, not a vote for socialism
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The American people sent a clear message in Tuesday's midterm elections. But Democrats would be making a serious mistake if they interpreted their victories as an endorsement of socialism.

Voters weren't demanding bigger government. They wanted relief from the affordability crisis.

Republicans shouldn't dismiss the results as a typical midterm setback either. The coalition that delivered President Donald Trump the White House and Republican control of Congress in 2024 expected results.

MEHEK COOKE: REPUBLICANS FAILED THE AFFORDABILITY TEST. THIS IS HOW TO WIN VOTERS BACK

The voters who hired Republicans to fix the affordability crisis are now holding them accountable for failing to deliver.

Americans were tired of inflation, unaffordable housing and watching their paychecks buy less. They believed Republicans would make their lives better.

FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

But somewhere between winning and governing, Republicans lost control of that message.

Trump had a legitimate argument for tariffs: rebuilding American manufacturing and bringing back jobs lost under decades of trade policies, including NAFTA, signed by President Bill Clinton. But Republicans never adequately explained the long-term benefits. Voters heard about tariffs while worrying about higher prices.

The same communications failure plagued the One Big Beautiful Bill.

Republicans made lower individual tax rates permanent, restored immediate expensing for qualifying business investments and prevented trillions in scheduled tax increases. Yet how many Americans could explain what that legislation actually did for them?

What good is passing legislation that helps working families and small businesses if you can't explain how it makes their lives better?

Healthcare was another squandered opportunity.

When enhanced COVID-19-era Obamacare subsidies expired, Republicans could have offered a serious affordability alternative built around price transparency, competition and consumer choice. Instead, they surrendered the conversation.

Healthcare is part of the affordability crisis. Families don't separate their mortgage, groceries, insurance premiums and deductibles into political categories. It all comes from the same paycheck.

Perhaps the biggest warning came from Hispanic voters.

The voters who hired Republicans to fix the affordability crisis are now holding them accountable for failing to deliver.

Trump made historic gains in 2024 by speaking to their economic aspirations, entrepreneurial spirit and desire for safe communities.

Following Trump's 2024 victory, his pollster, John McLaughlin, observed that Republicans had rented the Hispanic vote and warned they needed to work to keep it.

Unfortunately, they acted as though they owned it.

FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'

Economic frustration drove much of the erosion in support, but immigration enforcement contributed. Trump promised to secure the border and prioritize dangerous criminals. Instead, broader enforcement created fear in Hispanic communities, including among those who supported stronger border security.

Republicans worked hard to win those voters in 2024 and then seemingly forgot what brought them into the Republican column. They failed to maintain that trust, much less expand it.

My home state of Florida should be a wake-up call.

Republicans can celebrate electing Byron Donalds as Florida's first Black governor and holding major statewide offices. But Donalds narrowly defeated David Jolly despite a roughly 1.5-million Republican voter-registration advantage.

That advantage provided a cushion against the national Democratic swing, not immunity from it. Those margins should concern Republican leaders.

Then there's the war with Iran.

Whatever the administration's strategic justification, it failed to make a compelling case to Americans already struggling financially. Voters saw higher gasoline prices without a clearly articulated reason for the conflict.

None of this gives Democrats a mandate to push socialist policies.

A vote against Republican performance isn't necessarily a vote for higher taxes, more government spending or expanded bureaucracy. Many of these same voters supported Trump just two years ago because they wanted a different economic direction.

Democrats have earned an opportunity to address affordability, not a blank check for an ideological agenda.

Republicans, meanwhile, need to reconnect their policies to the people they're supposed to serve. Lower taxes, stronger small businesses, affordable healthcare and greater economic opportunity remain a compelling agenda. But voters need to see and feel the benefits.

Following Trump's 2024 victory, his pollster, John McLaughlin, observed that Republicans had rented the Hispanic vote and warned they needed to work to keep it. Unfortunately, they acted as though they owned it.

Tuesday's election was not a mandate for socialism. It was a demand for affordability, accountability and results.

Americans did not suddenly change what they wanted. They changed whom they trusted to deliver it.

And unless both parties understand that distinction, they risk learning the same lesson all over again.

World.title: High school athlete cursed out by Seattle Storm owner runs against trans athlete at state championship
World.content:
It was a cross-country course filled with twists, turns, hills and switchbacks. There was nothing round about it. But for Eastmont High junior Ahnaleigh Wilson, this was a case of things coming full circle.

More than two years ago, Wilson finished second to a trans athlete in a Junior Olympic track race. That set her on a path of speaking out against biological boys competing in girls' sports. If her name looks familiar, it's because she's the one Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton cursed out at a WNBA game in July for holding a sign reading, "Thank You Sophie (Cunningham) For Speaking Up For Girls!"

It brought a high school girl to tears, but as you'll learn, it takes a lot more than that to stop Ahnaleigh.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FAN WHO WAS CONFRONTED BY STORM CO-OWNER OPENS UP ON INCIDENT AND FACING TRANS ATHLETES

Since Keaton's tirade, quite a bit has happened in the world of Washington state transgender athletes. For the last month and a half, a male runner from Camas High who switched to the girls team midseason has dominated the headlines. After opening the season 76th in a boys' JV race, he crossed over to win a varsity girls' meet and knock female runners out of regional and state qualifying spots.

Well, guess who was lined up against him in Saturday's 4A girls state finals at Sun Willows Golf Course? That's right — one Ahnaleigh Wilson.

Wilson racing was no guarantee. Not just because she'd considered taking a stand against having to compete against a boy, but because she had a bone stress injury in her right fibula she feared might develop into a fracture. Her parents encouraged her not for health reasons. She didn't listen.

"I worked really hard this season, and I mean, I like running. So I wanted to run. I wanted to try at least," Wilson said.

It might have been good social-media material for activists had Wilson walked off in protest, but that wasn't going to happen. Plus, she'd already done enough in that department — regularly speaking in defense of girls and women despite her relatively shy nature.

She'd survived all the emotional abuse her detractors had thrown her way. Saturday was about surviving the physical.

BIOLOGICAL MALE COMPETING IN GIRLS' CROSS-COUNTRY RACE DENIES ANOTHER RUNNER AND HER TEAM A TRIP TO STATE

A healthy Wilson likely would have finished somewhere in the top third of Saturday's 155-girl field. Her usual time of 19:30 would have been good for 49th place. But this was not a healthy Wilson. This was a high school junior slogging through a 5000-meter course with searing pain every other step.

Ahnaleigh said she thought about quitting multiple times mid-race. But the cheers from the crowd kept her going. And we aren't talking about the ones from her parents, friends or coaches. We're talking about random supporters who knew her name because of everything she'd fought for.

"There were a few times I didn't know if I was going to finish, and I heard people I didn't recognize their voices, but there were people cheering for me, and that was really cool," she said.

Wilson's final time? 22:58.30 — which placed her 150th. The Camas male, meanwhile, finished 23rd, which wasn't fast enough to put him on the podium reserved for the top 16 runners.

This was his first race since Tuesday's election, when Washington voters decisively passed Initiative 638, which will enforce the separation of biological boys and girls in K-12 sports once it takes effect. And even though many runners at Saturday's race were relieved the measure got through, they were still motivated to outrun the boy in the girls race.

One was Skyview High runner Charlie Garrett, who, alongside teammate Sierra Retzlaff, walked off the start line in protest of the Camas runner last month. She'd heard that the boy told his teammates that his goal was to beat them every time since that act, and while he was successful in doing so Saturday (Garrett and Retzlaff finished 39th and 92nd, respectively), Garrett took solace in the fact that she wouldn't have to face him again.

WASHINGTON HS GIRLS BLAST MALE ATHLETE PARTICIPATING IN TRACK MEET: 'DON'T THINK THAT THAT'S RIGHT OR FAIR'

"I guess the motivation (to beat him) is just that I don't want my spot to be taken away by someone who shouldn't be in my race. That's my main motivation" said Garrett, a junior. "I didn't do it this season — and I won't have to this season. But I mean, me and my mom are very competitive people, so I think it just runs in the blood to try and do better than the person who's causing us stress."

Echoing that sentiment was Kamiakin High sophomore Lauren Baumann.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"My goal was to beat the guy from Camas because I don't think he should be racing in a girls race," said Baumann, who finished 11 spots behind him. "When he passed me at the 800 and I tried to stay with him but couldn't, it made me feel really really mad and just that I couldn't do anything to stop it. But I'm glad that he won't be able to run next year."

I-638 could go into effect as soon as December 3, although there may be legal challenges delaying its implementation. But girls such as Wilson, Garrett and Retzlaff — all of whom played critical roles in getting it passed — are taking their metaphorical victory laps.

That said, perhaps nobody was as emotional Saturday as Ahnaleigh's mom, Elizabeth, who broke down in tears after her daughter's race.

"I can't believe she went out and did that with a bone stress...that's just heart," Elizabeth said. "She started this journey racing a boy, and she ended it, and hopefully this will be the last time a boy competes against girls."

X-rays will reveal whether Ahnaleigh — who was limping after the race — has a stress fracture. But she proved something Saturday. Whether it's a state cross country race or a ballot initiative — no matter how painful, she is going to finish what she started.

World.title: Gulf War veteran left homeless after heart surgery details how he rebuilt his life from 'square one'
World.content:

Gulf War veteran Thomas Garrett Jr. returned home to celebratory parades, but years later, he found himself homeless after undergoing heart surgery.

Garrett’s efforts to rebuild his life after becoming homeless are highlighted in Fox Corporation’s sixth annual "Make Camo Your Cause" campaign with U.S.VETS, a nationwide initiative ahead of Veterans Day aimed at helping end veteran homelessness.

"The homecoming was a phenomenal event," Garrett said Saturday on "Fox News Live."

"I became homeless after having heart surgery. So that changed everything about my dynamic in life," he added.

AMERICA'S WOUNDED, STRUGGLING VETERANS GET BRAND-NEW HOMES BUILT BY FLORIDA TEENS

U.S.VETS, a national nonprofit dedicated to ending veteran homelessness, provides housing, food and career help to service members in need. According to the organization, it assists more than 20,000 veterans and their families each year. To date, U.S.VETS has served over 500,000 meals, provided 418,000 nights of shelter and placed 3,000 veterans into permanent housing.

Quandrea Patterson, executive director of U.S.VETS, explained that Garrett’s experience reflects a broader challenge facing veterans as they transition from military to civilian life.

NEW YORK JETS OWNER WOODY JOHNSON TO BE HONORED AT TUNNEL TO TOWERS GALA FOR DECADE-LONG PARTNERSHIP

"A lot of times when veterans are in service, they're told, and they know exactly what to do because they're mission-focused," Patterson said. "And then during that transition from active service to civilian service or veteran status, a lot of the information, a lot of the things to expect are unknown."

The uncertainty surrounding that transition can leave veterans vulnerable to homelessness, Patterson said.

For Garrett, U.S.VETS offered the structure and support he needed to move forward.

"U.S.VETS is a new starting point for veterans," Garrett said. "It's a square one to where you can build up your life the way the veteran themselves need it. It gives us good structure. It gives us a good routine to begin and to build from there."

TRUMP PROMOTES FREEDOM HAULERS INITIATIVE TO FAST-TRACK MILITARY VETERANS INTO TRUCKING JOBS

Ahead of Veterans Day, Patterson stressed that honoring those who served requires more than celebrating them once a year.

"Freedom isn’t free, and for the freedom that we're experiencing, that, there is somebody out there volunteering to put their life on the line and to navigate the unknown," Patterson said. "When they get out, we should wrap our arms around them to make sure that they know that that service was appreciated in more than just words, but in deed as well."

World.title: Blue Angels pilot removed from team for 'failing to uphold' standards, Navy says
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Blue Angels pilot was removed from the Navy’s flight demonstration team for "failing to uphold" its standards, leaving squadron with a five-jet show on Friday.

The dismissal comes just months after a controversial low Pensacola Beach flyover in July that sent debris flying, raising concern for public safety.

Maj. Scott Laux, a second-year member of the elite team, was identified as Blue Angel No. 6. The Chief of Naval Air Training (CNATRA) confirmed his removal to the Pensacola News Journal, saying the decision was announced Friday before the season finale at home in Pensacola.

NAVY SAYS NO REPRIMANDS OR FIRINGS AFTER BLUE ANGELS’ LOW PASS OVER BEACHGOERS

"Blue Angel #6 was removed from the team for failing to uphold the standards expected of members of the Navy Flight Demonstration Squadron and will not participate in the team’s remaining performance this season," CNATRA’s public affairs office wrote in a statement Friday.

Fox News Digital reached out for further information Sunday morning and has not yet heard back.

Laux previously defended the team’s low-flying displays after the July flyover over Pensacola Beach sent tents, beach chairs and umbrellas flying as sand swept across the shoreline.

"We appreciate the trust in support and it’s our privilege to be able to perform in that way," Laux told Rolling with Madrina after the incident. "We’re gonna keep bringing the heat and continue doing it safely."

VIRAL VIDEO OF JETS BUZZING DHL STADIUM IN CAPE TOWN PROMPTS AVIATION SAFETY INVESTIGATION

Navy and War Department leaders had previously defended the low flyovers.

"Flight debrief complete. No reprimands. No firings. No problem," Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao wrote on X in July. "That’s the sound of Freedom! Semper fi and Hooyah."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth had vowed more support.

"The flyovers will continue until morale improves," Hegseth wrote on X.

The White House posted a photo meme of the controversial flyover from its official X account.

"It's okay to love America," the post read.

HEGSETH STEPS IN TO ‘FIX’ SITUATION AFTER APACHE PILOTS SUSPENDED FOR ‘SALUTE FROM THE SHORES’ FLYOVER

The Navy has not said when Laux was dismissed or what conduct prompted the decision. His photo and biography are no longer featured on the Blue Angels’ website's team page

Laux was absent from the squadron’s NAS Pensacola Homecoming Air Show on Friday and Saturday, where the team performed with five jets instead of its usual six. Laux's role was the opposing solo, which flies with lead solo #5 in the head-on crossing passes and mirror-image maneuvers that fill the gaps between the four-jet Diamond’s routines.

The routines were adjusted to account for the missing jet, according to reports.

The 2026 narrator, Lt. Commander Ronny Hafeza, might replace Laux on the 2027 team. The Blue Angels officers serve three-year terms, one as a narrator as Laux did.

Laux, a native of Chantilly, Va., graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 2012 with a degree in Chinese and earned his wings in 2015, according to his bio, which as of Sunday morning could still be accessed on the site despite no longer being listed with the rest of the team. He flew F/A-18 Hornets with Marine Corps squadrons, deployed to Japan and aboard the USS Nimitz and supported three operations during the 2020 carrier deployment: Resolute Support, Inherent Resolve and Octave Quartz.

World.title: UFC’s Dana White says he will meet Trump on Monday to discuss press secretary offer
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Saturday said on Truth Social that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship.

“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” the president wrote.

Trump suggested in his post that White should bring several UFC fighters, including Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje and Amanda Nunes, as assistants to defend against the “Lunatic Left.”

“Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” he added.

White said at a boxing event in London Saturday evening that he was heading to Washington, D.C., that night and had a meeting scheduled with the president Monday.

Asked whether he could speak about conversations he has had with Trump so far, White declined.

“We have a meeting on Monday, so sure, I’ll have more to talk about after that,” White said.

When Trump posted on Truth Social earlier Saturday, it was unclear whether his offer to White was a serious one.

Shortly after Trump posted, White posted on Instagram what appears to be an AI-generated image of himself behind the podium in the White House briefing room, captioned, “On to the next chapter.”

White also added a screenshot of Trump’s post to his Instagram story.

Trump and White have long been friends and the president has attended many UFC fights while serving in the White House.

Earlier this year, White also organized a UFC fight on the South Lawn of the White House, an event that was part of a slate commemorating the United States’ 250th birthday.

Many Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers attended the fight in July.

A spokesperson for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The position has been vacant since Katie Zacharia departed the role after just five days in October.

Zacharia had replaced Karoline Leavitt, who served as White House press secretary since Trump returned to office in January of last year. Leavitt announced in August that she would leave her post to spend more time with her family.

The White House had another staff shake-up on Friday, when Chief of Staff Susie Wiles said she would be stepping down from her post. Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as her replacement.

Wiles’ departure made her the seventh woman to leave the Trump administration this year. So far, all of the women who have left have been replaced by men, with the exception of Zacharia and Leavitt, as a press secretary has not yet been named.

World.title: James Talarico kicks off ‘SNL’ days after historic Texas Senate win
World.content:
James Talarico, a Democrat whose U.S. Senate victory Tuesday was once thought improbable in the Republican stronghold of Texas, made a surprise appearance to help kick off the latest episode of “Saturday Night Live.”

The state lawmaker and seminarian’s defeat of Attorney General Ken Paxton was one of a slew of victories for Texas Democrats, who claimed every statewide office up for grabs, including state Rep. Gina Hinojosa’s gubernatorial win, after a decades-long drought.

“SNL’s” cold open featured New York’s Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (played by Kenan Thompson) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (Sarah Sherman) celebrating Tuesday’s wins, which helped to set up Jeffries as the likely House speaker in January.

Sherman’s Schumer introduced the pair as “establishment Democrats” and asked, “Do we even know how to lose?”

Thompson’s Jeffries answered: “Yes.” Still, he suggested a toast to victory.

“We flipped the House, we flipped the Senate, and how did we do it?” he said.

“Me!” said a party crasher, President Donald Trump, played by James Austin Johnson.

He called the Democrats’ victory wave a “blue Toonami,” referring to Cartoon Network’s late-night block of anime shows, and he indicated he wouldn’t challenge the midterm election’s results.

“I accepted the results, which is almost scarier in a way,” he said. “It’s like, ‘What the hell is he planning?’ I’ll tell you what I’m planning: Ballroom.”

Trump said he hopes voters enjoy the results of the election, including the victory in Texas by the man he calls “Talafreako.”

The real Talarico then moved into the spotlight in front of Trump to loud applause from the show’s New York City studio audience.

“Hi, America,” he said. “I’m James Talarico, the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for $5.”

Trump responded, “In this economy, who can blame you?”

Talarico, who campaigned on battling wealth disparity and political corruption, suggested working with the Republican president to “make life better for everyday Americans.”

“It’s clear people want something new,” the senator-elect said. “They want something different. I’m talking, of course, about ‘SNL’s’ cold opens.”

He suggested voters were tired of the comedy show’s political cold-open sketches, asking, “How many of these Trump freezers are they going to do?”

“Infinity,” Trump responded.

Both then joined voices in uttering the show’s trademark introduction, “Live from New York ... ”

“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

World.title: We want to hear your experience with changes to student loan repayment plans
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” has transformed the sprawling federal student loan system — and student borrowers are feeling the effects of the most consequential changes.

This year, the approximately 7.5 million student borrowers under the Biden-era Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE, plan had to select a new one. So far, about 2 million borrowers have done so, after the Education Department warned that the SAVE plan was “illegal” and would be discontinued. The remaining borrowers who did not select a new plan were set to start receiving notices this month informing them that they missed a final deadline and were automatically moved to a new plan.

The Trump administration has said ending the SAVE plan would help streamline repayment programs while ensuring borrowers are paying off what they owe to the federal government. But student advocacy groups fear lower-income borrowers who had benefited from smaller monthly payments — or even qualified to make no payments at all based on their income — will end up with significantly higher bills under the other available plans.

We want to hear from you, whether you’re in this situation or are facing another challenge related to the recent student loan changes. Please share your experience by filling out the form below.

World.title: The human touch: Luxury brands embrace craftsmanship as ‘AI slop’ floods the internet
World.content:
The sound of pencil putting lines to paper. The geometric shapes of a cartoon animal before it comes to life on the page.

Those were the opening shots of a teaser for Prada’s 2026 holiday campaign, which introduced a series of films made “using the anachronistic craft of hand-drawn animation,” working with longtime Disney animator John Pomeroy.

“I learned my craft with pencil and paper, old-school analog drawing with pencil and paper,” Pomeroy, who left Disney in 2003, says in the teaser video.

It’s that kind of skill that some artists say has become a greater asset than ever. In the age of widespread and accessible AI, artists say they’ve noticed more brands leaning into handcrafted art as a selling point.

In recent weeks, the luxury fashion houses Prada and Hermès touted their human-made art projects in social media campaigns — even tagging the artists behind the work to showcase their authenticity.

A still from the Prada Holiday 2026 campaign. Glen Luchford for PRADA

Alina Golovlova, a stop-motion artist in Prague, said that recently, she has felt that her work is actually “appreciated more than in previous years” as brands try to separate themselves from the AI content flooding the internet.

“In previous years, I felt like I was just some hired content creator. No one really cared to tag me or make a [collaborative post],” Golovlova said. “And I think now for brands, it becomes valuable to bring the artists together with the brand to show that they are working with real people.”

Golovlova directed a short film for Anthropologie last month, featuring a needle-felted bunny, embroidered stars and stop-motion movements — all designed and put together entirely by hand by a team of artists.

And the choice proved to be an effective marketing strategy, as support rolled in from commenters online.

“Beautiful! Love the creativity and seeing something human made and NOT AI 👏❤️,” a user wrote on Anthropologie’s post, accruing thousands of likes.

“AI = Broke, cheap, lazy,” another user posted in response to Prada’s campaign. “Art from human hands = High-end, luxurious, high quality.”

Animator Jon Densk, who worked on the hand-drawn Prada campaign under Pomeroy, said that while he suspects AI still has a way to go before it can be used successfully in animation, he has seen signs of it in commercials. Coca-Cola, he said, comes to mind as a major company that has leaned into AI for its s.

“After the first one I saw two years ago, I was like, I’m not buying Coke until they stop it. I still haven’t bought a Coke in two years,” Densk said. “So having a stance against [AI], I think, is a smart move for brands.”

Coca-Cola’s use of AI stirred some controversy, as attitudes about the technology remain divided over labor and environmental concerns, as well as fatigue over the swath of mass-produced content commonly described as “AI slop.”

Still, Densk said he wasn’t expecting the explosion of support that Prada’s hand-drawn campaign would attract online.

“I think people that see people like us who are still drawing things, and even people working in CG animation, as true craftsmen, because that stuff really does take hours and hours and hours of practicing to get to a proficient level,” Densk said.

World.title: Gov. Josh Shapiro urges Democrats to prioritize healthcare, food assistance
World.content:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January, though he urged them not to forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I hope one of the first things that the Congress does is to stop these Medicaid cuts, stop the SNAP cuts, roll back the cuts, the effective cuts in the Affordable Care Act,” Shapiro said in an interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that aired Sunday.

Shapiro noted that in Pennsylvania alone, 510,000 people are losing healthcare and 143,000 more are losing SNAP or food assistance due to cuts approved during President Donald Trump’s second term.

“In general, though, I think Democrats need to have an aggressive agenda that cuts costs, that ends the war, that gets put on the president’s desk,” he said. “Hopefully, he will sign it because it’ll be common-sense stuff that makes people’s lives better.”

Trump has said that he intends to work with Democrats when Congress begins its new term, though he has also touted a new “VETO”-branded hat since Republicans lost the majority in the midterm elections.

Shapiro said that if Trump chooses to veto Democrats’ legislation, “it’s yet another signal to the American people the president actually doesn’t care about their well-being.”

While the governor stressed the importance of revitalizing Medicare and SNAP programs, he also said Democrats shouldn’t forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I think the Congress needs to be responsive to where voters are on corruption, and there has to be real accountability for this administration,” Shapiro said, adding that Democrats need to “walk and chew gum at the same time” to pass effective legislation and also “have real accountability for the corruption that exists in Washington.”

“It can’t be either/or,” he said. “It has to be both/and.”

Shapiro added that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker of the House, “has made very clear that both are going to be on the agenda for the first 100 days and for these next two years.”

The governor said that he doesn’t think Democrats should be thinking about the 2028 elections yet. Instead, “we should be thinking about how to make people’s lives better in 2027,” he said.

“It’s incumbent upon the Congress to now do that, and it’s incumbent upon governors now to continue to lead the way in our states,” Shapiro said.

Shapiro, who has been floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, did not commit to running.

Asked whether he is more likely to run than not, Shapiro answered that his focus was on “figuring how we advance policies like raising the minimum wage and many other things that have been blocked by Republicans,” as Pennsylvania Democrats won a majority in the state legislature Tuesday.

He also did not directly answer whether he was committed to serving his full four-year term.

“Well, I committed to run for governor, and that’s the work I’m focused on doing,” Shapiro said. “And if I’ve got something to say about my future, I’d love to come back on your show and talk about it.”

World.title: The SS United States and her final destination
World.content:
Even with her paint peeling and rivers of rust, the queen of the North Atlantic – five city blocks long, 12 stories high – still strikes quite a pose in the setting sun. The SS United States quickly became the fastest ocean liner in history. On her maiden voyage back in 1952, she reached speeds topping more than 40 miles an hour – a record for a transatlantic crossing that's never been broken.

But she was elegant, too – stately and refined. During her nearly two decades in service, she carried four U.S. presidents, countless celebrities, and tens of thousands of happy voyagers.

But what was once glamorous and spacious, the jet age did away with. Speed won out over starry nights at sea. By 1969, the SS United States was withdrawn from service, and that's what gets us back to her currently forlorn state. She wound up in Philadelphia, where for almost 30 years she sat with only spiders and sunbeams booking passage.

The SS United States. CBS News

But she was still impossible to ignore.

"She still casts a spell; there's something about her," said Susan Gibbs, president of a non-profit called the SS United States Conservancy. "She has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together."

Gibbs knows every inch of this ship. Her grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the SS United States, with the U.S. military helping to foot the bill – a floating investment that could be converted in less than 24 hours into a troop ship to transport an entire division. "It may not seem that way now, but back then she was the space shuttle of her age," Gibbs said.

Only her bones are left, however – her once-grand staircase is bare; the indoor salt-water swimming pool is now just a ghostly abyss; the dance floor is still here, but nothing else.

Susan Gibbs, president of the SS United States Conservancy, and Lee Cowan tour what's left of the ship's bridge and indoor pool. CBS News

And yet, there was still enough that Gibbs was determined to save. There were all kinds of ideas – museums, restaurants, event spaces – but no takers.

Our one-time flagship seemed headed for the scrap heap. Until that is, one man had a wild idea: return the SS United States back to the Atlantic, not to sail, but to sink – sending her to the bottom of the sea where nature, instead of the wrecking ball, will take its course.

"This will be the largest purposely-sunk artificial reef in the world," said Alex Fogg.

As the natural resources chief for Okaloosa County, Florida, Fogg has sunk a lot of ships – in fact, dozens of them, smaller ones off the coast of Florida as part of the county's artificial reef program.

The vessels have created habitats that are a delight for fish, fisherman and frogmen alike. But sinking the SS United States is something entirely different. Just one look at her two massive engine rooms and you realize the enormity of the task ahead.

For Jennifer Adams, director of tourism for Okaloosa County, what better tourist attraction could she bring? When she was approached about buying the SS United States, she said her response was, "'How much?' And he told me and I said, 'Go get her.'"

That price tag? A mere $1 million for the legendary ship, plus another $13 million to ready her for sinking. But then, the idea of sinking her suddenly became a little too real.

"I cried this morning when I walked on board," Adams said. "I just, I got overwhelmed."

Her county now owned a historic ship, but one full of 1950s environmental contaminants; that's problem one. Problem two was the SS United States still had plenty of fans on land, people like Linda Sylva, who made her first voyage as a teenager. "She was made in America, made from American parts, all over America," Sylva said.

Joe Beaman was just an eight-year-old kid when he set sail. All these years later, he's never forgotten it. "Oh no, once that ship has your heart, you never lose it," he said. "I mean, it's a part of me."

Even those who never sailed on her, like Jeffrey Smith, felt some kind of pull: "I drove in from Detroit yesterday because I wanted to say goodbye."

He and the others were on a farewell cruise of sorts, organized by the Conservancy, to give fans one last look before her last port of call.

Fans of the SS United States cruise around the fabled cruise liner. CBS News

In 2025, crews cast off her lines and began towing the SS United States south, her funnels barely clearing Philadelphia's Walt Whitman bridge.

The ship leaving Philadelphia. Okaloosa County

Once at sea, she had all the majesty she always did, cutting the waves like a scalpel. She arrived almost two days ahead of schedule. "She's still breaking records, even today," Fogg laughed.

At a shipyard in Mobile, Alabama, she's undergone extensive remediation, from stem to stern, getting rid of those environmental contaminants. Holes were cut throughout to allow air and water to flow quickly and evenly during her sinking.

Removing the ship's funnels. Okaloosa County

If all goes well, she'll be scuttled this week about 20 nautical miles off the coast between Pensacola and Destin/Ft. Walton Beach, Florida.

CBS News

Her two funnels – some of the largest ever built – will become the bookends of a museum planned by the SS United States Conservancy that will eventually house one-of-a-kind artifacts, including the bar from the tourist class smoking lounge.

There will be plenty of salty tears when she's gone. Sinking seems contrary to everything she was designed to do. That said, the SS United States will remain a part of maritime lore forever.

After so many years alone, soon she'll become a place of life once again.

"She stood there year after year after year," said Linda Sylva, "waiting for somebody to say, 'Come here, you're welcome here.' And who is that welcome for? It's the ocean. What a perfect place for her to rest."
