World.title: As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The last time any British government launched a national public preparedness campaign was at the peak of the Cold War in 1980.

The “Protect and Survive” message was delivered in short, eerie-looking public information broadcasts and booklets, meant to advise people on how to prepare for a nuclear attack. The campaign — whose guidance included hiding under a heavy table or tips about how to store a dead body in the house for five days — backfired and was ridiculed. Brits realized little would protect them from a thermonuclear strike, leaving them feeling that preparation was pointless as survival would be futile.

Nearly 50 years on, the head of the British Army, Gen. Sir Roland Walker, addressed some 700 soldiers last month at Britain's biggest garrison in northern England. The "business of soldiering" had returned to the national psyche, he told members of the light, high-readiness global response force, adding that anyone following world affairs will realize there is “extreme jeopardy."

“The political leaders of this country,” he said, “will start to have a frank conversation with the citizens of this country about just what is going on, and where the risk lies, and what the nation ... must need to be prepared to do.”

Exactly one week later, Britain’s “Be Ready” campaign was unveiled, a guide on preparing for 72 hours of self-sufficiency in the event of an emergency, be it a climate crisis, cyber disruptions or threats by hostile states.

WATCH | A look at Protect and Survive from the 1980s:

“It’s something that emergency planners have been wanting for a very long time,” said Lucy Easthope, a global disaster recovery specialist. Easthope has advised in emergencies from the Novichok poisonings in Salisbury, England, to the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami and 9/11.

Easthope says what the public wants is reassurance — not negative and depressing messaging.

“Ancient DNA, by that I mean 30 years ago, is being reawoken,” she told CBC News. “This is reawakening the idea that it's perfectly survivable.

“I’m really pleased in the U.K. we haven’t resorted to fear messaging.”

Other European nations have also recently introduced or updated their emergency guidance, including France, Ireland, Sweden, Norway, Germany and Poland.

Ottawa, too, has reiterated its longstanding advice . But unlike Canada with its emergency preparedness week — an annual event since 1996 — Britain faces a cultural hurdle, with the word "preparedness" not even being in most Brits' vocabulary. The U.K. has largely relied on community resilience to short-term disruptions, rather than self sufficiency. Now, it faces the challenge of convincing people that they must be prepared for the worst — without sending them into a panic.

Widespread warnings

In Hertfordshire, north of London, family physician Nyari Matebwe says her first reaction was to roll her eyes and ignore it.

“I feel like it’s scaremonger-y, or the skeptic in me thinks maybe they’re hiding something from us … another distraction from the real issues,” she said.

The recent suspected hacking attacks on supermarket freezers in multiple European countries and attempts to raise temperatures in French medical fridges containing critical blood donation stocks have made her question her own skepticism.

“After the recent airplane bomb hoaxes, I did start to think about it a bit more,” said Matebwe, whose teenage daughter is pushing her to take the prepping message seriously.

Sweden is advising seven days , Germany up to 10 , but the U.K., like Canada, has settled on three days' survival off-grid.

WATCH | Recent bomb threats in Europe: Europe's wave of bomb threats spreads from airports to newsrooms | Duration closed caption 2:12 The wave of bomb threats targeting European airports has now spread to newsrooms, including broadcasters in Ireland and Bulgaria. It's unclear who's behind these threats or the cyberattacks on grocery store freezers earlier this week.

School parents’ WhatsApp groups are lighting up with conversations

“I want to stockpile but I’m in a state of inertia,” one parent wrote. “My husband is totally unbothered.”

Another asked, “How will we cook if there’s no gas or electricity?” while one raised concern about rising crime rates and the risk of keeping cash at home.

Warnings have been widespread recently.

Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which is part of the government’s signals agency GCHQ and the Five Eyes intelligence sharing group that includes Canada, told CBC News: “This is a moment of urgency.”

The NCSC says AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the power stations, airports and hospitals in the U.K. within two years.

In Horne’s annual state of the cyber nation address, he said “military networks are subjected to sustained and persistent, widespread attempts to penetrate our systems."

That included Russian hybrid warfare campaigns, he said.

“All countries need to be taking this moment seriously," he told CBC News. “There are loads of vulnerabilities that do not need to be there,” which he said the country's adversaries are exploiting.

'Hard times have been forgotten'

Outside the need for companies to keep their technology safe, Horne said at home it is a case of keeping devices up to date and using passkeys.

“You do need to be thinking about, 'do I need to be having the levels of connectivity of devices across my house, apartment' … not unnecessarily introducing potential vulnerabilities.”

There are some who see the “Be Ready” messaging as another example of the "nanny state," or the government telling them how to live.

Others think cultural attitudes play a part.

WATCH | How to prepare for an emergency: Getting prepped to deal with emergencies | Duration closed caption 4:11 Emergency Preparedness Week aims to educate people about how to ready themselves for the unexpected, whether it’s a house fire, severe weather or a power outage. Thunder Bay Fire Rescue encourages residents to take a few simple steps now that could make all the difference later.

Luis Martinez Arnal, an IT professional from Spain now based in London, says his Mexican wife automatically prepares for emergencies, having grown up in a country prone to earthquakes.

“But in the U.K.,” Arnal said, “hard times have been forgotten.”

The accessibility of everything, he added, “psychologically is making us feel more comfortable.”

The recent cyberattacks have created a heightened sense of anxiety across Europe, and as people grow more reliant on the internet, questions are being asked how anyone can prepare to stay connected if it went down. Those haven't been easily answered — especially as Britain has long planned to switch all copper-wire landline phones to internet use-only from the end of January 2027.

“Call me crazy, but following the new guidelines, I do feel a bit nervous,” said one London mother, Amee Doshi, pointing to talk about the potential for a world war.

A Tesco grocery delivery vehicle is seen stopped at a police roadblock on Sept. 27, in Fairford, U.K. Police declared a major incident after evacuating residents from their homes in Whelford, a village about 1.6 kilometres from RAF Fairford, a military base that hosts U.S. Air Force bombers involved in the Iran conflict. (David Bown/Getty Images)

Others appear to be taking to it like true preppers.

“We bulk-buy,” said Preyal Shah, a working mother from Harrow in northwest London.

“I even now have 10 kilograms of rice, five kilograms of pasta … multiple cases of tinned food, each type being 12 tins.”

Preyal said she is also stockpiling newspapers to light a coal-burning stove: “Back to basics.”

Competing crises

In October, British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned that the country needs to be “ready for war in 1,000 days," flagging the potential of Russian aggression.

“To prevent the worst, we have to prepare for it,” he said.

“We’ve just got so many competing crises at the moment … and war in Europe,” said Reena Patel, a lawyer from north London, referring to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“It’s not necessarily that I’m thinking war is coming but…” she said, listing off all she wants to buy, from a wind-up radio to water purification filters.

“The only thing I have in my control is to try to be a little bit prepared.”

World.title: What needs to happen for Canada to join Europe's flagship student exchange program?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada is negotiating to be a part of a major European exchange program that could give Canadians more opportunities to study, work and live in Europe.

At last month's Canada-EU summit and in his 2026 budget, Prime Minister Mark Carney reaffirmed the government's interest in expanding Canada's participation in Erasmus+, Europe's internationally recognized student and skills exchange.

"Through this program, a Canadian student can pursue their studies in Barcelona just as easily as they could at McGill," Carney said at the summit in Montreal.

An expert in European integration says the prospect is complex and likely to be expensive — but that it would come with major benefits for Canada's youth and deepening ties with the EU.

Through Erasmus+, students in the EU and select other countries have direct access to funding, institutions and grants that help cover travel and living costs when participating in exchange programs between institutions.

Students are also exempted from the fees for tuition, registration and exams that a Canadian exchange student might typically pay to study in Europe.

But Erasmus+ isn't just an opportunity for students. Its benefits extend to people starting their careers across a wide range of fields, including trainees, apprentices, youth workers and academic staff.

"An apprentice welder in Manitoba could bring or complete their placement with an employer in Italy, bringing new skills home," Carney said.

Many Canadian universities are already partnered with Erasmus+ through independent agreements, but they're limited mostly to exchange opportunities for master's students and faculty members.

Further participation in Erasmus+ could expand funding opportunities for undergraduates as well as youth, training and sport exchanges — all of which are available to EU members and the program's current six associate countries.

How would this work?

Oliver Schmidtke, a University of Victoria professor specializing in European integration, called Canada's proposed involvement in Erasmus+ "a lot of ambition."

"Education is largely a provincial thing in Canada, so how this would land and how the federal government would interact with provincial governments in trying to regulate this … that's a whole range of questions that are open," Schmidtke said.

WATCH | More about Canada's closer ties with EU: What could EU associate membership look like for Canada? | Duration closed caption 17:00 CBC's David Common speaks with International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu about Canada’s trading relationship with the EU and beyond. Then we hear from Joost Korte, special envoy for the EU-Canada partnership, from the Canada-EU summit where Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is seeking to become the European Union's first associate member.

And buying into an international exchange program isn't exactly cheap. The United Kingdom is rejoining in January and will pay over $1 billion for its first year.

Canadian universities would have to "pay substantial amounts to be eligible for the full array of services" and provide housing supports and staff to accommodate the Erasmus+ students coming to Canada, Schmidtke said.

The provinces and European Union would also have to iron out credit transfers for participating students — no simple feat.

All current Erasmus+ members and associated third countries follow the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS), simplifying the academic credit transfer process.

When the United Kingdom rejoins, it will be using its own system, but has set up a national framework for how credits will be transferred.

In Canada, even credit transfers between institutions within the same province aren't consistent.

This work would come at time of "a lot of financial stress at Canadian universities," Schmidtke said.

He said some of that comes from a reduced number of international students in Canada in recent years — who generally pay higher tuition rates directly to the institutions.

Carney has indicated that the expected costs of joining Erasmus+ won't stop Canada from pursuing that goal. Joining was one of the most concrete examples Carney gave when he announced in September that Canada was pursuing an "alliance for the future" with the EU.

"We don't view this as paying for something," Carney said in Montreal about the overall costs of closer EU integration. "We view this as coming together."

Despite these potential complications, Schmidtke believes integration with Erasmus+ will be an "invaluable opportunity" for Canadian students.

"Canada is a bit behind the curve when it comes to internationalizing student experiences, mobility and so forth," Schmidtke said. "So the Erasmus+ program could be a great incentive to expand the international experience of many Canadian students."

Some Canadian universities already involved

The University of Victoria, University of Waterloo, McMaster University, Simon Fraser University, University of Toronto, University of British Columbia and the University of Calgary told CBC News they would be open to exploring participation — or further participation, as some already partner with Erasmus+ — as more details become available.

Western University president Alan Shepard said international engagement is a key part of the student experience at Western, and the university was excited about the opportunities Erasmus+ could create.

"We encourage our students to see themselves as global citizens through opportunities to study, conduct research and gain hands-on experience around the world," Shepard said.

WATCH | More about Erasmus+: How Canadian students could benefit from EU 'associate member' status | Duration 2:00 In his speech to the European Parliament, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canadian membership in the EU's student exchange program, Erasmus+, would give students an opportunity to 'broaden their horizons' and build lasting ties to sustain the alliance between Canada and Europe.

In late October, Université Laval rector Sophie D'Amours and Sorbonne University president Nathalie Drach-Temam penned an open letter in La Presse encouraging the government to integrate Canadian universities into the program.

"The Sorbonne is the oldest French-language university in Europe. Université Laval is the oldest French-language university in the Americas. Our traditions are strong, as is our capacity to help address the challenges of tomorrow," the letter said.

By joining forces, we will be even better placed to promote the common good that universities represent for society."

World.title: Injured Wainwright soldiers benefit from cutting-edge Canadian burn research
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Cutting-edge Canadian burn research is being used to help victims of the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright. Scientists are using soldiers' own skin cells to grow permanent, human-like skin substitutes that their bodies won't reject.

When news broke about the deadly training exercise at CFB Wainwright that killed four soldiers and sent dozens more to hospital with severe burns, Véronique Moulin knew she had to help.

Her research group is nearing the end of clinical trials on a ground-breaking process to reconstruct and manufacture a permanent, human-like skin substitute by taking a toonie-sized biopsy of the patient's healthy skin and extracting the cells.

"If everybody can survive and [I] can help to treat some, I will be happy," said Moulin, head of the regenerative medicine division at the CHU de Québec-Université Laval research centre.

Unlike other lab-grown skin technologies, Moulin's method coaxes the patient's own cells to create a completely natural skin tissue containing both the dermis and epidermis layers.

Véronique Moulin, head of the regenerative medicine division at the CHU de Québec-Université Laval research centre, is seen placing cells into liquid nitrogen for long-term preservation. (CBC)

While it's not completely identical to the patient's skin because it doesn't have pigment and sweat glands, Moulin said it's useful in cases where the burns cover too much of the body to harvest skin for grafts.

Clinical data on 50 Canadian burn patients treated since 2005 shows that, unlike grafts from cadavers, their body doesn't reject the skin substitutes. The tissue grows, fuses and stays flexible, which means less scarring and reduces the need for repetitive surgeries as the patient heals, she said.

Lab now growing skin from wounded soldiers

As of Nov. 4, the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) said 25 soldiers remain in hospital. Four have been moved to health-care facilities in British Columbia and Ontario to continue treatment closer to their home communities and families.

Skin biopsies from several of the hospitalized soldiers have been taken, and cells are now growing in Moulin's lab.

But it takes up to eight weeks to grow the first batch of skin substitute grafts from the initial biopsy — which is only enough to cover part of a torso — and her lab is already running at capacity.

"Usually we have three, sometimes four, but it's very rare that we have so many patients at the same time," Moulin said.

"But at least we can start, and after the first one, we can continue and send them every two weeks, we can send the same surface area."

WATCH | Family details soldier's ordeal: Family of soldier severely burned at CFB Wainwright describes his ordeal | Duration closed caption 2:22 The family of a Canadian soldier severely burned during the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta tells CBC News they're just as worried about his mental health as they are about his physical trauma. With catastrophic burns over much of his body, Pte. Liam Ramage can barely move or speak.

Burn research advancing across the country

Moulin is just one of the Canadians on the front lines of research meant to help burn patients heal faster, with less pain and fewer scars.

Halfway across the country, in a University of Manitoba lab, an interdisciplinary team of researchers is also developing skin substitutes that mimic the features of human skin, including its layers, blood vessels, nerves and different skin colors.

A close-up of the skin substitute that an interdisciplinary team of researchers is developing in a University of Manitoba lab. It mimics the features of human skin, including its layers, blood vessels, nerves and different skin colors. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)

"Currently, we are working on one type of skin substitute that we are planning to test on animals. So that is the first step. You test on animals, then if it works, we will go to clinical trials," said Hamed Alizadeh Sardroud, a postdoctoral fellow and researcher in biomedical engineering and tissue engineering.

The lab is also exploring ways to engineer donor cells to be compatible with the recipient’s immune system and avoid rejection. They're using a 3D printer to create patches that would be used for burn wounds.

"Those cells are live and they can grow. And when you implant it, transplant [it] on the skin, they will just regenerate," Alizadeh Sardroud said.

WATCH | How the researchers are using 3D printing: 3D printing skin substitutes for grafts | Duration closed caption 1:25 Researchers at the University of Manitoba are fabricating skin substitutes that mimic human skin, including its different layers, blood vessels, nerves, and different skin colors. They are also exploring ways to engineer the substitutes using donor cells in a way to be compatible with the recipient’s immune system and avoid rejection.

Just a few doors down, one of his colleagues is testing a biosensor that can detect bacteria causing infection in a wound.

"You can see it's yellow and then as soon as it's in contact with bacteria and their enzymes, it becomes green," said Farinaz Jonidi Shariatzadeh, a post-doctoral researcher, as she did a demonstration.

"It's like an early warning system that shows you that the bacteria are present in the wound and … infection is going to start soon."

WATCH | Inside Farinaz Jonidi Shariatzadeh's lab: Infection detection and management | Duration closed caption 1:24 Researchers at the University of Manitoba are creating biosensors that can detect bacteria and the start of infections in wounds, and smart dressings that will release antibiotics to start treating the infection.

The postage stamp-sized nanofibre membrane can be placed in the top layer of a dressing so it doesn't have to be removed to keep an eye on the wound. A patient can monitor it at home, and contact their doctor when they see the colour change.

It has already been licensed by an American medical technology company that has begun clinical trials, Jonidi Shariatzadeh said.

"Compared to what's commercially available, it is groundbreaking because none of the available biosensors can actually show the colour change in real time that can be observed with the naked eye."

The University of Manitoba team is also developing a smart dressing that will release an antibiotic as soon as an infection is detected, said Dr. Sarvesh Logsetty, a burn surgeon and director of the Manitoba Firefighters Burn Unit at Winnipeg's Health Sciences Centre.

"The science fiction of yesterday is the treatment of today," he said.

"The goal is to decrease the pain and suffering and improve the quality of life and the quantity of life of individuals that have burns and also injuries of any kind."

Dr. Sarvesh Logsetty, a burn surgeon and director of the Manitoba Firefighters Burn Unit at Winnipeg's Health Sciences Centre, leads a multi-disciplinary team of researchers that's become a hub for clinical innovation. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)

'The journey is a long and painful one'

It's welcome news for Tyler Pelke, who survived third-degree burns over 25 per cent of his body more than 35 years ago.

"The journey is a long and painful one," said Pelke, a former firefighter who is now a CAF reservist and head of Alberta's Emergency Health Services. He spoke as a burn survivor, not on behalf of those organizations.

"So yeah, some pretty amazing advancements, but it's a pretty impactful and horrific injury, especially when a large burn."

Pelke said he was lucky because doctors were able to take skin grafts from his own legs, but he dreaded the bandage removals and dressing changes.

Anything that can help ease the physical and mental suffering for burn patients is welcome, he said.

World.title: Ramayana: Part 1 has the muscle, but lacks a certain epic soul
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Growing up in Toronto, my family got our Indian cinema fix in the late ‘90s by renting bootleg VHS tapes from the basement of a shop on Lawrence Avenue. Usually, that meant fanciful Bollywood romances, but occasionally we'd pick up an episode of an 1987 TV series depicting the ancient Hindu epic poem, the Ramayana.

It was full of telenovela-esque facial reactions, tinfoil jewelry and my favourite: arrows that transformed into other things through the awesome magic of jump cuts. It was appointment viewing for millions of people in India, where it originally aired, and for the diaspora for years to come.

Now, nearly 40 years later, there's the first of two mega-budget adaptations in theatres, Ramayana: Part 1. And despite how visually impressive and modern it is, it's missing the soul found in that melodramatic low-budget TV series.

Believed to have been written several thousand years ago, the Ramayana is a story rooted in Hinduism. But it extends beyond one religion, culture or country. Generally, it's the journey of Prince Rama, a god in human form, as he is drawn into a war with the villainous King Ravana, who abducts the noble princess Sita. The film was directed by Nitesh Tiwari with actors from across Indian cinema — the Hindi-language A-lister Ranbir Kapoor, the Kannada-language star Yash and the Tamil- and Telugu-language actor Sai Pallavi, respectively.

The story's details change across South and Southeast Asia so much that, to quote the scholar A.K. Ramanujan , "one conception [of the story] is quite abhorrent to those who hold another."

And yet the characters are part of everyday life for millions of people, says Aparita Bhandari, an arts and culture reporter in Toronto who grew up in New Delhi.

"You go to the temple, the idea of Ram/Sita, this whole thing is just there in your kind of collective consciousness," she said.

Ranbir Kapoor stars as Prince Rama, a god in human form who is drawn into a war with the villainous Ravana. (Sony Pictures)

Beyond entertainment, the story is full of parables, dealing with struggles and ethics. For example, Prince Rama sacrifices his birthright to be king to his brother, Bharat, and accepts an unfair exile to satisfy his stepmother.

But even with a runtime of over three hours for the Hindi version — and much less for the English dub — some major characters had to be erased or sidelined.

"They had to really cut a whole bunch out of it. You know, like Kaushalya and Sumitra just never spoke," Bhandari said, referring to Rama's birth mother and another stepmother.

Shiv Reddy, a film reviewer who watched both the Hindi and English versions, says the latter even removes a scene with Bharat begging his brother to come back.

A shadow puppet theatre group performs the Ramayana in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Feb. 9, 2025. Southeast Asian cultures have many versions of the myth, which are told in various ways. (Yayuyoshi Chiba/Getty Images/AFP)

"It immensely changed my perception of Ranbir Kapoor's performance as Rama, and also his duty as a king," Reddy told CBC News from Orange, Calif. "And to remove it entirely feels like that conflict that [Rama] faces is removed also."

The end result feels like it's hurrying audiences along, with characters rarely dissecting their motivations, instead telling you something to get you to the next part.

Some glory

And in between that stiff dialogue were often-bombastic action sequences.

From the opening moments, we're greeted with a fantastical battle of angels and demons on an icy battlefield, with war rhinos and a flying elephant battling like Lord of the Rings met God of War and 300.

A flying war elephant arrives on a frigid battlefield in a scene from Ramayana: Part 1. (Sony Pictures)

Loud and crunchy sound design, punctuated by a score from Hans Zimmer, who co-composed it with the equally legendary A.R. Rahman, helped drive these scenes.

For a kid who grew up on that ‘80s series and comic book adaptations, the graphics were impressive (save for a few facial expressions of some demons).

Meeting the moment

The film is timely not just because it's out in theatres for the Diwali weekend — a holiday that celebrates Rama's victory.

It also meets a need for international audiences expecting grand action from the Indian film industry ever since S.S. Rajamouli's RRR in 2022 — and in the process brought together talent from across India and the world to work on both films, which together reportedly cost $500 million US.

Part 1 is playing in more than 50 theatres across this country. Part 2, which has a lot more of the story to cover, has now been delayed to 2028.

"The ambition helped…to tell this grand story," Bhandari said, adding that the money went to a whole wall of artists featured in the end credits. "There's a lot of people that have put a lot of effort into making this work. And I guess to a certain extent, it shows."

WATCH | The English-language trailer for Ramayana:

But one aspect of the film that some critics feel missed the mark was the use of AI, in post-production, to try to give this story more universal appeal.

In the English dub, which used human voice actors, AI changed the mouths of the actors on-screen to appear as if they were speaking English.

Tiwari, the director, said during the L.A. premiere that this was to "present the film to the world in their language."

For Reddy, it didn't work.

"It's uncanny, for sure," Reddy said. "Because the face is also changing, it feels like it's just not their performance."

Ultimately, AI is an apt analog for this adaptation. Ramayana: Part 1 feels like an AI-generated summary of the ancient epic. You get the gist, you get the polish, but none of the depth until you choose to seek it.

World.title: Poilievre pans Liberal budget's $15M capital gains exemption, calls for 'simpler' plan
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is criticizing a key feature of the Carney government's latest budget, arguing the proposed $15-million capital gains exemption on the sale of qualifying shares from a Canadian company applies too narrowly, excluding key businesses.

"Basically, I can't figure out who actually qualifies," Poilievre said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live airing Sunday morning. "I suspect no one does, and you have to be able to stand on one foot and count backwards from a thousand with your finger on your nose before you could qualify for that break."

In the 2026 federal budget, tabled on Thursday , the Canada Growth Incentive excludes businesses operating in the agricultural, fishing, forestry, financial, insurance, utilities, real estate, food and accommodation, arts, recreation and entertainment sectors.

Because of that, Poilievre said he views it as "insignificant and irrelevant and adds more complexity to the system." The budget states that the measure is expected to bring $715 million in tax relief over the next four years, beginning next fiscal year.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's Liberal government is touting the incentive as a way to encourage Canadian founders to build a valuable company in Canada. Early-stage employees can receive more equity as part of their compensation, and investors get a better after-tax return for backing the business.

WATCH | Breaking down Budget 2026: Budget 2026: Carney makes 'big bet' for investment, opposition blasts affordability moves | Duration closed caption 6:43 The Carney government's second budget lays out over $150 billion in spending to attract investment, accelerate nation-building projects, boost housing and tackle the affordability crisis. The NDP says it favours the rich, while Conservatives call it a 'credit card budget Canadians can't afford.'

The budget calls the $15-million exemption "substantial" because founders would retain nearly 96 per cent of the company's value when they exit, compared with the current 71 per cent.

The move was met with praise by some business groups, including the Council of Canadian Innovators, which advocates on behalf of 175 high-growth companies in Canada. The group said the incentive would create the conditions companies need to attract talent and scale.

Poilievre did express support for Carney's productivity mega-deduction — expected to cost about $36 billion over five years — saying he believes anything that cuts taxes on investment is "positive."

But Poilievre's approach would allow businesses and individuals that reinvest their capital gains back in Canada to fully defer the tax.

"And that would bring back the hundreds of billions of dollars of investment that companies and individuals have parked abroad.... I think that that would be economic rocket fuel. It would be a lot simpler than what Mr. Carney and the Liberals are proposing," the Opposition leader said.

Poilievre said he personally proposed the idea to Carney and encourages the prime minister to "steal my idea because we desperately need job-creating investment in Canada."

NDP criticizes affordability measures

The New Democrats have seized on the budget's tax cuts for new business investment, arguing that the affordability measures for Canadians pale in comparison. In a video statement posted on Thursday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis said, "If you're a billionaire, this budget is Christmas come early."

After the budget was read in the House of Commons by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne , Lewis acknowledged it earmarks new funds to address homelessness but said it "doubles down on shovelling more money to the biggest CEOs and investors, with the promise that all of us will be better off for it. This has never worked."

Lewis also pointed out a chart in the budget that shows the spending composition of announced measures. In the chart, $98 billion is listed as "Growth and Investment," while $48 billion is listed as "People."

WATCH | Champagne, Lewis spar over government's second budget: Champagne walked into the NDP leader's interview — and Lewis had questions | Duration closed caption 1:56 In an unexpected encounter, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne joins NDP Leader Avi Lewis's interview on Power & Politics and the two argue about the federal budget.

In an interview, Champagne said affordability is "top of mind" and that the budget boosts Canada's grocery benefit, extends the suspension of the federal excise tax on fuel and includes other measures on dental care and pharmacare.

"So we say two-thirds of the additional revenue we're getting, we're going to put that into growth and investments so that our economy will grow," the finance minister said. "But at the same time, we took one-third and we say, 'This is where we need to support people.'"

Poilievre criticized the government's borrowing, saying "government debt does not bring investment. It brings inflation, it brings stagnation and it brings failure."

"We need to get the government out of the way and off the backs of Canadians so that we can have real free-enterprise growth that pays the bills and puts food on the table," the Conservative leader said.

Champagne told host Rosemary Barton that it will take time for the government's proposed tax cuts and productivity measures to translate into tangible benefits for everyday Canadians, but he was bullish on the impact the budget will have in due course.

"This is going to be making us stronger and more resilient," Champagne said.

World.title: How the Democrats' midterm wave shows a path back to the presidency
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Although thrilled by their sweeping defeat of U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the midterms, Democrats remain cautious about jumping to conclusions of what it could mean for the next presidential election campaign.

Still, the dramatic scale of the victory has some seeing a potential path back to the White House in 2028.

The Democrats won the popular vote for House districts by 13 percentage points, the biggest margin for either party in 50 years.

They ousted Republicans in Senate races in the red states of South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, which haven't sent a Democratic senator to Washington since 1998, 1988 and 1932, respectively.

Strategists are busy analyzing both what went so wrong for the Republicans and what went right for the Democrats. If there's one consistent thread in this midterm post-mortem, it's that cost of living concerns made all the difference.

That's why leading Democrats believe the pocketbook populism that worked at the midterms in both swing states and red states is a message that could work in the next presidential election.

WATCH | The Democrats' midterm wins go well beyond Congress: Democrats prepare to flex new power — not just in Washington | Duration closed caption 2:05 The Democrats' gains in Tuesday's midterms go beyond Washington, as three-quarters of Americans now have a Democratic governor and more than half live in a state where Democrats hold the governorship and both branches of the state legislature.

Mo Elleithee, former spokesperson for the Democratic National Committee (DNC), says his party "isn't always the best at message discipline," but its candidates stayed solidly on-message in the midterm campaign.

"Candidate after candidate, the most progressive to the most moderate, from Kansas and Texas to Maine and Michigan, every Democratic candidate was talking about cost of living and corruption, and, in many cases, tying those two things together," Elleithee told PBS News Hour.

'What the future looks like'

Democrats who want to run for president will need to show voters their vision for the post-Trump era, Elleithee said.

"For the past decade, what we have mainly been doing is playing opposition to Donald Trump," he said. "Now we can paint a picture of what the future looks like."

For a decade, Democrats have been searching for ways to win back the many working-class voters who had abandoned them in favour of Trump.

Their winning candidates in the midterms in red and swing states focused relentlessly on pocketbook issues in a way that could seize the terrain of economic populism back from the Trump GOP.

"The biggest divide in this country is not left versus right. It's top versus bottom," the Texas Democrat senator-elect James Talarico said frequently from the very launch of his campaign.

James Talarico, the Democratic senator-elect for Texas, thanked supporters in Austin after his win on Tuesday. (Eric Gay/The Associated Press)

DNC chairman Ken Martin says the midterm victories were in part a repudiation of Trump, but also a consequence of Democrats talking about affordability.

"Our candidates across the board ran for something, not against something," he told NPR. "They gave people a sense of a positive vision of what Democrats would do while we're in power."

The three priorities that Democrat leaders have said they intend to pursue immediately once the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3 are all aimed at bringing down costs for Americans: repealing Trump's tariffs, restoring health insurance subsidies cut by the Republicans and ending the war in Iran that triggered big jumps in fuel prices.

Midterm results shift electoral college map

Midterm wins at the state level mean next year will see Democrat governors in power in all seven swing states that Trump won in 2024: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.

Democrats also now envision Ohio, which has voted solidly for Trump in three straight elections, to be a potential target in 2028 after midterm wins for both governor and Senate.

WATCH | As Republicans point fingers, Trump defends his team: Trump defends Hegseth as Democrats prepare for political war | Duration closed caption 2:19 U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed calls for Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's resignation, despite more Republicans blaming the Iran war for their massive midterm losses. Meanwhile, Democrats are gearing up to flex their new power after taking both houses of Congress.

Some are even dreaming that Texas, with its shifting demographics and its 38 electoral college votes, may no be longer a lost cause, after a Democrat sweep of statewide races.

It remains to be seen how long the Democratic Party's midterm-fuelled unity will last once the fight for the 2028 nomination begins.

That could start as soon as next spring, given the track record of would-be presidential candidates announcing their intentions roughly a year and a half before election day.

The dominant theme in the nomination race could be the competing visions of centrist and progressive Democrats.

Progressive icon Bernie Sanders — the independent U.S. senator from Vermont who the Democratic Party spurned in 2016 as presidential nominee in favour of establishment candidate Hillary Clinton — argues the midterm results show there's only one route to victory.

"We can win over millions of Republicans and independents who are struggling economically if we focus on the issues that are important," Sanders told Politico Playbook this week.

Sen. Bernie Sanders campaigned for the Michigan Democrat Senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, at a rally in Grand Rapids on Oct. 25. (Kristen Norman/The Associated Press)

Sanders said Democrats need to have the courage to tell big-money donors, "Thank you very much for your help, but right now we are going to focus on the needs of the working families of this country, whether you like it or not."

Warnings abound for the Democrats abo ut what lessons they should and shouldn't draw from the midterm result and how it may apply to 2028.

David Plouffe, who served as Barack Obama's campaign manager in 2008 and advised Kamala Harris in 2024, says the Democrats can't count on voter sentiment in this year's midterms being the same in the next presidential election.

"I would say this was a vote against Trump more than a vote for the Democratic Party. Our brand is still quite weak," Plouffe told a post-midterm forum at Harvard University's Institute of Politics.

Mark Leibovich, a journalist who has extensively covered the party's Trump-era struggles, has a message similar to Plouffe's.

"Democrats should avoid the obvious trap of thinking that their victory means they've magically solved their 'brand problem,' 'trust problem,' or 'working-class-voter problem,' among various others," Leibovich wrote in the Atlantic this week.

World.title: Poland in mourning after shooter with 'ultranationalistic' views killed 6, wounded 15 in Krakow
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, after a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him.

The attack, which Poland’s defence minister described as an "act of terror," happened on Saturday in Main Square in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town. The area is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city.

By evening, mourners had left candles in memory of the victims. The square remained partially closed on Sunday morning as authorities continued their investigation.

WATCH | Shooting in Krakow leaves 6 dead, more than a dozen injured: Krakow shooting leaves 6 dead, more than a dozen injured | Duration 0:44 Six people were killed and more than a dozen wounded after a gunman opened fire Saturday afternoon in a busy market square in Krakow, Poland, authorities said. The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a gunfight with officers a short distance away from the initial violence, police said.

Marie-Ange Collaer wrote on Facebook that she and her family survived the shooting during a trip to Krakow from Brussels.

"We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around," she wrote. "Lying on the floor in a shop like in a bad police movie whilst you hear bullets everywhere."

Collaer said her family was "quite in shock" after returning to their hotel but everyone was grateful to be alive.

"We saw a few that did not make it, true horror," she wrote.

St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight in tribute to the victims. It is the first time the call has been missed since the Second World War.

Attacker’s sister and parents found dead

Four women and two men were killed in the Main Square shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from an unidentified foreign country were also among the dead.

The two police officers who stopped the attacker remain in hospital. One of them is still in a coma while the other woke up from a coma, Klęczar said. Officials launched an appeal for blood donations for the benefit of the most seriously wounded policeman.

Cordoned-off areas at Krakow's Main Market Square following Saturday's mass shooting. (Jakub Porzycki/Reuters)

"If it weren’t for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher," Klęczar said.

Five non-Poles are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

The attacker is also in a critical state, having been operated on multiple times.

There was confusion on Saturday about the shooter’s age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24.

The prosecutors said on Sunday they started an investigation for murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act "constituting a terrorist offense."

Authorities also found three dead bodies at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers northeast of Krakow. The police said on Sunday they were the bodies of the attacker’s sister, mother and father.

The family members likely died from gunshot wounds, the police said.

The mass killing marks a grim first for Poland

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the attacker holds "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Videos posted on social media by witnesses show people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims. In one video, a police officer is seen repeatedly shooting the attacker, who is lying on the street, only to later slowly collapse to the ground himself.

People stand near candles and flowers left near the Main Market Square in tribute for victims after Saturday's mass shooting. (Jakub Porzycki/Reuters)

Klęczar said the attacker’s father owned over 10 guns legally and that the attacker also owned guns. Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found in the possession of the attacker in Krakow or in his car.

Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising, particularly because of Russia's invasion of Ukraine and fear of instability in the region.

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The young attackers used knives or other sharp objects.

The Krakow attacker’s military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other "extreme-right lone actors" committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague.

" We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland."

World.title: Kite flying in Ukraine: One N.S. veteran's mission to help children in a war zone
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At a summer camp in western Ukraine, children run through a field, pulling kites behind them. Smiles light up their faces.

Their instructor, Seth Congdon, cheers them on. He might have the biggest smile of all.

The 49-year-old military veteran from Nova Scotia brought these kites to the kids. He wanted them to see the sky as a place of beauty and freedom, not just a potential source of danger filled with drones and missiles.

“Nothing should be above your head but clean air and shelter. And they’re literally being rained death from above," Congdon said.

"What better way to stand up, stick your chest out and say, ‘I’m here, and this is me, and I’m not going anywhere.’"

In July, Congdon travelled from his home near Lunenburg to Ukraine with fellow Canadian veteran Royce Roberts, bringing 130 handmade kite blanks to the summer camp for children living with the daily realities of war. For three weeks, the pair taught the children how to assemble, decorate and fly the kites in workshops Congdon called Reclaim Your Sky.

LISTEN | Seth Congdon's Ukraine mission: Atlantic Voice 26:10 The freedom of kite flying in Ukraine Ukraine's sky is a place of danger, drones, and missiles. Seth Congdon of Nova Scotia's south shore wants to change that, for a small group of children whose parents are on the frontlines. This is the story of a veteran's mission to share his love of kites with these children, and bring a bit more peace to his own struggles with PTSD. A documentary by Erin Moore.

“We call them camps, but they’re really trauma rehabilitation programs,” said camp director Oksana Hrycyna, a Ukrainian-Canadian teacher from Toronto.

Forty of the 120 children who attended camp this summer had a parent killed on the front lines, she said. Others had parents who were missing or being held as prisoners of war.

From Hirtles Beach to Bagram

For Congdon, kites go back much further than Ukraine. He grew up in Kingsburg, N.S., flying them at Hirtles Beach with his mother, Marilyn Congdon, a well-known kite maker who has taught the craft across the Maritimes.

Congdon shakes hands with the colonel-in-chief of the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry during a military tour in Bosnia in 2002. (Submitted by Seth Congdon)

When he grew up, kites took on another meaning. During his 15-year military career, Congdon served in Afghanistan in 2002 with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry. Returning from the Battle of Takur Ghar, he remembers seeing kites from the back of his helicopter.

“You could tell where the green zone was — the protected area around Bagram — because there were kites or people were wearing colour,” he said. “Colour was outlawed, and music was outlawed, and kites — absolutely outlawed.”

The kites stayed with him, along with everything else he saw in Afghanistan.

Weight of war

Months after he returned home, it all caught up with him while he was driving alone on a highway outside Winnipeg.

“I had to pull off on the side of the road, feeling every emotion at once — anger, fear, aggression— for about 10 seconds,” he said. “And then click, the switch went off, and I was like, ‘What was that?’”

He said he didn’t tell anyone, including therapists, for close to a decade.

Congdon was released from the military in 2014 and now works with veterans and first responders living with post-traumatic stress disorder. He uses creative work like painting, writing and building kites to help others process what they carry.

“We’re basically using art and creativity and positivity to heal trauma,” he said. It's that same idea that took him to Ukraine.

Royce Roberts, front left, and Seth Congdon, front right, pose with some of the Ukrainian campers and their decorated kites. (Submitted by Seth Congdon)

Despite a language barrier, Congdon said his own combat experience gives him an unusual connection with the children at the camp.

“We know what artillery sounds like. We know what bombs sound like,” he said. “That being a given, you can sit in that same place, and now, let’s talk about flying a kite.”

Most of the children had never flown a kite before, he said. In the workshops, they decorated theirs with flowers, butterflies, rainbows, hearts and, in some cases, warplanes.

Hrycyna said it was powerful to watch the campers fly their kites.

“They’re not cowering in fear, and they’re watching their kites playfully dart and dip and dive with the wind," she said.

"It really warms your heart to see kids being kids, and doing something so simple as flying a kite that they constructed themselves with their own two hands,” she said.

Congdon said that, despite growing up around kites, this trip to Ukraine helped him understand what they truly meant.

“Kites have been in my life my entire life, with mom and how she’s made them. But I never really truly got the significance. The gravity didn’t hit until, honestly, this trip,” he said.

Besides giving the kite workshops, Congdon raised $11,000 through local fundraisers for the camp.

Seth Congdon flies a kite at Hirtles Beach, N.S., after returning from leading kite workshops in Ukraine. (Erin Moore)

What came home

A week after returning to Nova Scotia, Congdon joined his wife, Janna, their two sons and Roberts’ family at Hirtles Beach to fly kites.

He said being able to go back into a war zone to help children has reshaped how he thinks about his military past.

“If a trauma or something really difficult, something that taxed your spirit to the point that you can’t function anymore, made it possible to do something like this, to throw yourself back into service for a positive return, then maybe it doesn’t make the trauma OK,” he said.

“But it makes the good thing possible.”

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: Why the Embargo Does Not Explain Repression in Cuba
World.content:
Berta Soler (left), photo: AP / Desmond Boylan. Camila Acosta and Yoani Sánchez, photos: taken from Facebook.

By Eloy Viera Cañive (El Toque)

HAVANA TIMES – When the Cuban government arrests a journalist or puts citizens on trial for organizing independently, a familiar explanation tends to resurface: Cuba faces exceptional circumstances because of the United States embargo, and those circumstances justify restricting rights. That argument can be challenged using legal and theoretical reasoning.

The starting point does not deny that sanctions have consequences. Recognizing that a foreign policy can harm a country is one thing; accepting that this conflict requires its rulers to persecute journalists, prevent independent associations, or prosecute people who organize on their own is quite another.

What Is the Argument for Exceptional Circumstances?

The argument works in three steps: Cuba is under threat, Cuba is subject to an embargo, and therefore those in power can do whatever is necessary to defend themselves. The practical consequence is that Cubans who disagree with government policies are expected to wait until the embargo ends before demanding their rights.

This idea is an old one, and at its core it has a concrete effect: if everything that happens on the island is the fault of the embargo and the exceptional circumstances it creates, then no one bears individual responsibility for what they do in the name of those circumstances. Defending exceptional circumstances as a justification for restricting rights amounts to defending impunity for those who carry out repression.

What Lies Between a Sanction and an Arrest?

Between a US sanction and the arrest of a journalist in Havana lies a series of decisions. Those decisions are made by people and are political in nature: officials issue orders, police officers carry them out, and authorities make choices. For that reason, the embargo cannot erase the individual responsibility of each link in that chain.

An ongoing case illustrates the point. Four men, members of the Freemasons, faced trial on November 5, 2026. The formal charge was an illegal dollar exchange transaction. The amount involved: US $300, which was used to purchase powdered milk for elderly residents of a nursing home. This is a political operation presented as a currency-related crime, and the connection between this case and any US sanction once again runs through a decision made inside Cuba.

The second example involves the independent press. Journalists Camila Acosta and Yoani Sánchez were detained on the street, prevented from moving freely, and had their equipment confiscated. Anyone who justifies these actions by invoking the embargo is siding with those who carry them out.

What Does Hannah Arendt Explain About Terror?

Hannah Arendt, the political thinker who developed the concept of totalitarianism, helps answer the fundamental question: Is violence by a totalitarian state a response to an external enemy? According to Arendt, it is not. Terror under totalitarianism does not arise solely as a reaction to adversaries who threaten the government. Rather, it is part of a system of domination that seeks to destroy pluralism and the individual’s capacity to act independently.

This leads to a conclusion applicable to Cuba: if the objective is to dominate through fear, rather than merely defeat the opposition, repression will continue even after organized opposition has been defeated. Cuba has lacked an organized opposition for years, yet repression continues.

A farm analogy helps explain it: repression functions like herbicide sprayed over an already plowed field to prevent anything from growing except what the owner wants. This interpretation is not new. It has been described since the 1940s by authors who understood totalitarianism as a model for organizing power, rather than a phenomenon tied to any particular country.

Why does a One-Party System clash with any form of autonomy?

A system that claims the right of a single party to direct society has a problem with any space for autonomy. Two examples illustrate this. The independent press is troublesome because it decides for itself what to investigate. Freemasonry is troublesome because its members chose their own leaders regardless of what the Ministry of Justice might say.

Neither case has anything to do with the embargo. With or without a blockade, with or without an embargo, any citizen who decides to organize without asking and receiving permission will run into trouble.

All states have policing functions and use force to maintain order, but that order must be enforced within legal and legitimate frameworks. Political repression in Cuba is not legitimate and often is not even legal under the island’s own laws. Regimes of this kind repress because they need to preserve their existing power structure intact. Allowing citizens to organize, obtain information, and compete politically would mean accepting the possibility of losing control.

Havel and the Independent Life of Society

To conclude, it is worth returning to The Power of the Powerless, the essay by Václav Havel, the first president of post-communist Czechoslovakia. Havel spoke of what he called the “independent life of society”: the lives of those who write, teach, create, practice their religion, or organize according to their convictions. Havel showed that, for regimes such as Czechoslovakia’s at the time or Cuba’s today, that autonomy, that independence of ordinary people, could come into conflict with the system even before it developed into explicit political opposition.

That is the conclusion tying together the arguments presented here. If conflict with those in power begins the moment someone acts independently, as with the Freemasons who buy milk for a nursing home or the journalists who go out to report, the embargo may worsen the country’s difficulties, but it does not explain why people are arrested, prosecuted, or have their belongings confiscated. Those are decisions made by people who bear responsibility for them.

First published in Spanish by El Toque and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.
