World.title: Carlota de Limón: The Mexican cocktail that transported me to my mother’s kitchen
World.content:
“You have to try one of these; it’s like a refreshing key lime pie,” a hotel guest at the bar said. I walked over to the friendly group, all with the same drink in hand. The cocktail in front of them resembled a blended piña colada that was pale yellow and frothy on top, garnished with a thin lime wedge on the rim.

My friend and I were staying at the Dreams Estrella del Mar in Mazatlán, Sinaloa, for a few days to check out the hotel and all its amenities. After the nightly show, we stopped by the bar for a drink and tasted what would ultimately be the most memorable part of the trip.

The cocktail was tangy from the lemon, sweet from the sugar, and instantly took me to something very familiar. The creamy texture and the balance of tart and sweet also felt familiar, as if I had tasted this combination many times before.

Then it hit me: It was a dessert my mom used to make growing up, and one I’ve always requested when I’m home. It was a favorite of mine that she called “lemon dessert,” which I know now as a Carlota de Limón.

Back in my mother’s kitchen

Carlota de Limón is a Mexican icebox cake made with lemon juice, Galletas María (sweet, thin vanilla cookies), and a creamy mixture of evaporated and condensed milk. Layered and chilled until set, it has the perfect balance between sweet and tangy.

It was one of my favorite desserts growing up. I remember eating it by the spoonful, freshly made and the day after, as well as the feeling of disappointment when it was gone. It wasn’t reserved for special occasions, and my mom made it regularly whether we were having dessert at home or sharing a meal with guests. It was a dish that was made on a whim, ingredients almost always on hand, and one that didn’t last long.

In other words, it was always a hit.

My mother’s kitchen was where our family came together and where some of our deepest conversations happened. While water boiled for pasta or soup simmered in spices, we would all gather around the island, almost like magnets pulling us closer, filling the space with conversation, laughter and connectedness. That feeling is still there today when I visit my parents, especially around the holidays or special occasions.

An unexpected connection

At the hotel, I pulled up a bar stool and watched the bartender make another drink. Curious about its inspiration, I struck up a conversation with him. He was 23 and working his first hotel bartending job, where he had been experimenting with flavors and creating cocktails, something he found to be a fun, creative outlet.

When I described the dessert the cocktail reminded me of, he recognized the Carlota de Limón, a favorite of his, too. He had been experimenting with ingredients to create the drink, combining Licor 43, the vanilla and spice notes echoing the María cookies, and the fresh lemon juice, sugar and heavy cream to match the creamy layer. He would then shake it vigorously with ice until the mixture turned frothy and cold, adding a simple lime wedge as the finishing touch.

What began as an experiment in flavors had unexpectedly recreated something familiar to me. The bartender didn’t know my personal backstory of the dessert, but his experimentation with a new cocktail and my memories of my mother’s kitchen had led us to the same place.

Why flavors stay with us

Research from the National Library of Medicine has a name for the way a familiar smell or taste can bring back a personal memory: the Proust effect, named after the French writer Marcel Proust. The theory is that taste and smell can trigger autobiographical memories, leading to powerful emotions. Research on the brain’s olfactory pathways also shows direct connections between smell processing and the regions involved in emotion and memory, which makes sense given my strong and positive response to the citrus cocktail.

To me, Carlota de Limón was more than just a dessert; it was something my mother made regularly, in a kitchen where conversations and laughter occurred. The flavor was familiar, but so was everything I associated with it.

When I returned home, I found myself thinking less about the resort’s beautiful pools, manicured grounds or nightly shows, and more about that cocktail. A drink I’d encountered on vacation that had brought back a dessert so familiar that I hadn’t thought much about what it meant to me until that moment.

On the drive home from the airport, my husband asked how the trip went. My answer was simple: “Do we have any lemons? I have a drink in mind.”

Sandra Lee is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: My family always travels during Día de Muertos. Here’s what we’ve enjoyed most
World.content:
There are certain magical aspects of living in Mexico that simply cannot be replicated elsewhere — its foods, traditions and seasons. And because of Mexico’s vast geography and cultural topography, many of those elements can be heightened by being in the right place at the right time.

In that regard, nothing compares to Día de Muertos: A time of year in which colors are blooming, communities are celebrating and honoring loved ones, and regional gastronomy, customs and superstitions are on display for everyone to be collectively immersed in.

Beyond the obvious, increasing importance of the Mesoamerican holiday in Mexico for so many native families and local households, Día de Muertos means something especially personal for me and my family since it marks our anniversary of having moved to Mexico from California. The holiday always reminds me of arriving in Mexico after having gained dual citizenship and being received by festive parades, open-armed friends and relatives, and getting a dose of Mexico’s fullest, most complex flavors that have come to define what we most enjoy about living on this side of the border.

Building our own annual tradition

My wife’s and my own appreciation for Día de Muertos extends further back, years before we had fully relocated to Mexico. In 2019, we visited my mom, who is Mexican-born and was living on my abuelo’s ranch in Oaxaca at the time. We spent a month traveling the state of Oaxaca with her. The highlight? A full week of Día de Muertos in Oaxaca City.

I’ll never forget when we arrived, hopped off the bus, dropped our things off and went into the loud, colorful streets as Oaxaqueños had already kicked off their days-long celebration in the middle of the afternoon. A man wearing a Spider-Man mask saw us standing among the crowd, and as we soon found out would be a common occurrence and part of the local hospitality, he offered to pour out a shot of mezcal from the bottle in his hand.

As an outsider, there is no warmer welcome on the planet than someone picking you out of the masses on the street and pouring you mezcal. It’s a spirit and energy that would come to embody every Día de Muertos holiday we’ve experienced — the sense of connection and togetherness.

Since then, we’ve turned it into our own tradition to celebrate the holiday in different parts of Mexico as often as we can.

The regional nuances of Día de Muertos

My wife recently shared a visual map with me that outlines the different kinds of pan de muerto that are prepared throughout Mexico, based on each state’s history and gastronomic influences. Her point, besides nudging me to pick up another round of pan de muerto for our house, was that Mexico offers more to try than we know, especially whenever Día de Muertos rolls around.

It’s true. Everywhere we’ve been during this season has always presented a new way through which to experience and understand the multidimensionality of how the holiday is celebrated and revered.

Nearby, in the town of Naolinco, Veracruz, and its surrounding mountain communities, the festival is largely centered on the cempasúchil. This year, the community of San Pablo Coapan welcomed thousands of visitors for its fifth annual Festival del Cempasúchil, in which the local cempasúchil farms open to the public with a festival-like array of activities, food and Instagrammable photo ops.

The flower fields are decorated with playful calaveras that are decorated in Veracruzano style, ranging from a 25-foot-tall Jarocho skeleton to a human-sized fútbolero in the afterlife wearing a Tiburones Rojos soccer uniform from the 1990s (a team that no longer exists but certainly evokes memories for anyone who recalls the historic Veracruz team and grew up watching Liga MX).

In the pueblo of Naolinco proper, just a few miles up the mountain, Día de Muertos is celebrated with “La Cantada” (or a townwide serenade), where locals go around singing from the cemeteries to the streets throughout the night.

Major cities and regional rituals

Of course, there are the more globally popular and large-scale interpretations of Día de Muertos that can be seen in Oaxaca or Mexico City. In both cases, the holiday draws countless international and domestic visitors who join in on the fun and traditions as local families honor their deceased relatives with a mix of humility and bombast.

In both Oaxaca and Mexico City, expect massive gatherings of happy-go-lucky tourists and locals, as you’ll have to shuffle your way around the crowds and generally pay higher prices. The celebrations are bigger, louder and, to a degree, more capably geared toward tourism than other locales. I’d say for starters, both Oaxaca’s capital and Mexico City are a comfortable entry point into Mexico’s sprawling multiverse of Día de Muertos, as they provide broadly appealing and easy-to-navigate celebrations, both of which my family has enjoyed and experienced ourselves multiple times.

Of course, we still have a bunch of places to visit on our wishlist that I’ve been told about by my Mexican family members and other travelers. In the Huasteca jungles, “Xantolo” brings the holiday to life with “La Viejada,” a regional masked dance in which townspeople dress up as elders (similar to Veracruz’s “El Viejo del Año Nuevo” custom at the end of every year) to remember their relatives.

1 of 17

Indigenous customs from Huasteca to Campeche

In parts of Michoacán, there is a lake procession where the Purépecha fishermen use torches to light their path across the water and celebrate with all-night vigils.

Choo Ba’ak, a bone-washing ritual that happens every year in the Campeche pueblo of Pomuch, is part of Hanal Pixán (the Maya Day of the Dead) and offers an idiosyncratic version of the holiday unlike the contemporary mainstream version that is usually portrayed.

National Geographic described the ceremony as such: “…families wash the tombs and clean the bones of their deceased. After the cleaning they keep the ossuaries, or the box where the bones are deposited, open so the skulls and bones receive sun and air, as dictated by tradition. Relatives also arrange, paint and adorn the ossuaries and cover them with an embroidered white tablecloth bearing the name of the deceased.”

In Huaquechula, Puebla, unique altars — three to four stories tall, resembling a pyramid — are on display inside homes, with each layer of the altar representing a different aspect of life and death (the earth, the heavens and a celestial summit). The elaborate designs are typically defined by white cloth and marigolds.

As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me, you’d need more than a few lifetimes to truly experience all that Mexico has to offer regionally for Día de Muertos.

Our highlights from this year in the mountains of Puebla

The Pueblo Mágico of Cuetzalan del Progreso is tucked away in the northernmost edge of the state of Puebla, high up in the Sierra Norte mountains.

Unlike the majority of Puebla, which is commonly known for its arid plateaus and Talavera pottery in its state capital and surrounding areas, northern Puebla offers a microclimate and culture of its own that more closely resembles the humid, tropical and high-altitude Indigenous communities of Papantla in northern Veracruz, which is located just a few miles away on the other side of the mountain.

It’s not what one might think of when thinking of Puebla. And yet, it’s where regional customs for Día de Muertos are flourishing. We drove roughly four hours north of Xalapa (or about five hours northeast from Mexico City) to experience it for ourselves this year.

We weren’t disappointed, to say the least.

The town’s architecture alone is worth the winding mountain curves that one must navigate to reach the small, ages-old village that is — because of its elevated location in the mountains — famously drenched in drizzly mist and rainfall. The narrow alleys and steep, cobblestone paths (which all lead to the gorgeous Parroquia de San Francisco de Asís and its Totonac voladores, who perform their flying ritual on a sky-high wooden pole at the center of the plaza) resemble a miniature version of Guanajuato’s capital city, without the overcrowded tourism and with a hyper-local texture.

Flying globos de Cantoya into the night

I was told by a couple of young locals that families don’t commonly celebrate Día de Muertos by visiting the graveyards overnight (which is the tradition elsewhere). Instead, they light “globos de Cantoya” (miniature hot-air balloons made from paper and other materials) and send them off into the night.

From groups of high schoolers to older professionals who’ve mastered the craft, the town gathers on Día de Muertos weekend, as everyone takes turns setting up and sending off hundreds of their custom, artisanal balloons. The balloons — and their makers — vary in style, decoration and success (often, the small balloons will self-combust in flames and come burning back to earth, which can sometimes cause fires in the area). But generally, it’s a safe and spectacular tradition to witness in person.

The tradition, as it was explained to me in the pueblo, is meant to represent a path back to the heavens for the souls who are visiting their altars to enjoy the ofrendas laid out. Each globe, as it ascends brightly and colorfully into the night sky, is meant to guide family members back to the spiritual realm.

In recent years, Cuetzalan has turned the tradition into a legitimate state-funded festival, known locally as “El Vuelo del Quetzal” (The Flight of the Quetzal), and officially as Festival Internacional de Globos Artísticos de Papel. Surprisingly, the festival is only in its second year of formal operation, which helps it retain a charmingly niche, DIY feeling.

Local flavors and looking ahead

During the day, it is all preceded by local dances, voladores, Catrina costume contests and the general ambiance of a Pueblo Mágico worth its salt: excellent food, tianguis and a dense number of historic stairways and nooks to explore.

Among the standouts in town, you cannot skip TAOL, which is led by Chef Adriana Márquez and offers elevated, accessible takes on local dishes, including tlayoyos, chilpozontle, itacate, pipián, coffee and more. It’s the kind of chic eatery that would draw lines out the door in Mexico City, but since it’s hidden behind an unassuming stone exterior in Cuetzalan, it is able to offer ample space and friendly prices for what I would consider among the best cuisine I’ve tasted this year.

Paired with Día de Muertos activities and the hordes of costumed kids making their rounds on Halloween night to ask for their calaverita at local shops, which my son participated in, a few nights in Cuetzalan is a slept-on destination for late October and early November.

Though we elected to stay home last year to dedicate our time and resources to building and decorating an altar inside our home — with the help of my mom, who supplied many photos of our relatives — we’ve enjoyed going on the road to see how others embrace the spirit of the tradition.

I’m already thinking about where we might end up next year and what it will impart.

World.title: Why Tuesday’s US midterm results are a historic opportunity for Mexico-US relations: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Most of us intently watched Tuesday night’s midterm election results in the United States, regardless of political affiliation. As the MND team is committed to remaining apolitical, I will not weigh in on my personal thoughts on the results. I will, however, comment on what they mean for Mexico and for Mexico-U.S. relations.

It’s important to understand that the hardline approach of the Trump administration over the past two years against both Mexican immigrants and Mexico effectively silenced leaders on both sides of the border. Mexico was constantly on the defensive against the U.S. on tariffs, cartels, deportations, the rights of Mexican citizens abroad and many other topics. Mexican Americans, regardless of status, watched with anxiety as their communities came under threat from aggressive ICE raids. For many people and for Mexico in general, it was a time to keep your head down and stay quiet. The focus became on surviving the storm rather than thriving, leading or growing.

But the midterm election results have dramatically changed that dynamic.

First of all, I am happy for Mexican Americans. They will hopefully no longer have to fear the heavy-handed tactics often deployed by members of ICE. I recently wrote about the death of the 18th Mexican-American in ICE custody here: Yet another Mexican national dies in the custody of ICE: A perspective from our CEO.

People living in the United States — either legally or illegally — shouldn’t have to fear for their lives at the hands of the government. The data shows that the raids have often gone far beyond focusing on criminals, as the administration suggested it would do. Too many good people have been demonized by ICE as the agency has become increasingly extremist.

I am also happy for Mexico. The country has been the brunt of countless threats by the Trump administration on everything from tariffs to immigration to drug policy and cartels — despite historic cooperation from the Sheinbaum administration on many of these issues. Businesses on both sides of the border have had to deal with near-constant tariff threats, which oftentimes defy standard logic and strategic rationale for the North American region. Both Trump and members of his administration have repeatedly claimed that Mexico is run by the cartels, that President Sheinbaum is “afraid of the cartels,” and threatened to take unilateral action in the country. Hopefully, the unprecedented cooperation will continue and the unhelpful threats will diminish.

I am happy for the states of California and Texas, which both elected Mexican American governors. These two states — the largest and most economically prosperous in the United States — now account for more than half of the people of Mexican origin in the United States. Mexican Americans represent 40% of the total population in those states, which, if they were stand-alone counties, would be the fifth- and eighth-largest in the world in terms of GDP. Children of Mexican immigrants to the U.S. now lead both states. The newly elected lieutenant governor of Nevada is also of Mexican heritage.

Mexican Americans stood up, voted, and were heard — loudly and clearly. Their collective action presents a tremendous opportunity for Mexico. Let me give two examples:

1. I recently wrote about the huge, untapped opportunity that the Mexican diaspora in the U.S. represents for Mexico. The engagement of Indian American businesspeople with India stands in stark contrast to the lack of engagement of many Mexican American businesspeople with Mexico. Post-election, the timing is perfect for this to change. The opportunity for Mexican American businesses to further connect with Mexico to find talent, suppliers or customers is massive and could unleash economic growth in both countries.

2. It’s time for Mexico and the U.S. to think BIG on binational projects and initiatives. If not at the national level, most certainly at the state level. Some great examples already exist or are in process. In California, think of the Tijuana airport, which actually straddles the border into California. The airport has experienced phenomenal growth and is a perfect example of how the two countries can work strategically to develop closer ties. In Texas, think of the newly-opened second railway between Laredo and Nuevo Laredo or the proposed expansion of the World Trade Bridge from eight to 18 lanes. Think of the soon-to-be-opened Pharr project adding a four-lane bridge in Reynosa, or the Colombia-Solidarity highway projects to better connect Nuevo León and Laredo. Or even consider the Green Corridors planned project for an autonomous system to transport cargo from Monterrey to Laredo.

It’s a historic time for real leadership — strategic, long-term, big thinking that can foster engagement and economic prosperity between the two countries. Far too much time has been lost dividing, threatening and silencing bilateral collaboration and cooperation. The current circumstances offer an opportunity to take the relationship to a whole new level. Leaders on both sides of the border, stand up! The time is now.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Mexican Border Mayor Reported Kidnapped
World.content:
Key Facts Who. Miguel Ángel Almaraz, opposition National Action Party (PAN) mayor of Río Bravo, a Tamaulipas border city facing Texas.

What. Reported as a suspected kidnapping victim on Saturday 7 November; his whereabouts are not officially confirmed.

Where. San Luis Potosí officials say the abduction happened in Zacatecas; a search is under way.

Why it matters. Río Bravo lies across from Texas, near Reynosa (Mexico) and McAllen (Texas).

As of 8 November 2026, 13:00 GMT

The mayor of Río Bravo, a Mexican city across the border from Texas, is reported kidnapped. Officials are searching the border zone between two Mexican states, and many basic facts remain unconfirmed.

Miguel Ángel Almaraz Maldonado, mayor of Río Bravo in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas, is reported as the victim of a suspected kidnapping. Tamaulipas is a state in north-east Mexico that borders Texas.

San Luis Potosí’s state security ministry (Secretaría de Seguridad y Protección Ciudadana, SSPCE) said on Sunday 8 November 2026 that its civil guard is working to locate the people involved. Río Bravo sits across the border from Texas, near Reynosa, a Mexican border city, and McAllen, a Texas city, so the case matters to US residents and travellers near that border.

What We Know

The SSPCE said that, on first data, the alleged abduction took place in Zacatecas, a central Mexican state, on the highway between San Tiburcio and Vanegas. The people affected were abandoned on the road, asked for help and reached Cedral, a town in San Luis Potosí.

The Guardia Civil Estatal, San Luis Potosí’s state civil guard, set up an operation in the border zone between San Luis Potosí and Zacatecas. It is coordinating with Zacatecas authorities and other bodies to locate the people involved.

The ministry described the case as a “presunta privación ilegal de la libertad”, meaning an alleged illegal deprivation of liberty. In plain terms, that is a suspected kidnapping.

Elefante Blanco, a Tamaulipas news outlet, reported that his family was with him and was released at the site, and early information said they were heading to Real de Catorce, a town in San Luis Potosí. The San Luis Potosí ministry says the people affected were left on the road, and they reached Cedral to ask for help.

Elefante Blanco reports that armed men in two pickup trucks stopped the group on Saturday 7 November 2026, citing judicial sources. Officials have not confirmed that account.

The National Palace in Mexico City, seat of the federal government. File photo, Wikimedia Commons.

What Is Not Known

No official source has confirmed where the mayor is. Jesús Govea Orozco, state attorney general of Tamaulipas, said he had no conclusive information and could not rule out a kidnapping.

Also unknown are who took him, the motive and how many people were in the group. Any ransom demand and any arrests have not been reported either.

One Mexican outlet reported unofficially that he regained his freedom around 22:00 on Saturday. Neither the San Luis Potosí ministry nor any other official source has confirmed that, so we treat it as unverified.

Who Is Miguel Ángel Almaraz

Almaraz belongs to the National Action Party (PAN), an opposition conservative party. He won the Río Bravo mayor’s office in 2024, backed by the Fuerza y Corazón por Tamaulipas coalition.

That coalition united the PAN, the Institutional Revolutionary Party and the Party of the Democratic Revolution. Elefante Blanco describes him as politically and legally at odds with Tamaulipas governor Américo Villarreal Anaya and with Morena, Mexico’s ruling party.

These are the outlet’s descriptions. Nothing reported so far establishes a motive.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

Río Bravo lies across the border from Texas, in the same broader region as Reynosa (Mexico) and McAllen (Texas). A case involving an elected border official draws attention from residents, businesses and travellers who follow security there.

The city shares its name with the river that Americans call the Rio Grande. That river marks the border between Texas and Mexico at that point.

We know of no change to any travel advisory linked to this case. Anyone planning border travel should check official government guidance and local conditions before setting out.

Security on the northern border is a recurring story. Our earlier report, Girl Dies as Cartel Blockades Matamoros, covered a cartel blockade in another Tamaulipas border city.

Our Mexico coverage follows the wider security and political picture. We will report confirmed developments as officials release them.

The next signals will be official: confirmation of the mayor’s whereabouts and statements from Tamaulipas or Zacatecas authorities. Until then, the search in the border zone between San Luis Potosí and Zacatecas is the main thing to watch.

Sources

San Luis Potosí Secretaría de Seguridad y Protección Ciudadana (SSPCE) statement, 8 November 2026; Elefante Blanco (Tamaulipas) reporting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Miguel Ángel Almaraz?

He is the National Action Party mayor of Río Bravo, Tamaulipas, a Mexican border city across from Texas. He is reported as the victim of a suspected kidnapping.

Where did the alleged abduction happen?

The San Luis Potosí security ministry says it happened in Zacatecas, on the highway between San Tiburcio and Vanegas. Reports say the mayor was intercepted on Saturday 7 November. One outlet says he may have regained freedom that night, which officials have not confirmed.

Have there been arrests or a ransom demand?

No arrests and no ransom demand have been reported. Authorities have not said who took him or why.

Has the US changed its travel advice?

We know of no travel advisory change linked to this case. Check official government guidance before border travel.

World.content:

ARGENTINA · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts The country Argentina adopted a US trade-body security standard for state telecom purchases.

What happened An order published Friday 6 November 2026 makes SCS 9001 certification the test for suppliers.

Who is covered State bodies and state companies, such as network operator ARSAT, fall under the rule.

The clock Within 90 days, the cybersecurity agency must list which networks count as critical.

Power Index Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 60.2 points (November 2026 edition).

Argentina has made a United States industry standard the yardstick for the telecom equipment its government buys. The order, Disposición 7/2026 of the National Cybersecurity Centre (CNC), the state agency that sets security rules for critical networks, appeared in the Official Gazette (Boletín Oficial) on Friday 6 November 2026.

For US readers, the move ties Argentina’s state telecom buying to a standard written by a US industry body. Chinese telecom makers such as Huawei and ZTE may struggle to obtain the certification, although the order itself names no company or country.

What Happened

The order is titled Technical Supply-Chain Security Requirements for Equipment Intended for Critical Telecommunications Infrastructure. It was signed by Walter Fabián Agüero, executive director of the CNC.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 60.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

It takes as its reference SCS 9001, a standard created by the Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA), a US trade body for the telecom industry. The standard certifies a manufacturer’s processes across the supply chain, and it does not test individual devices.

Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Who Must Comply

The rule binds the national public sector, including state-owned companies, when they buy, contract or operate equipment for critical telecom networks. State companies such as ARSAT, the state-owned network operator, fall inside its scope.

Private companies are not directly bound for now. They can still be affected if they sell to the state, because state tenders will carry the requirement.

The Timetable

Within 90 days of taking effect, the CNC must identify which networks are critical and sort equipment into criticality levels. Reports on the order’s annex describe four levels, with SCS 9001 certification required for the top two.

Reports on the annex also describe a 36-month transition, during which proof that certification has started is enough. Equipment already installed may get adaptation plans, and replacing it requires a reasoned decision.

Where Huawei and ZTE Come In

The order excludes no supplier by nationality and names no company. Local reports note, however, that TIA does not certify companies on US government restriction lists, which include Huawei and ZTE.

More than 1,200 small internet providers operate in Argentina, according to the country’s internet providers’ chamber. Reports on the order mention no cost estimate for operators, so the price of any switch is unknown.

What It Means for You

For US investors in Argentine telecom and infrastructure, the order adds a compliance step for suppliers that sell to the state. Costs could rise if networks must replace installed equipment.

Non-Chinese suppliers could gain ground in state tenders, since certification is open to firms outside the US restriction lists. Consumers see no immediate change, because the order does not directly bind private companies.

What Is Not Known

The list of critical networks is not published, and the CNC has 90 days to draw it up. It is also unclear how many suppliers hold or can quickly obtain SCS 9001.

Enacom, the national communications regulator, has been asked to assess whether to extend the requirements to equipment approvals for the private sector. No decision is public, and Costa Rica and Paraguay have already used the same certification, with a Costa Rican court partly suspending its decree.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times. See also Argentina’s plan to swap Chinese technology in state networks.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is SCS 9001?

It is a supply-chain security certification created by the Telecommunications Industry Association, a US trade body. It audits a manufacturer’s processes rather than testing individual devices.

Does Argentina’s Rule Ban Huawei?

No, the order names no company or country. Certification is open to any supplier, but TIA does not certify firms on US restriction lists, which include Huawei and ZTE.

Who Must Follow the Rule?

The national public sector and state-owned companies must follow it when buying equipment for critical telecom networks. Private firms are affected only through state contracts for now.

When Do the Requirements Start?

The CNC has 90 days to list critical networks and classify equipment. State purchases that begin after that period must follow the rule.

Sources: Argentina, Boletín Oficial, Disposición 7/2026 of the National Cybersecurity Centre, 6 November 2026 (boletinoficial.gob.ar); Telecommunications Industry Association, SCS 9001 standard; Enacom, National Communications Agency of Argentina.

World.title: Senegal Migrant Boat Wreck Leaves 21 Dead
World.content:
Fishing pirogues on the beach at Kayar, Senegal (Photo: Ibrahima khalilpro diop, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

An official source cited in Senegalese reports put the toll from a migrant boat shipwreck off the Atlantic coast at 34 dead on Sunday 8 November 2026. That replaces Senegal’s Interior Ministry provisional count of at least 21 dead and one survivor, issued on the evening of Saturday 7 November 2026.

Who: Presumed migrants aboard a pirogue; 34 dead in the latest official count.

Presumed migrants aboard a pirogue; 34 dead in the latest official count. What: A presumed shipwreck of a pirogue, a long wooden fishing canoe, carrying would-be migrants.

A presumed shipwreck of a pirogue, a long wooden fishing canoe, carrying would-be migrants. Where: Off Lompoul, on the coast of the Kébémer department, a district in the Louga region, north-west Senegal.

Off Lompoul, on the coast of the Kébémer department, a district in the Louga region, north-west Senegal. When: Bodies found from Saturday 7 to Sunday 8 November 2026. As of 8 November 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET (15:00 GMT).

Bodies found from Saturday 7 to Sunday 8 November 2026. As of 8 November 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET (15:00 GMT). Earlier count: The Interior Ministry’s provisional toll on 7 November was at least 21 dead and one survivor.

A stretch of Atlantic beach in northern Senegal has become a place of mourning. The bodies lie near Lompoul, a coastal spot between Dakar, the capital, and Saint-Louis, a northern port city.

The shore matters to US readers because boats leave this coast on the Atlantic route. That sea path leads toward Spain’s Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago off Morocco.

What We Know

A pirogue carrying would-be migrants reportedly capsized off Lompoul, a coastal spot in the commune of Léona. A commune is a local council area, and Léona lies in the Kébémer department, an administrative district of the Louga region.

The cause has not been officially stated, and authorities describe a presumed shipwreck. Local reports speak of a capsizing.

On Saturday 7 November the toll rose sharply, as many more bodies were found near Lompoul, also spelled Loumpoul. The Interior Ministry’s provisional count that evening was at least 21 bodies and one survivor.

On Sunday 8 November an official source cited in Senegalese reports put the toll at 34 dead after further bodies were recovered. That figure replaces the earlier counts and must not be added to them.

The number of people aboard has not been given. Searches continue for possible further victims.

The governor of Louga, the region’s top state official, went to the site on Sunday 8 November. The Interior Minister, who heads the ministry, is expected at Lompoul on Monday 9 November to assess the situation and bring state support to families.

Identification of the bodies was under way on Sunday. Gendarmes and firefighters took part in the recovery.

What Is Not Known

The toll is not final, and the figure may change. Officials have not confirmed where the boat left from, and its destination is unconfirmed, though boats leaving this coast typically head for the Canary Islands.

The number of people on board is not known. The identities of the dead are also unknown.

Officials describe the cause as a presumed shipwreck. Nothing further has been confirmed, and we will not speculate.

An aerial view of Dakar, Senegal’s capital, showing part of the Cheikh Anta Diop University campus, the capital’s main public university (file photo; the shipwreck was some way up the coast to the north). Photo: Ji-Elle / Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)

Why This Route Keeps Claiming Lives

The Atlantic route runs from West African coasts to the Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago in the Atlantic. It is widely regarded as one of the most dangerous migration routes.

Crossings often use pirogues, wooden boats built for coastal fishing rather than long ocean journeys. Open water, strong currents and long distances leave little room for error.

Earlier arrivals on the Canary Islands are covered in Senegalese Migrants Among 77 at El Hierro. Our explainer on the route follows below.

Our Senegal coverage hub carries more background. It includes our explainer on Senegalese migration to Spain.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

For readers in the United States, the sinking shows how far migration pressure from West Africa reaches. It belongs to the wider flow toward Europe that readers following migration policy watch closely.

The incident took place on a coast between Dakar and Saint-Louis. We have no confirmed information on any change to travel conditions there.

The count may change as rescue services continue their search. The Interior Minister’s visit on Monday 9 November is the next scheduled step.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened off Senegal’s coast?

A pirogue carrying presumed migrants reportedly capsized off Lompoul. By Saturday 7 November 2026 the Interior Ministry’s provisional toll was at least 21 dead and one survivor.

Is the toll 21 or 34?

An official source cited in Senegalese reports put the toll at 34 dead on Sunday 8 November 2026. That replaces the provisional count of at least 21 from the evening before.

Where is Lompoul?

Lompoul is on Senegal’s Atlantic coast between Dakar, the capital, and Saint-Louis. It lies in the Kébémer department of the Louga region, in the north-west of the country.

Do officials know why the boat sank?

No, officials describe a presumed shipwreck and the cause is unconfirmed. The departure point, the number on board and the identities of the dead are also unknown.

Sao Paulo in November: holidays and still running

December stacks CCXP (3–6 December) and Primavera Sound with Gorillaz and The Strokes (5–6 December) into one week at two of the city’s biggest event venues, São Paulo Expo and the Interlagos track. Both sit outside the central districts, so plan transport early.

Weather in Rio in November

Brazil’s national weather institute, INMET, and the city’s Alerta Rio service publish the official forecasts and storm alerts. No alert for the coming days was confirmed at the source on Tuesday 3 November 2026.

Afternoon storms are common in Rio as spring turns to summer, so plan beach hours for the morning. Forecasts change daily, so check both services before outdoor events.

This Weekend in Rio: 7 and 8 November

CASACOR Rio, an interior design show in its 35th year, fills the Aliança da Bahia building in Centro until Sunday 8 November. Tickets cost 120 reais (about US$22), or 60 reais (about US$11) half price; it opens Tuesday to Sunday, noon to 8pm.

The fifth Festival Gastronomia Sem Fronteiras fills the rooftop of the Fashion Mall shopping centre, Estrada da Gávea 899 in São Conrado, on Saturday 7 and Sunday 8 November, from 1pm to 11pm. Kitchens from Germany (Herr Pfeffer), Italy (Babbo), Portugal (Barsa), Japan (Jappa da Quitanda) and France (the Franco-Brazilian chefs’ association led by Frédéric Monnier) cook beside Rio’s São Miguel and QuiQui, with a market of producers from Rio de Janeiro state and cooking classes by the Senac RJ school.

The band Últimos and Rodrigo Santos play the Sesc stage on Saturday, and rock singer Paulo Ricardo closes the festival on Sunday with his voice-and-guitar show “Voz, Violão e Rock’n’Roll”. First-batch tickets cost 40 reais (about US$7), or 20 reais (about US$4) half price, and rise as batches sell; children up to 10 enter free, and food and drink are paid separately.

“Tom na Fazenda” (“Tom at the Farm”), an award-winning stage drama adapted from a play by Canadian writer Michel Marc Bouchard, plays the Teatro da Ilha on Ilha do Governador, the large island in Guanabara Bay that holds Rio’s international airport, on Saturday 7 November at 8pm. It is the first time the touring production, starring Armando Babaioff and directed by Rodrigo Portella, stops on the island; the dialogue is in Portuguese, and ticket prices are available from the venue.

The Bossa Nova Sessions festival enters its final week at the Teatro Café Pequeno in Leblon and runs until Sunday 8 November. Ticket prices are available from the venue.

Pianist Osmar Milito, a jazz and bossa nova figure who died in 2024, is remembered in “Saudades de Osmar Milito” at Acaso Cultural in Botafogo on Sunday 8 November at 6.30pm. The Augusto Mattoso Trio, with Cliff Korman on piano and Xande Figueiredo on drums, plays his arrangements; ticket prices are available from the venue.

“Cordélia Brasil”, a tragicomedy by Antonio Bivár about a woman who carries the care of her household, runs at the Teatro Glauce Rocha in Centro on Thursdays at 7pm: 12, 19 and 26 November. João Fonseca directs and Paula Goja plays the title role; the dialogue is in Portuguese, and ticket prices are available from the venue.

“Embarcação Perdue”, a stage comedy-drama about a mysterious expedition searching for what was lost in life, opened on Thursday 5 November at the Teatro Glaucio Gil in Copacabana. It runs Wednesday to Friday at 8pm until 27 November; the dialogue is in Portuguese, and ticket prices are available from the venue.

Vasco da Gama host Palmeiras in the Copa do Brasil semi-final second leg on Sunday 8 November, planned for São Januário at 5pm Brasília time (3pm US Eastern).

Concerts and Opera: 9 to 22 November

Turandot, Puccini’s last opera, plays the Theatro Municipal at 7pm on 13, 14, 18, 20 and 21 November. A school matinee is on 17 November at 2pm.

Individual Turandot tickets run from 20 reais (about US$4) in the gallery to 90 reais (about US$17) in the boxes. The Gilsons, a family trio, play Vivo Rio with Gilberto Gil as special guest on Friday 13 November at 9pm.

Half-price Gilsons seats start at 160 reais (about US$30) and full price at 320 reais (about US$59). The venue says last tickets remain.

Soul singer Decco Torres presents his new album “Neo” at the Teatro Rival Petrobras, a Rio music hall, on Friday 13 November at 7.30pm, his press office says. The show mixes soul, disco funk, trap and MPB (Brazilian popular music) and includes classics by the Brazilian soul singers Tim Maia and Sandra Sá; ticket prices are available from the venue.

Bar Bukowski, a rock bar in the Botafogo district at Rua Álvaro Ramos 270, says it turns 29 on Friday 13 November. The band Os Gradientes plays 1980s and 1990s classics and there is cake for everyone; the price of the party was not announced.

Singer-songwriter Naiara Martins, a Jabuti Prize nominee (Brazil’s main book award), debuts her show “Terras do Sem-Fim” at the Dolores Club in Lapa on Thursday 12 November at 8.30pm. The programme blends bossa nova and samba with classics by Gilberto Gil, Baden Powell and Marcos Valle; ticket prices are available from the venue.

The Associação de Canto Coral, a Rio choral society, marks its 85th year with a concert of José Maurício Nunes Garcia’s Missa de Santa Cecília on 12 November and again on 22 November; the venue and times were not confirmed, so check with the society.

Singer-songwriter Nando Reis plays his romantic tour “Pra Você Guardei o Amor” (“I Kept the Love for You”) at Qualistage, a large concert hall in the Barra da Tijuca district, on Friday 13 November at 9.30pm (doors 7.30pm). Ticket prices are available from the venue.

Country singer Simone Mendes brings her show “Intimidade” to Rio for the first time at Qualistage on Saturday 14 November at 10pm (doors open 8pm), with seated tables; tickets start at 130 reais (about US$24).

Mariah Carey brings her Christmas show to the Farmasi Arena’s outdoor area in Barra da Tijuca on Saturday 21 November. Standing-floor tickets cost 247.50 reais (about US$46) half price and 495 reais (about US$91) full price, with gates at 4pm.

Rio Tap Beer House, a craft-beer bar in the Flamengo district, says it marks its seventh anniversary on Saturday 21 November with an afternoon open-bar party serving draught beer from Brazilian and foreign breweries; ticket prices are available from the venue.

Seal, with Seu Jorge opening, plays Qualistage in Barra on Thursday 26 November. Seated tickets start at 197.50 reais (about US$36) half price and 395 reais (about US$73) full price.

The 31st Rio Pride parade, the Parada do Orgulho LGBTI+, takes over the Copacabana seafront on Sunday 22 November. Organisers had not published a start time at the time of writing.

O Grande Encontro (“The Great Meeting”), a night of Umbanda music, fills Qualistage on Sunday 22 November. Umbanda is an Afro-Brazilian religion, and the singers Sandro Luiz and Tião Casemiro play with guests Leci Brandão and Luan Pureza as part of Black Consciousness celebrations; prices were not confirmed, so check the ticket seller.

Free Things to Do in Rio in November

The Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, a downtown arts centre, shows the Amazônicas exhibition free until Monday 16 November. It opens Wednesday to Monday, 9am to 8pm, and free tickets are online or at its box office.

The Theatro Municipal also runs a free midday opera series, Ópera do Meio-Dia. Its November dates were not confirmed on 3 November, so check the theatre.

Late November: Bethânia, Clássicos do Brasil and Sailing

The Festival Clássicos do Brasil fills the Marina da Glória on Saturday 28 November from 5pm and Sunday 29 November from 3pm. Saturday brings Maria Bethânia, Alceu Valença and Vanessa da Mata, and Sunday brings Alexandre Pires, Péricles and Ferrugem.

Tickets start at 120 reais (about US$22) on the festival’s own site. The festival returns on 5 and 6 December, and no line-up has been published for those dates.

Holidays, Money and Getting Around

Sunday 15 November, Proclamation of the Republic Day, falls on a weekend and gives no extra day off. Friday 20 November is Black Consciousness Day, a national holiday, and banks and public offices close.

The Banco Central do Brasil dollar rate was 5.4212 reais on Friday 30 October, so 100 reais is about US$18. Half-price tickets, the legal meia-entrada, go to students, people over 60 and others with ID.

What It Means for You

For US visitors, the busiest weekend is 20 to 22 November, when a holiday, Mariah Carey and Pride overlap. Book hotels early; the dollar has bought more reais since the 25 October runoff.

Buy tickets only from the venue or its named ticket seller. Carry photo ID, and keep a rain plan for afternoons.

What to Watch Next

Watch Friday 13 November for the Turandot premiere and the Gilsons concert, then Friday 20 November for the holiday. The Pride start time and the December Clássicos line-ups are still to be confirmed.

The central bank publishes a new dollar rate each business day, and this guide returns in December. Football dates for rounds 35 to 37, between 18 and 28 November, are not yet fixed.

What Is Not Known

Organisers had not published a Pride start time or the Ópera do Meio-Dia dates. The theatre site could not be opened on 3 November, so Turandot prices rest on published listings.

Gilberto Gil’s own site does not list the Vivo Rio date, which rests on the venue’s listing. The ticket seller shows 198 to 396 reais (about US$37 to US$73) with fees.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the holidays in Rio in November 2026?

Sunday 15 November (Proclamation of the Republic) and Friday 20 November (Black Consciousness Day) remain; Monday 2 November was All Souls’ Day. Banks and offices close on the 20th.

What are the best things to do in Rio in November?

The top picks are Turandot at the Theatro Municipal from 13 November and Gilberto Gil at Vivo Rio on 13 November. Pride on 22 November and the Clássicos do Brasil festival on 28 and 29 November follow.

What is free to do in Rio in November?

The Amazônicas exhibition at the Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil is free until 16 November. The Theatro Municipal also runs a free midday opera series; check its dates.

What is the weather in Rio in November?

Warm and humid, with afternoon storms common as spring turns to summer. Check INMET and Alerta Rio for the daily forecast and storm alerts.

Sources: Banco Central do Brasil (dollar rate, 30 October 2026); INMET, Brazil’s national weather institute (alerts); Riotur, Rio city tourism agency (Clássicos do Brasil); Vivo Rio concert hall (Gilsons with Gilberto Gil) (all accessed 3 November 2026).

GHANA · MEDIA

Key Facts The country Ghana, a West African democracy, held the 30th awards of its national press union in Accra.

What happened Radio host Philip Osei Bonsu, known as O.B., won the top prize on Saturday 7 November 2026.

The warning The Ghana Journalists Association says security officers were allegedly involved in three of five attacks on reporters in January 2026.

The money President John Dramani Mahama pledged 10 million Ghanaian cedis (GH¢10 million, about US$860,000) to a fund for journalists.

What next The 2027 national budget is meant to carry that seed money.

Ghana has named radio host Philip Osei Bonsu, known as O.B., its Ghana Journalist of the Year for 2026. The Ghana Journalists Association (GJA), the country’s national press union, announced the prize on Saturday 7 November 2026 at its 30th Media Awards in Accra.

For US readers, the night is a health check on the press in a West African democracy at a time when its own union warns of attacks on reporters. It also brought a pledge of public money for the news industry from the head of state.

What Happened

O.B. hosts Ekosiisen, a late-afternoon current-affairs show on Asempa FM, a Ghanaian radio station. He received the GJA/P.A.V.

Ansah Journalist of the Year award, named after the late Ghanaian journalist P.A.V. Ansah and the highest individual honour of the evening.

The ceremony took place at the Palms Convention Centre of the La Palm Royal Beach Hotel in Accra. Its theme was “Celebrating Excellence, Advancing Media Freedom and Combating Hate Speech in the Digital Age”.

President Mahama, Ghana’s head of state since January 2025, spoke at the event. Judges had weighed 327 entries from 206 applicants before the winners were named.

Who Else Won

Nabil Ahmed Rufai, a freelance reporter, won Best in Television News for “Stolen Childhood”, a report on child labour in Ghana’s fishing industry. Mohammed Fugu won Best in Print News.

Clinton Yeboah won Best Radio Feature. Nathaniel Attoh of Joy FM won the sports reporting award, one of the beat prizes handed out on the night.

A Warning About Attacks on Reporters

The GJA president, Albert Kwabena Dwumfour, used the evening to raise the safety of journalists. He said three of the five attacks on reporters recorded in January 2026 allegedly involved security officers.

Dwumfour said journalists are not enemies of the state but partners in national development. He added that an attack on a journalist is an attack on press freedom.

The association made the same January count public at the time. It said the three attacks were allegedly carried out by state security agencies.

A Fund for Journalists

Mahama told the audience that the 2027 national budget includes GH¢10 million (about US$860,000 at the market rate of 8 November 2026, US$0.086 per cedi) as seed money for a Media Development Fund. He said the fund will support journalist welfare, professional training, investigative reporting, digital literacy and safety training.

The president said he had announced the fund’s revival at the 29th awards a year earlier. He also said he would personally ask companies and the central bank to contribute, and promised that editorial independence would be respected.

Why It Matters

Press freedom shapes how reliably the world hears about Ghana’s economy, from the central bank’s gold accounts to the end of its IMF loan. Reporters are the people who check those stories.

The warning about attacks comes from the union that speaks for them. The pledge of money comes from the president whose government is often the subject of their work.

What It Means for You

If you follow Ghana as an investor, a traveller or a family member abroad, the awards show where independent reporting stands. Stories on mining, child labour and public accounts are the kind of work that holds institutions to account.

A press that can report safely is easier to trust when you read about the cedi, Ghana’s currency, the budget or local risks. The 2027 budget will show whether the media fund receives the money Mahama promised.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how the fund will be run, who will oversee it, or when the first payments will reach journalists. The GJA has not said whether it considers GH¢10 million (about US$860,000) enough.

It is not known whether any officer has faced action over the January attacks. It is also unclear whether the award for O.B. changes how the GJA presses its case with security agencies.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Is Ghana’s Journalist of the Year for 2026?

Philip Osei Bonsu, known as O.B., of Asempa FM won the GJA/P.A.V. Ansah Journalist of the Year award. He hosts the current-affairs show Ekosiisen.

When Were the 30th GJA Media Awards Held?

They were held on Saturday 7 November 2026 in Accra. The venue was the Palms Convention Centre of the La Palm Royal Beach Hotel.

What Did President Mahama Announce?

He said the 2027 budget includes GH¢10 million (about US$860,000) as seed money. It is for a Media Development Fund for journalists.

What Is the GJA?

The Ghana Journalists Association is Ghana’s national press union. It runs the yearly media awards and speaks for reporters on safety and press freedom.

COLOMBIA · SECURITY

Key Facts The place Southern Bolívar, a gold-mining region in northern Colombia, where armed groups fight for control.

The attack Drones hit an army base in Santa Rosa del Sur on Saturday 7 November 2026.

The toll The Army confirms three soldiers dead and eight seriously wounded; local officials count 35 hurt.

The warning The state ombudsman counted 11,135 people hit by confinement or displacement from May to September 2026.

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.1 points (November 2026 edition).

Southern Bolívar violence is now at the centre of Colombia’s security debate after drones hit an army base on Saturday 7 November 2026. The region, in the north of the country, is a gold-mining area where three armed groups compete for land, roads and income.

For US readers, the story matters because Colombia is a close security partner of Washington. The ELN, a Colombian guerrilla group, is the main suspect, and the United States lists it as a terrorist organisation.

What Happened on Saturday

Drones carrying explosives hit the military base in Santa Rosa del Sur, a town in southern Bolívar department, around midday. The Army says three soldiers were killed and eight were seriously wounded, and it calls the attack a grave violation of international humanitarian law.

The strike came while local officials were holding a security meeting after three people were killed in the town on Friday 6 November. The mayor counted 35 injured, and later military tallies were higher.

Why Southern Bolívar Is a Flashpoint

The Defensoría del Pueblo, Colombia’s state ombudsman for human rights, says the attacks are not isolated events. It says illegal armed groups in the Serranía de San Lucas mountain range are fighting over territory, mining income and strategic corridors.

Three groups are involved: the ELN, the Clan del Golfo, a large drug-trafficking gang that calls itself the Gaitanista Army of Colombia, and FARC dissidents under a commander known as Calarcá. The FARC dissidents are fighters who rejected or abandoned the 2016 peace deal.

The Human Cost in Numbers

Between May and September 2026, the Defensoría learned of 22 humanitarian emergencies in southern Bolívar. They involved confinement, when people cannot leave their villages, and mass forced displacement, and they affected at least 11,135 people from 4,939 families.

The ombudsman also reports landmines, limits on movement, shortages of food and medicine, and interrupted schooling in rural communities. It says Santa Rosa del Sur sits under Early Warning 034 of 2023, a formal risk alert about civilians, which it last updated in August 2026.

Why It Matters

Saturday’s attack follows our report on the first hours after the strike, and it is the deadliest of its kind we have covered this year. It adds to pressure on a government that has also targeted the Clan del Golfo.

Our guide to Colombia’s key players shows who holds power in Bogotá. The southern Bolívar fight tests whether the state can reach remote mining zones.

What the Government Says

President Abelardo de la Espriella, a conservative who took office this year, condemned the attack on social media and said terrorists would not intimidate or push the state back. He ordered the security forces to step up the pursuit of those responsible and to retake territory.

Colombia’s defence minister said the ELN is the likely culprit, possibly in revenge for the capture of a regional ELN leader known as Carrito. The Army said hours before the attack that his arrest would cut the ELN’s income from illegal gold mining, but no group has claimed the strike.

The Defensoría said no one has yet convened the national commission that coordinates rapid responses to early warnings. It asked the Interior Ministry to do so urgently.

What It Means for You

If you hold Colombian stocks or bonds through US funds, a deadly strike on troops raises security costs but does not alter the main economic outlook. The risk is concentrated in a remote mining region, not in Colombia’s big cities.

Travellers should check official travel advisories before visiting rural Bolívar, which is not a typical tourist destination. The attack also tests how the new government keeps its promise to retake territory held by armed groups.

What Is Not Known

It is not known who carried out the attack, because no group has claimed it and the revenge theory is unconfirmed. Final casualty numbers are also still being settled.

It is unclear whether the Interior Ministry will convene the early-warning commission, or what new troops or air defences the government will send. The security plan for the region has not been published.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where Is Southern Bolívar?

It is the southern part of Bolívar department in northern Colombia. Towns such as Santa Rosa del Sur sit in the Serranía de San Lucas, a gold-mining mountain region.

Who Is Fighting in Southern Bolívar?

The ELN, the Clan del Golfo and FARC dissidents led by Calarcá are fighting for control. The state ombudsman says the dispute is about territory, mining income and strategic corridors.

How Many People Has the Violence Affected?

The Defensoría counted at least 11,135 people from 4,939 families in 22 humanitarian emergencies between May and September 2026. These involved confinement and forced displacement.

Who Carried Out the Drone Attack?

No group has claimed it. The defence minister named the ELN as the likely culprit, possibly in revenge for the capture of a regional leader known as Carrito, but that is not confirmed.

World.title: Israel Pick Sends Netanyahu Exit Odds to 68%
World.content:
File photo: the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, in Jerusalem.

Published Sunday, 8 November, 4:30 a.m. Eastern Time (ET) · Source: Office of the President of Israel, public prediction-market data

Traders now bet that Benjamin Netanyahu is likely to lose Israel’s top job within eight months. On Polymarket, a crypto-based trading platform, the price that he is out as prime minister by 30 June 2027 is 68%.

The contract for the end of this year jumped about 26 points in a week to 44.5%, after President Isaac Herzog said on Saturday that Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief and Netanyahu’s main rival, gets the first try at forming a government. It matters for US readers because Israel’s next government will shape Washington’s talks on Gaza and Iran.

Key Facts Prediction markets. Polymarket: Netanyahu out by 31 December 2026 at 44.5%, up 26 points in seven days (4:25 a.m. ET, 8 November).

Trigger. President Isaac Herzog said on Saturday that Eisenkot, a former army chief, will get the mandate to form a government.

Next. The formal handover is set for Sunday, 8 November, at 5 p.m. in Jerusalem (10 a.m. ET); Eisenkot then has 28 days.

Volume. About US$35,000 changed hands on the three live contracts in 24 hours, so they are thinly traded.

What the Traders Now Expect

Polymarket runs a market called “Netanyahu out by…?” with one price for each deadline. At 4:25 a.m. ET on 8 November the 30 June 2027 contract read 68%, the 31 March 2027 contract 66% and the 31 December 2026 contract 44.5%.

A week earlier the same three contracts stood at about 37%, 24.5% and 18.5%. The 31 December price therefore gained 26 points in seven days and 6 points in the last 24 hours, while the March contract gained about 41 points in the week.

The market has drawn about US$125 million in bets since it opened. In the last 24 hours the three live contracts saw only about US$35,000 of trading, almost all of it on the December one, so a few bets can move the short-dated prices.

Why the Odds Moved

Israel’s president holds a mostly ceremonial office, but he decides who gets the first chance to build a government after an election. On Thursday, 5 November, Herzog’s office said lawmakers holding 67 of the 120 seats had recommended Eisenkot, 46 had recommended Netanyahu, and one seven-member faction named no one.

On Saturday, 7 November, Herzog’s office announced that Eisenkot, who leads the opposition party Yashar, will receive the mandate. It is the formal task of trying to assemble a majority of at least 61 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament.

Eisenkot has 28 days, and Herzog can add up to 14. Herzog has also said the recommendation count does not settle who can govern, because parties on both sides refuse to work with some of the others.

Prediction markets do not explain their moves. The timing fits this news, but it is not proof of what traders were thinking.

In Plain English Netanyahu out. Polymarket’s “out” contracts are bets on whether Netanyahu has left the prime minister’s job by the date shown.

Mandate. The president’s formal task for one politician to try to build a majority government.

Caretaker. A prime minister who stays in office, with limited powers, until a new government is sworn in.

61 seats. The majority needed in the 120-seat Knesset.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, “Prime Minister of Israel after the next election?”: Eisenkot 66.8%, Netanyahu 18.6%, Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beytenu party, 6.6%, Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister, 2.8%. About US$89.8 million has traded on that market overall.

Kalshi, an exchange regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), asks who will succeed Netanyahu: Eisenkot 82% on the last trade, Bennett 3.3%. Only about 790 contracts of the Eisenkot contract traded in 24 hours, with a wide gap between buyers and sellers, so that market is thinly traded.

The “out by” contracts and the “who is next” markets ask different questions, so their numbers should not be added together. These prices are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Why the Odds Stay Below 50% for 2026

The 31 December price is below even odds because a mandate is only a chance to build a majority, not a government. Netanyahu stays caretaker prime minister until a new cabinet is sworn in.

Traders are splitting the timeline. They put the chance of an exit by mid-2027 at about two in three, but give this year’s deadline less than a coin flip.

What It Means for US Readers

Israel is one of Washington’s closest partners, so a change of prime minister would reach US policy on Gaza, Iran and defence aid. Eisenkot’s party says it will govern only with partners who accept his four principles, including destroying the military and governing power of Hamas, the Palestinian militant group.

Investors in Israeli assets should watch the Sunday ceremony and the first coalition talks. Markets are bets, not votes, and the odds can reverse quickly if Eisenkot cannot reach 61 seats.

What It Means for Latin America and Africa

The direct effect is limited. Israel’s next government will set its stance on Gaza and Iran, and Middle East tension is one of the factors that can move oil prices.

Oil exporters such as Brazil, Colombia and Nigeria, and oil importers across Africa, watch those prices. We found no report of an oil-market reaction to this decision, so this is a channel to watch, not an observed effect.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Eisenkot can reach 61 seats, or which parties will join him.

We also could not confirm the exact rules Polymarket uses to settle “out” if a caretaker government stays in place.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do prediction markets say about Netanyahu leaving office?

On Polymarket, a crypto-based platform, traders price 68% that he is out by 30 June 2027 and 44.5% by 31 December 2026. These are bets, not polls or forecasts by The Rio Times.

Why did the odds rise again?

No trader explanation is published. The rise came as President Herzog said he would task Gadi Eisenkot, not Netanyahu, with trying to form a government.

What does the mandate actually do?

It gives Eisenkot the first chance to assemble a majority of 61 of the 120 seats in the Knesset. He has 28 days, which Herzog can extend by up to 14.

Does the mandate mean Netanyahu is out?

No. Netanyahu stays caretaker prime minister until a new government is sworn in, and Eisenkot can still fail. Markets price that risk, which is why the 2026 contract sits below 50%.

Can I trade on these markets?

This article gives no trading advice and links to no betting site. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the CFTC; Polymarket is a separate crypto-based platform.

Sources: Office of the President of Israel; Knesset, Israel’s parliament; Polymarket and Kalshi public market data (read 8 November 2026, 4:25 a.m. ET).
