World.title: Messages from Khankendi: Symbols of occupation become symbols of victory
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. The address delivered by President of Azerbaijan and Supreme Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Ilham Aliyev in front of the Victory Arch in Khankendi on November 8, marking Victory Day, highlighted not only the military outcomes of Azerbaijan's historic victory in Karabakh but also its political and moral significance.

Key points in President Ilham Aliyev's speech show that, for Azerbaijan, Victory did not end with the liberation of its territories. It has continued through the restoration of sovereignty, the elimination of separatism, and the transformation of former sites of occupation into new symbols of statehood.

President Ilham Aliyev's decision to deliver his address in Khankendi, in front of the Victory Arch, carries particular political and symbolic significance. Once presented as the center of separatism, the city has now become a place where the restoration of Azerbaijan's sovereignty and state authority is being demonstrated.

In this regard, the location itself forms part of the message. Khankendi is no longer being presented in the context of conflict and separatism, but rather as part of Azerbaijan's historic victory and post-conflict reconstruction.

The symbolic fulfillment in Khankendi on September 20, 2023, of President's earlier declaration that "Karabakh is Azerbaijan, an exclamation mark" is also particularly significant in this context. It demonstrates how a political statement was subsequently translated into concrete events and outcomes. In other words, the political resolve expressed in 2020 entered a new phase in 2023 with the restoration of Azerbaijan's sovereignty throughout Karabakh.

One of the most striking messages in the President's address was his announcement that the building once occupied by the former separatist entity would eventually house a Victory Museum.

The head of state recalled that when he visited the building in October 2023, he opened its windows and said he wanted the "evil spirit" to leave the premises. He then emphasized that a Victory Museum would be established there, giving the site profound symbolic meaning.

This is not simply a matter of changing the building's function. Transforming a site that once served as the center of separatist administration into a museum preserving Azerbaijan's historical memory creates a symbolic dividing line between the past and the future.

The central message is that the legacy of the occupation period is being replaced not only physically but also in the realm of public and historical memory. A building that once symbolized the past will become a place where future generations can learn about the history of Victory.

The President's remarks that war criminals are now serving their sentences in Baku prisons also complete the legal dimension of this message. Thus, the address draws attention both to the fate of the political center of separatism and to the accountability of those who led it.

The figures cited by the President regarding the outcome of the 44-day war were among the key points illustrating the scale and results of Azerbaijan's military operations.

More than 300 cities and villages were liberated on the battlefield during the war, while the liberation of Shusha on November 8 marked a decisive stage in the military campaign. The liberation of Shusha demonstrated Azerbaijan's military and political superiority and played a crucial role in the process leading to the end of the war.

In this context, Shusha's historical and geographical significance should be considered alongside its status as Azerbaijan's cultural capital. Its liberation carried meaning far beyond the military outcome, representing an important moment in the restoration of national memory and historical justice.

The return of other territories to Azerbaijan without a single shot being fired or a single casualty being suffered, following Armenia's signing of the act of capitulation, illustrates the distinction between the military phase of the war and the subsequent political agreements. This was an important demonstration of how Azerbaijan's battlefield advantage shaped the developments that followed.

Another point highlighted in the President's address was the comparison between the Azerbaijani and Armenian armies during the war.

According to the head of state, not a single Azerbaijani serviceman deserted during the fighting. Armenia, meanwhile, acknowledged that nearly 12,000 of its soldiers had deserted.

This comparison underscores that wars are not fought solely with weapons and technology. The fighting spirit, discipline, and confidence of military personnel in their mission also influence the outcome. The combat capability, military preparedness, and determination of Azerbaijani servicemen are presented as among the key factors behind the results of the 44-day war.

Taken together, these points in the President's address reflect several stages of Azerbaijan's path in Karabakh: military victory in 2020, the full restoration of sovereignty in 2023, and the ongoing reconstruction of the liberated territories.

The address delivered in front of the Victory Arch in Khankendi, the plan to establish a Victory Museum in the former separatist building, and the particular emphasis on the liberation of Shusha are all elements of the same political and historical narrative.

Its central message is that, for Azerbaijan, Victory is not limited to the memory of a past war. It continues through the consolidation of state sovereignty, the preservation of historical memory, and the building of Karabakh's future.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev's speech in Khankendi was powerful and emotional - Mikhail Gusman
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. We are all deeply moved by the incredibly powerful speech delivered by President and Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev in Khankendi, and it was a very powerful and emotional address, a distinguished journalist, radio and television host, writer, and public figure, Mikhail Gusman, told Trend.

"I congratulate the entire Azerbaijani people on this historic day – Victory Day," he said. He noted that one of the key points in President Ilham Aliyev's speech was that Azerbaijan's historic victory had been achieved through the unity and struggle of the entire nation.

"The President once again emphasized that this victory belonged to the entire Azerbaijani people and had not come easily. The enemy was strong and cunning and had been preparing for war for 30 years. The bravery of Azerbaijani soldiers, the courage of the entire Army, and the Supreme Commander's outstanding leadership produced the desired result. The Azerbaijani Army, backed by its people, emerged victorious. This victory will be remembered for centuries, and the Azerbaijani people will always be grateful to those who made it possible," he said.

Gusman stressed that one of Azerbaijan's main objectives now was to fully restore life in its native Karabakh.

"Today, our main goal is to bring life back in full to our native, liberated Karabakh. Nearly 100,000 people are already living and studying there, and new jobs are being created. Every day, Karabakh is becoming more and more the vibrant and significant part of Azerbaijan that it was before the occupation," he said.

The journalist also said that President Ilham Aliyev's remarks explaining the essence of the Azerbaijani identity and ideology, known as Azerbaijanism, had made a particular impression on him.

"What especially touched me was President Ilham Aliyev's explanation of the importance and philosophical essence of the idea of Azerbaijanism. Being a citizen of Azerbaijan is not enough; calling yourself Azerbaijani is not enough; even being ethnically Azerbaijani is not enough. Azerbaijanism must become deeply ingrained in a person's very being as an ideal of profound humanism and the highest values.

I would like to express my special gratitude to the President for articulating the essence of this great concept – the idea of Azerbaijanism – with such mastery," Gusman added.

World.title: Live: Wallabies open spring tour at Twickenham against England
World.content:
(Getty Images)

Former Wallaby Berrick Barnes has revealed how even Springboks and All Blacks greats "hero-worshipped" Mark Nawaqanitawase upon his arrival in Japan.

Fresh off becoming the only player to capture this year's NRL premiership after completing an Ashes and State of Origin series-winning double, Nawaqanitawase has begun the latest chapter of an already-decorated career at the Saitama Wild Knights.

Barnes is the backs and attack coach under the club's director of rugby, former Wallabies mentor Robbie Deans, and couldn't be happier to have the freakish code-hopper on board.

"We're so lucky to have him. Forget the player, there's an aura and energy about him which is rare. He's a rare human being," Barnes told AAP from just outside Tokyo. "He's just really positive around the group and lifts the Japanese boys up. He only lobbed on Thursday and already knew a lot of the boys' names. "He'd even watched some footage and was over how we played. Not many guys come in and do that. Like, you'd think that's the bare minimum, mate, but that's pretty rare."

Barnes, a one-time Wallabies vice-captain after starting in the NRL as a teenage wonder at the Brisbane Broncos, has played with and under an endless list of legends of both codes.

Yet he was still blown away by the way Nawaqanitawase was feted by teammates and Wild Knights staff, including two-time Rugby World Cup winners Damian de Allende and Sam Whitelock.

(Getty Images)

"The aura he's got, he walks into a building and he even gives you belief as a coach, which is pretty rare from a player," Barnes said. "I'm just excited for him to be around the boys. They're a great bunch we've got here and they'll welcome him in, but I've never seen a bunch of foreigners in our team actually genuinely excited to see someone in the building — and genuinely nervous. "The Kiwi boys included. They deal with some pretty famous Kiwi guys — All Blacks or whatever — but Mark's status in what he's done in rugby league, it's ridiculous and, for a lot of those boys, there's a bit of hero worship there. "We've got Damian de Allende, Lood de Jager, two players probably most considered like Mark in South Africa. We have Sam Whitelock, who came up and coached. "So guys who've done a lot in the game, but I'd say there's not many that have had that 'Marky Mark' presence with guys. It's like 'holy shit, this guy's that good and we get to have him on our team'. That's pretty bloody cool."

Barnes believes the dual international will revel in Japan — and become an even superior player without the spotlight, glare and pressures from NRL or Australia's Super Rugby Pacific fans.

"Honestly, he'll get around with anonymity, seriously," Barnes said. "That's what people don't get about Japan. It is an island unto itself. It's culturally unique. "Yeah, on game day for sure he'll get mobbed by fans. The rugby fan base here is strong and they're passionate. But outside of games, he'll get around as if he's just an everyday bloke. "After a while fans will recognise him, but people have to understand no-one watches rugby league over here. It's a weird thing because in Australia it's on everything and it's our main sport, especially on the east coast. "But over here, mate, no one even knows who Nathan Cleary is."

AAP

World.title: Against Samoa, Australia's old power conquered the new world
World.content:
They say you can't fight city hall, but sometimes against Australia, it feels like you're flat out breaking a few windows.

The Kangaroos cruised into the World Cup final by turning Samoa's dream into a recurring nightmare via their 44-12 win in Sydney on Sunday night.

As New Zealand did the night before, Australia won this on the finer margins.

Spirit filled the night through the anthems, where tears again flowed freely, and the Siva Tau, which ended with Brian To'o and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui sharing a moment more powerful than words can say.

Moments like that are the big things, the reason these matches matter in the first place. And it's what makes them feel like more than a game but through the blinding emotion there is still a game to be won.

To do it when it really matters, you need to do all the little things and Australia proved it's the little things that make up life right from the start as, not for the first time, its science defeated Samoa's magic on the big stage.

Against any other team, it might not matter that Francis Manuleleua and Jazz Tevaga, two middle forwards, found themselves defend together off a scrum. It's not the done thing, but you can get away with it.

But the Kangaroo punished Samoa for that lapse when Tom Dearden took them and threw a dummy everyone knows is coming but nobody seems to know how to stop for the first try of the night.

Like the hardest teachers, Australia stressed the same lesson over and over again and Samoa's inability to change the course meant frustration took hold, which only made things worse.

Three times in the first half alone, Samoa conceded a penalty, a set restart and a try in quick sequence. For the final 19 minutes of the half, they got to their kick just twice.

Give Australia that much ball and field position and you're asking for punishment.

The Kangaroos ran up the tries and carried a 26-2 lead into the break that killed off the game as a contest and robbed the blue wave in the stands of their power.

Samoa's army of fans were silenced by Australia. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The harder the Samoans tried and the more venom they played with, the more it turned to a choking bile in their throats.

Spencer Leniu dropped the ball with his first touch, got sin-binned for dissent, then dropped the ball with his first touch on return.

They did what they could to the end, and twice had tries chalked off by the barest of margins. But in the end Australia were too clinical, too clever, too willing and able to exploit every little edge on offer until it all added up to a comfortable win.

Samoa's poor discipline — Adam Gee pinged them for a combined 12 restarts and penalties in the end — and errors would have been much to overcome against most sides and most sides aren't packing Australia's heat.

RLWC live The Kangaroos will face New Zealand in the final of the Rugby League World Cup after overwhelming Samoa 44-12 at Sydney Football Stadium. Follow live.

Reece Walsh, raced in a brilliant hat-trick to continue his dazzling tournament and put himself right in the frame to be awarded the Golden Boot on Thursday as the best international player of the year.

The Broncos firecracker was the explosion and the fuse was lit by Cameron Munster and Harry Grant, who were in total control of every aspect of the match throughout.

Pat Carrigan and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui were both strong in the middle in a performance that should help restore a little of the Australian forwards battered reputation.

The win would have been a personal triumph for Fa'asuamaleaui given the Samoa international copped plenty from the crowd.

The Pacific nations have given this World Cup so much and they feel like the future of Test football. But this game was a reminder of the power of old money and that the most dangerous creatures in these waters are still Kangaroos.

There is a reason, for all the improvement Samoa and Tonga have made in recent years, they only have one win over Australia from a combined 10 attempts.

It's the same reason Australia has only lost one game from 18 starts in the set restart era, which is the same reason they haven't lost a game on home soil in 11 years.

Samoa's frustration was palpable as the game slipped away. (Getty Images: Spencer)

To climb the green and gold mountain, you need to be as close as perfect as reality can allow because need a way to douse their firepower and blunt their smarts while getting just about everything right yourself.

New Zealand have the team to do it, to the point they should be favourites for the final. But it's no guarantee they will because team as fierce and skilled as Samoa, for all their might and power, couldn't really get themselves in the fight.

After all their growth, it is the last step they need to take but perhaps the longest of all.

The Kangaroos are as ruthless as they are well-drilled, as fast as they are merciless.

That is why, even as the Davids have gotten bigger, Goliath still reigns.

World.title: Strong earthquake rocks central Japan, injuring at least 22
World.content:
A strong earthquake has shaken central Japan, shattering store windows, causing people to flee buildings and leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media.

Japan's Meteorological Agency said Sunday's quake was a magnitude-5.7, while the US Geological Survey reported it at magnitude-5.5.

Smaller aftershocks were reported.

A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara and nearby prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, as well as Gifu.

Japanese TV footage showed shattered store windows and scattered shards of glass on the streets.

A bookstore was left with mounds of books that had flown off the shelves.

The injuries included people who fell from stairs while they were trying to flee.

The quake, which struck at 1:04am (local time), was located about 40 kilometres below the Earth's surface in Shizuoka Prefecture.

Aichi and Shizuoka are neighbouring regions. They are far enough from Tokyo that the quake was not felt there.

Experts warned residents of the possibility of more earthquakes in central Japan this week. (AP: Kenzaburo Fukuhara)

The meteorological agency warned people to brace for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially the next two to three days.

"Please be on the lookout for mudslides, falling rocks and the possible effects from rainfall," Ayataka Ebita, an agency official, said.

He said no apparent change was detected to the Nankai Trough plate, where scientists say a megaquake can possibly hit.

The Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in the affected areas as a precautionary measure. Sometimes quakes can damage the railways the trains run on.

A book store employee had to clean up after the earthquake in Toyota in Aichi Prefecture. (AP: Kyodo News)

Japan is located in an area that is prone to earthquakes.

Authorities frequently instruct people to stock up on bottled water, food and batteries, have plans ready to hide under tables and keep comfortable walking shoes at hand.

AP/ABC

World.title: Wounded Jillaroos into World Cup final after Fiji smackdown
World.content:
Facing the Jillaroos at this Rugby League World Cup has been like heading straight into the eye of the storm.

Those who have dared to venture there have emerged either gallant in an ultimately big defeat, like Fetu Samoa, or humbled into merciless submission, like England and Wales.

But the Fiji Bulikula storm chasers stared the beast down in the semi-finals, and rattled them. Not besting them this time, but firing a warning shot that their time is coming.

This will be sold as a Jillaroos' scare or wake-up call, but this was more like much-needed proof of life for the international women's game.

Fiji's time is coming

Most fans and experts predicted another Jillaroos' trouncing.

The three-time defending champions steamrolled their opposition in their three pool games, with a combined score of 242-6.

SYDNEY, AUSTRALIA - NOVEMBER 08: Isabelle Kelly of Australia is tackled during the 2026 Women's Rugby League World Cup Semi Final match between Australia Jillaroos and Fiji at Allianz Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Sydney, Australia. (Photo by Mark Metcalfe/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

They have lost only one game in a decade, and that was to their long-time nearest (and truthfully only) rival, New Zealand.

The two-horse race in the women's game has been holding it back, and this tournament has had some ugly scorelines, showing much more investment is needed.

But Fiji, in its first World Cup appearance, could be the one that can finally break the Australia-New Zealand duopoly.

Where no other side has made the slightest dent in the Jillaroos' machine, the Bulikula turned it into a write-off in the first half.

The Fijians brought incredible defensive intensity; they crunched the Australians in tackles with perfect technique as they forced countless uncharacteristic errors.

The Australians' completion rate was around 40 per cent, a figure unheard of for the best side in the world, as the visitors executed to perfection.

Their long kicking game in particular was on point. They consistently pinned the Australians back, then regained possession deep into their opposition's half.

Un-Jillaroos-like things were happening. Tamika Upton failed to collect bombs. Jocelyn Kelleher dropped the ball unchallenged. Abbi Church was stopped dead in her tracks, sprinting towards the tryline.

This was Fiji's first appearance at the women's World Cup. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Five-eighth Luisa Yaranamua, destined for the NRLW sooner rather than later, played the game of her life, as she orchestrated an 8-0 lead.

But the Australians did not have to be perfect to come back and win this one.

They started to wipe out the unforced errors, the completion rate improved, and when they entered the red zone, they scored.

Church was the stand-out with four tries, including one where she steamed into the in-goal to collect a kick which almost any other player surely would have dropped.

But the gritty win took its toll; Jamie Chapman left the game early with cramp, and the Australians will come away with bruised bodies, if not slightly bruised egos. All for the greater good of the game.

Fiji players perform the hymn Noqu Masu before the game. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Fijians tired in the second half, unable to hold back the Australian wave, but they kept turning up till the end, and were rewarded by a late try.

Their contributions extended to the pre-game too, as they performed their moving hymn, the Noqu Masu.

Another reminder of the power of the Pasifika nations in this World Cup, where culture, faith, and footy collide.

The Jillaroos' juggernaut may have stuttered for the first time in what feels like an age, but it ultimately remains on track for its final destination.

A final against the Kiwi Ferns in Brisbane next Sunday, and a fourth straight World Cup trophy beckoning.

World.title: Two Australians rescued after helicopter crashes into Borneo river
World.content:
Two Australians have survived a helicopter crash after it nosedived into an Indonesian river while fighting fires on the island of Borneo.

Video shows the helicopter collecting water for water-bombing operations from a river in Indonesia's South Kalimantan province.

The aircraft then loses control, losing altitude and crashing into the river.

Indonesia's National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB) said two Australians survived and the cause was being investigated.

Late on Sunday night, personnel from Indonesia's search and rescue agency Basarnas confirmed they found the body of an Indonesian crew member who was in the helicopter when it crashed.

Loading...

Video shows local residents helping to pull the wreckage out of the river.

The two Australian men are receiving medical attention while personnel from Indonesia's search and rescue agency, Basarnas, are heading to the scene.

The helicopter was contracted by Indonesian authorities as the country faces its worst forest and land fire season in more than a decade.

The firefighting helicopter crashed into the Barito River in Borneo while scooping up water. (AFP: Reina)

"In Indonesia, the helicopter frequently supports various disaster response missions of the National Disaster Management Agency, with flight routes covering Banjarmasin, Pontianak, and Surabaya," BNPB spokesperson Berton SP Panjaitan said.

"The relevant team is currently on stand-by in the field, and a complete report detailing the chronology and exact cause of the accident is being compiled for immediate release to the public and authorities."

The helicopter lost control and nosedived into the river. (@joneshop via X)

Flight tracking data shows the helicopter leaving Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan this morning and heading to fire-affected areas before the crash.

The crash comes after three Indonesian crew were killed after a separate water-bombing helicopter crashed earlier this week in Central Kalimantan.

The helicopter was carrying eight crew and also crashed while loading water.

Indonesia battles supercharged fires

Intense forest and land fires have been burning across large swathes of Indonesia, particularly in the Indonesian portion of Borneo, known as Kalimantan, in Sumatra and in Papua.

Haze crisis reignites regional frustration Widespread fires in Indonesia are prompting calls for legal action or boycotts in neighbouring countries blanketed by the smoke, ahead of an ASEAN foreign ministers' meeting.

The fires often burn on peatland, which can be notoriously difficult to put out as embers can burn far below the ground.

Environmental monitor Nusantara Atlas said satellite monitoring data shows more than 1.9 million hectares have burned across Indonesia up to September this year.

The country's environment minister said more than 100,000 personnel have been involved in fighting fires across the country.

The fires have spewed a toxic smoke haze across parts of the region and in Indonesia alone more than 400,000 cases of acute respiratory infections have been recorded according to the country's health ministry.

The country has a fire season annually, but this year has been supercharged by drought and heat caused by a Super El Niño.

The fires are commonly linked to land clearing operations, particularly to clear land for plantations.

Indonesian police have named more than 240 people and 20 companies as suspects, accused of deliberately or negligently lighting fires.

World.title: Jillaroos avoid all-time upset to progress to World Cup final
World.content:
The Jillaroos have qualified for the Rugby League World Cup final, but only after surviving an almighty scare against tournament debutant Fiji at Sydney Football Stadium.

The world champions conceded first and were level at half-time, but surged clear after the break to triumph 30-14 and avoid one of the sport's all-time upsets.

Winger Abbi Church scored four tries as the Jillaroos booked a date with old foe New Zealand in next Sunday's final in Brisbane.

Speaking on Channel 7 at full-time, Fiji captain Sereana Naitokatoka was bristling with pride for her team, which provided one of the World Cup's great storylines in its run to the semifinals.

"I'm so proud of all my lewas [girls], they put in the hard work from the first minute of the game to the very end, and I'm very proud of them," Naitokatoka said.

Luisa Yaranamua gave Fiji a shock early lead. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

After cruising through the group stage with an aggregate scoreline of 242-6, the Australians were challenged for the first time in the competition, caught off guard by a disciplined, aggressive Bulikula outfit.

A penalty goal from five-eighth Luisa Yaranamua earned Fiji a shock 11th minute lead, before the same player dummied and then slid over to provide one of the most sensational scorelines in international rugby league history.

8-0 down after 16 minutes, the Jillaroos were far from their best and clearly rattled, with their hopes of a fifth-straight World Cup final seemingly under threat.

Two unconverted tries, courtesy of Church and Tamika Upton, ensured scores were level at half-time, but the hosts reached the break having completed just 12 of their 19 sets.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

An improved second-half showing saw the Jillaroos hit the front and then find some breathing space, Church striking three times in the second 35, including one spectacular aerial effort.

Player of the match Church was full of praise for Fiji, saying it was a much needed test ahead of her side's clash with the Kiwi Ferns, who qualified for their seventh straight decider with victory over Samoa on Saturday.

"Fiji did exactly what we thought they were going to do," Church said on Channel 7.

"They came out hard and gave us a real fight and a real arm wrestle.

"I think it was an incredible game, we really needed that going into next week and they really tested us."

A cause for concern was the absence of star winger Jaime Chapman, who crossed early in the second period but spent much of the half off the field, struggling with what was reported as cramp.

Fiji was able to conjure a second try, but Maria Paseka's late four-pointer, scored after a neat short-side play, was quickly cancelled out by Church's fourth effort of the day.

World.title: SA government plans to ban ticketless parking fines
World.content:
The South Australian government plans to ban councils from issuing ticketless parking fines.

Under the planned reforms, councils would be banned from posting fines to drivers after a camera car has driven past, and it would be mandatory for inspectors to leave a physical ticket on the car or hand it to the driver.

The South Australian premier highlighted the City of Adelaide's Park Safe program — which uses a car with cameras on top to scan for illegally parked cars and take high-quality photos — as an example.

The council has previously said the images are reviewed by trained officers to verify whether an offence has occurred.

A recent council report showed that on average, 25 per cent of contested fines were withdrawn following requests for reviews by parking information officers so far this year.

Dallas Coull says he never received fines before the City of Adelaide's Park Safe car came into effect. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Tour bus operator Dallas Coull, who spoke at the government's press conference about the reforms, said he had never received fines before the Park Safe program but had received "dozens and dozens" since its implementation.

"There's actually a hotel in the CBD that don't pick up [at] anymore because we get kept getting fines," he said.

Fiona Garwood says she welcomes the proposed ban on ticketless parking fines. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

In nearby Rundle Mall, shopper Fiona Garwood welcomed the planned changes, saying she would "rather have things done by a person".

Fellow shopper Levi Adams said he had seen the council's Park Safe car in the CBD before and agreed with the government's proposed reforms.

"I'm concerned about AI in every aspect of life, so I really don't need it to be in parking fines as well. The less, the better, in my opinion," the 23-year-old said.

Peter Malinauskas says the regulation was modelled on similar reforms in New South Wales. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Mr Malinauskas said AI technology could still be used, but any ticket would need to be physically issued by a council inspector at the time of the alleged offence.

"If they've got someone in the car and someone gets out of the car, looks at the circumstances … that's OK," he said.

"It's the practice of the car and the AI machine only forming the judgement that we are regulating out."

Heather Holmes-Ross says people can contest ticketless parking fines as they can with other fines such as red light speed cameras. (Supplied: Local Government Association of South Australia)

Local Government Association of SA president Heather Holmes-Ross said it was "unusual" that the state government had not consulted them on the planned reforms, and questioned whether it would extend to other ticketless fine systems.

"The technology we're talking about is the same technology that's used by red light cameras, phone detection — it's all the same software — so we're a little confused about why it would be that just parking data is being attacked here and not all data that's collected by AI," she said.

But the state government said there was an "important distinction" between enforcing parking restrictions and road safety laws.

"Parking fines are mostly issued to stationary cars whereas that is clearly not the case for a speeding car," a spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said the state government would consult stakeholders, including the LGA.

Ms Holmes-Ross, who is also the mayor of Mitcham in Adelaide's inner-south, said there were several councils trialling the technology around the state in a bid to improve efficiency, with human oversight.

"If you drive past 10 or 20 cars, then that video can be viewed, and those fines can be mailed out," she said.

"If you're stopping and you're giving out those 20 individually, it just takes more time.

"So if there's a way of doing it accurately and more efficiently, it's better for everyone."

World.title: Kangaroos cruise into World Cup final with victory over Samoa
World.content:
The Kangaroos will face New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup final after overwhelming Samoa 44-12 at Sydney Football Stadium.

Fullback Reece Walsh crossed for a hat-trick and five-eighth Cameron Munster was influential with three try assists as Australia produced by far its most convincing performance of the tournament.

It sets up a rematch of the tournament opener, when the Kangaroos snuck past the Kiwis 24-22 four weeks ago, but Sunday night's win over a poor Samoa side was a comfortably better performance for Kevin Walters's side.

The fireworks started before the game when the teams came face to face during a dynamic siva tau, with winger Brian To'o touching foreheads with Kangaroos prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, who is eligible to play for Toa Samoa.

It was one of the moments of the World Cup and ignited the atmosphere at the Sydney Football Stadium, sold out and dominated by Samoa fans.

Samoa drew first blood with a penalty goal, but the next time the crowd favourites troubled the scorers early in the second half they had conceded five tries and were down to 12 men courtesy of prop Spencer Leniu's dissent to referee Adam Gee.

The Kangaroos, who had looked so clunky for the first three matches of their campaign, clicked almost every time they were given chances by an error-riddled and ill-disciplined Samoa.

Jarome Luai and Samoa fell afoul of the officials. (Getty Images: Spencer)

Tom Dearden's opener, using Walsh as a distraction to allow the halfback to scythe through off a scrumbase play, set up the onslaught as Samoa seemed powerless to stop the surging Australians.

Munster and Walsh wreaked havoc with their footwork and ball playing to lead Australia to a 26-2 advantage at half-time.

Samoa crossed twice in the second half, through Stephen Crichton and Izack Tago, but the comeback attempt never really got off the launchpad as Walsh completed his hat-trick and Jack Bostock dove in late while the game devolved into messy footy and occasional spot fires.

Earlier, the Jillaroos were caught cold early by a red-hot Fijian outfit and trailed 8-0, but ultimately hold off the Bulikula to win 30-14 and set up a fifth straight World Cup final against New Zealand.

The women's and men's finals will be played at Brisbane's Lang Park next Sunday at 4:10pm and 7:35pm AEDT respectively.

World.title: Walsh sinks Samoa as Kangaroos set up blockbuster World Cup final showdown with Kiwis
World.content:
A backflipping Reece Walsh has helped put Australia within touching distance of their fourth-straight World Cup crown as the Kangaroos dismantled Samoa 44-12 in their semi-final.

In their most complete performance of the tournament to date, Kevin Walters’ outfit put an ill-disciplined Samoan side to the sword, running in eight tries at Sydney’s Allianz Stadium on Sunday night.

Led by fullback Walsh, who scored a hat-trick, the Kangaroos rarely looked troubled.

Reece Walsh celebrates after scoring Australia’s fourth try. Getty Images

Australia will face New Zealand at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane in next Sunday’s final as they look to extend their stranglehold on the World Cup that stretches back to 2013.

As fluent as Australia were, Samoa were all at sea in one of their most underwhelming showings since their surprise run to the 2022 final.

With a side stacked with NRL talent and a groundswell of support from their diaspora community, Samoa have a realistic hope of breaking international rugby league’s glass ceiling in the years to come.

But on Sunday they made nine errors and gave up 12 set restarts or penalties, while prop Spencer Leniu was sin-binned for dissent late in a disastrous first half.

The Kangaroos soared into the World Cup final after smashing Samoa in Sydney. Getty Images

After a lively pre-game siva tau where they came face to face with the Kangaroos, Samoa were first on the board when Stephen Crichton kicked a fourth minute penalty.

But it was all one-way traffic from then on as Australia asserted their dominance, starting when Tom Dearden scythed through some feeble defence off a scrum play to put the home side on the board.

Jacob Preston pinballed his way over from close range before Tom Trbojevic, Walsh and Bradman Best all crossed to push the Kangaroos out to a 26-2 halftime lead.

Walsh - chosen ahead of James Tedesco for the starting No. 1 spot - celebrated his try with a backflip.

But he was left red-faced soon after halftime when he leapt to claim a Samoa bomb, which Crichton scooped up to score.

The Brisbane fullback soon made amends by slaloming his way through the Samoan defence and palming off Brian To’o to add his second.

Izack Tago barged his way over as Samoa showed something of a fightback.

But again, Walsh was the man in the right place at the right time.

The fullback backed up a Cameron Munster break to add his third before having a hand in Australia’s final try to winger Jack Bostock.

World.title: Australians walk away from helicopter crash while fighting fires in remote Indonesia
World.content:
WorldAsiaAviation Australians walk away from helicopter crash while fighting fires in remote Indonesia Karuni Rompies November 8, 2026 — 9:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Two Australian pilots have escaped with minor injuries after their helicopter plunged into a remote Indonesian river while fighting fires that have raged across the island of Borneo, as authorities search for a third crew member. The Super Puma H225 helicopter was supporting forest and land fire-extinguishing operations and can be seen in video footage attempting to collect water for water-bombing when it loses altitude and nosedives into the river. Loading A spokesman for the National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNBD), Berton Panjaitan, said initial reports from the search and rescue office said both Australians “have been found in good health”. He named them as Hugh Andrew John Page and Michael John Betterridge and said they were receiving medical attention and their families had been contacted. He said the third crew member, Indonesian national Yayan Supyansuri, who was serving as the helicopter landing officer, was missing.



“We have also ensured that the two crew members who have been found receive medical examinations and any necessary medical care,” Panjaitan said. “We have conveyed to the families of those involved that the government is placing serious priority on the search, rescue, and care of all the helicopter’s crew members.” Related Article Climate crisis How monster El Nino is causing havoc around the world An 18-strong team has been dispatched from the South Kalimantan Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD) to the scene for the rescue effort. Panjaitan said the first priority was to locate Supyansuri and “ensure that the entire search and evacuation process is conducted safely”. “Second, we are ensuring proper care for the crew members who have already been recovered. The BNPB is coordinating with relevant parties to ensure that both pilots receive necessary medical examinations and treatment,” he said. The helicopter has been moved to the riverbank for further investigation. Panjaitan said it was too early to say what caused the crash and he did not wish to speculate before the official investigation results are available.



“This incident is a matter of serious concern for the BNPB, particularly regarding air operations for forest and land fire management,” he said, promising a “comprehensive evaluation of safety aspects in our air operations”. The scale of this year’s fires in Indonesia is unprecedented, and comes after months of drought fuelled by what is shaping up to be the strongest El Nino on record, as well as underlying climate change. From January to September this year, 1.9 million hectares of land burnt across Indonesia, according to satellite imagery analysed by Nusantara Atlas using peer-reviewed methodology. That is 38 per cent higher than the comparable period in 2019, the previous worst year on record for fires in Indonesia. World.title: Three times the rebate and way above inflation: the medical specialties with sky-high fees
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHealthcare Three times the rebate and way above inflation: the medical specialties with sky-high fees Brittany Busch November 8, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australians are paying 20 per cent more to see some specialists than they were a year ago as rising fees outpace inflation, reinforcing calls for the government to do more to rein in extravagant charges. New analysis from the Grattan Institute reveals some specialists are consistently charging patients much more than their colleagues. The most expensive 5 per cent of psychiatrists, for example, charged a median out-of-pocket fee of $669 for an initial consultation – more than double their peers. The most expensive paediatricians and cardiologists also charged three times more than their peers, setting median fees of $362 and $265 respectively for initial consults. Some specialists charge far more than their peers. Gabrielle Charotte The influential policy think tank is arguing that Labor should make specialists who charge the most extreme fees repay their Medicare rebates to the government.



Their intervention builds on momentum to overhaul specialist fees, an issue Minister for Health Mark Butler said would be a priority for Labor’s second term. He launched an inquiry into specialist affordability and accessibility in March, triggering a stoush with doctors who accused the senior frontbencher of blaming practitioners while neglecting real reform. More than 800,000 Australians skip or delay specialist care every year because of the cost, harming patient quality of life and further burdening under-pressure hospitals, the Grattan Institute said on Monday. Related Article Health Five graphs that show how the cost of seeing a doctor has skyrocketed The report into what it describes as a broken market builds on previous research that found specialist fees soared 73 per cent between 2010 and 2025 – three times faster than inflation, wages or other Medicare service fees. The latest report found specialist fees grew 4 per cent faster than inflation in the past year. The median fee for a first visit to a psychiatrist jumped 20 per cent, or $50 a year, while a dermatologist’s rose 7 per cent, and for most specialities, the highest fees grew the fastest.



“This policy failure is hurting patients and exacerbating the cost-of-living crisis,” Grattan Institute health program director and the report lead author Peter Breadon said. “Well over two million Australians now pay at least one extreme specialist fee a year – more than double the number in 2020.” Some specialties are more likely to charge “extreme fees”, which the think tank defines as more than triple the Medicare Benefits Schedule. This is the amount the government contributes to the cost. “More than 60 per cent of dermatologists would be classified as extreme-fee chargers, and more than a quarter of obstetricians and gynaecologists,” the report said. The think tank called for schedule fees to be reviewed to ensure doctors are fairly compensated, starting with those specialties. Fees vary both between and within specialties, and workforce shortages and swamped public care can exacerbate high costs and long wait times for patients.



Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Out of control’ specialist fees will be Labor’s next health priority The Australian Medical Association argued in its submission to the parliamentary inquiry that access and affordability issues were driven by government underfunding over many years, while private health insurance benefits were also failing to keep up. The peak body said Medicare had not matched rising costs of providing services after a freeze on rebates and subsequent slow indexation. “The growing shortfall must be absorbed by medical practices or passed on to patients,” the submission said. But the Grattan Institute said on Monday that specialists had on average recouped Medicare losses and then some, while rising costs also could not explain the highest fees. The median profitability of specialists grew more than that of GPs.



“The real problem is a market with almost nothing to restrain fees, which has been left on autopilot for far too long,” the report said. The institute said Labor’s moves to improve fee visibility and speed up the recognition of overseas qualifications were the simplest steps forward and called for the government to go further. “Rising fees and wait times won’t be reversed by cheap and easy reforms,” the report said. The Grattan Institute wants the government to require the “small minority” of specialists charging an average of three times more than the schedule fee to repay those Medicare rebates. Less than 6 per cent, or 2000 specialists, would be affected, and the annual assessment would avoid penalising genuine high fees needed for complex or lengthy consultations, the institute said. All GPs should also have easy access to specialist advice to avoid unnecessary referrals while a shortfall of 7000 specialists by 2033 had to be urgently addressed.



“No one is accountable for how many specialists are trained, in which specialties, or where,” the report said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Brisbane Lions close in on a successor to AFL coaching legend Fagan
World.content:
SportAFLBrisbane Lions Brisbane Lions close in on a successor to AFL coaching legend Fagan Peter Ryan November 8, 2026 — 7:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Brisbane Lions are expected to announce a replacement for three-time premiership coach Chris Fagan this week as they ponder whether to appoint internal candidate Cameron Bruce or take the club into a new era under external candidates Nathan Buckley, Hayden Skipworth or Adam Simpson. Despite Bruce being considered the favourite, the Lions have been adamant that they had not settled on a successor for Fagan who retired soon after leading the Lions to their third consecutive flag when they overcame Fremantle with a barnstorming finish in the final minutes of an epic grand final. The club is looking not just to 2027 – where they remain a strong premiership chance – but beyond into the next era. This group reached eight consecutive finals series and four straight grand finals under Fagan and have played in four finals in each of their past three premiership campaigns. Brisbane assistant coach Cameron Bruce is a candidate for the vacant Lions gig. Getty Industry sources with knowledge of the process and who wish to remain anonymous said the club need to be convinced an internal appointment is at least as capable as external candidates available.



They also want the new coach to meet the challenge of maintaining the momentum Fagan’s extraordinary record of success created for the club in Queensland and nationally with the position one of the most high profile in Australian sport. Alongside football manager Danny Daly, the club has created a well-led program which is, to a large extent, player driven. The Lions selection panel includes chair Andrew Wellington, CEO Sam Graham, Daly and coaching mentor Phil Smyth. Board member and four-time premiership coach Leigh Matthews is acting in an advisory capacity and Simon Black and Matti Clements are being consulted. Bruce has been involved in six premierships as a development and assistant coach at the Lions, Carlton and Hawthorn since 2013 and the players hold him in high regard. He played 224 matches for Melbourne and 10 games at Hawthorn before retiring in 2012. He joined the Brisbane Lions in 2022 and was responsible for midfield and centre bounces at the Lions in 2026. Chris Fagan left behind big shoes to fill after winning three flags as the Lions coach before retiring. AFL Photos via Getty Images Buckley and Simpson coached against each other in the 2018 premiership with the Eagles winning the flag with Simpson at the helm. Simpson finished at West Coast in 2024 with a 50 per cent winning record after 242 matches. He has worked in the media since finishing.



Buckley returned to coach as an assistant coach at Geelong in 2025 after finishing at the Magpies in 2021, having coached them to a 54 per cent winning record in 218 matches. He was a candidate for the Tasmania Devils job, having also met with Melbourne and North Melbourne when their coaching jobs were vacant. He played with the Brisbane Bears in 1993 before joining Collingwood, where he started his career under Matthews. He has also been Fox Footy’s On the Couch with Matthews this season. Skipworth is a well-credentialled assistant who started his stint at Collingwood in the coaches’ box with Buckley after coaching at Essendon, including stints coaching his own team in the VFL. He also played at the Crows and the Bombers and is considered a good communicator. It is rare for clubs to appoint a new coach following a premiership, with Allan Jeans returning to coach the Hawks in 1989 after Alan Joyce stepped in to coach the team to a flag in 1988 when Jeans took a break for health reasons. Peter Jones replaced Alex Jesaulenko as coach in 1980 after a board coup following the 1979 flag resulted in Jesaulenko leaving the job. Fagan announced last week he was joining Carlton as their director of coaching in 2027 after 243 matches with a winning percentage of 61.32.



Meanwhile, former Blue and Giants utility Zac Williams announced his retirement from the AFL on Sunday following a 183-match career. He played just 70 matches in an injury-riddled six seasons at Carlton and 113 matches at the Giants. His high point was a best on ground performance for the Giants in their 2019 preliminary final win over Collingwood. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Get your Windex ready: The Sydney school that has a brush with destiny
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation Get your Windex ready: The Sydney school that has a brush with destiny Christopher Harris November 8, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s just past noon on a Friday and a small army of students clutching bottles of spray and wipe, buckets and brooms spreads across the playground at Chatswood High, led by a man in a black suit with a commanding voice. Meet Robin Chand, the public school principal not afraid to make students clean. Other students operate mechanical claws to pick up litter. They have a few minutes to clean an area before Chand leads them, like a benevolent Pied Piper, to their next spot. Their 45-minute cleaning shift began with a small speech. Year 7 Chatswood High students collecting litter under the direction of principal Robin Chand, pointing in the background. James Brickwood “I give them a talk about the importance of looking out for our environment, and that the responsibility is on each of us,” he says. There have been no complaints from the school’s 2287 students since the cleaning regime was introduced about three months ago. Teachers sign up their classes to clean with two sessions a week.



Word has spread quickly on the north shore. Prospective parents are now less interested in NAPLAN or HSC results than they are in cleaning. “When we go to parent information sessions at primary schools and in the community, when we show a slide of kids cleaning – it is a huge attraction point,” he says. Teachers say the initiative has made students more mindful of their physical environment. James Brickwood The origins of the cleaning policy at Chatswood High can be traced back two years, when Chand visited a Japanese high school where students mopped the floors. “I just thought it was just beautiful. It was just amazing. There was no discussion about why. It was just understood that the school is here for all of us,” he says.



That stuck in his mind. But it was not until the Bondi massacre last December spurred him on to adopt the unconventional cleaning regime. The school teaches manners, respect, gratitude and resilience under its new Just Be Kind curriculum. James Brickwood A contingent of Chatswood High students, parents and teachers visited Bondi Pavilion in the aftermath and Rabbi Dovid Slavin spoke to them. “He always talks about light beating darkness, and I thought to myself: ‘What’s something that we can do, that I can do as a principal, that will have some sort of effect of planting a seed of kindness and respect?’” They created a curriculum called Just Be Kind – which explicitly teaches manners, respect, gratitude and resilience, out of which the unconventional cleaning roster was born.



Related Article Education Meet the private school girl on a mission to make everyone use good manners After a shift with the dustpan and brush, year 9 student Hillary Zhu, 14, says the exercise had opened her eyes. “Only after you start cleaning the school, you realise how much rubbish there is,” she says. “I told my parents about it, and they were like, ‘These children are so disciplined, they follow their principal. Very good, very good.’” When Supreme Joshi, 14, heard about the cleaning plan, he was happy because he could see the school was dirty. He estimates he has picked up between 10 and 15 scraps, explaining that finding litter has become trickier since the initiative was launched.



“I’ve tried hard … There’s not much rubbish around here,” he says. Rachel Benny, 14, says it helps her feel more part of a community. “It’s also pretty calming.” Adriana Figueroa Gonzalez, 15, pulls a sparkly gold-backed playing card from her pocket. “I mean, it was on the ground,” she says as she places it back into her pocket. Parents emailed to thank Chand, saying cleaning activities were standard practice at their high schools in Asia. James Brickwood She says the mechanical claw tools (which a local Bunnings donated) alleviated the ickiness she felt about touching other students’ rubbish. But she thinks the cleaning regime helps everyone appreciate the work of others.



“I feel like a lot of times, people forget about the people who actually clean the school, like the janitors. I really want people to notice and appreciate these people,” she says. Not everyone was initially impressed, says computer science teacher Imogen Harding, who signed one of her classes up for a cleaning session this year. “There was a repeat of grumblings around ‘Why are we doing this? Shouldn’t the younger students be picking up the rubbish?’ ” But students’ attitudes changed, saying at the end it was enjoyable and satisfying. An email from a parent this month thanked Chand: “Growing up in Asia, cleaning activities were a normal part of our school life. We learnt that keeping our school clean was not just about personal hygiene, but also about respecting and taking care of the environment around us.” Student Luke McDermott, 15, notes there were good reasons students did not simply pick up rubbish of their own volition.



“I think there’s more stigma around it that if you do it without being told, you’re viewed as more of a goody-two-shoes,” he says. But that might change too. “Respect is cool,” Chand says. “Respect is courageous.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Jacob Preston pinballed his way over from close range before Tom Trbojevic, Walsh and Bradman Best all crossed to push the Kangaroos out to a 26-2 halftime lead.

Walsh - chosen ahead of James Tedesco for the starting No. 1 spot - celebrated his try with a backflip.

But he was left red-faced soon after halftime when he leapt to claim a Samoa bomb, which Crichton scooped up to score.

The Brisbane fullback soon made amends by slaloming his way through the Samoan defence and palming off Brian To’o to add his second.

Izack Tago barged his way over as Samoa showed something of a fightback.

But again, Walsh was the man in the right place at the right time.

The fullback backed up a Cameron Munster break to add his third before having a hand in Australia’s final try to winger Jack Bostock.

Two Australian pilots have escaped with minor injuries after their helicopter plunged into a remote Indonesian river while fighting fires that have raged across the island of Borneo, as authorities search for a third crew member. The Super Puma H225 helicopter was supporting forest and land fire-extinguishing operations and can be seen in video footage attempting to collect water for water-bombing when it loses altitude and nosedives into the river. Loading A spokesman for the National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNBD), Berton Panjaitan, said initial reports from the search and rescue office said both Australians “have been found in good health”. He named them as Hugh Andrew John Page and Michael John Betterridge and said they were receiving medical attention and their families had been contacted. He said the third crew member, Indonesian national Yayan Supyansuri, who was serving as the helicopter landing officer, was missing.



“We have also ensured that the two crew members who have been found receive medical examinations and any necessary medical care,” Panjaitan said. “We have conveyed to the families of those involved that the government is placing serious priority on the search, rescue, and care of all the helicopter’s crew members.” Related Article Climate crisis How monster El Nino is causing havoc around the world An 18-strong team has been dispatched from the South Kalimantan Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD) to the scene for the rescue effort. Panjaitan said the first priority was to locate Supyansuri and “ensure that the entire search and evacuation process is conducted safely”. “Second, we are ensuring proper care for the crew members who have already been recovered. The BNPB is coordinating with relevant parties to ensure that both pilots receive necessary medical examinations and treatment,” he said. The helicopter has been moved to the riverbank for further investigation. Panjaitan said it was too early to say what caused the crash and he did not wish to speculate before the official investigation results are available.



“This incident is a matter of serious concern for the BNPB, particularly regarding air operations for forest and land fire management,” he said, promising a “comprehensive evaluation of safety aspects in our air operations”. The scale of this year’s fires in Indonesia is unprecedented, and comes after months of drought fuelled by what is shaping up to be the strongest El Nino on record, as well as underlying climate change. From January to September this year, 1.9 million hectares of land burnt across Indonesia, according to satellite imagery analysed by Nusantara Atlas using peer-reviewed methodology. That is 38 per cent higher than the comparable period in 2019, the previous worst year on record for fires in Indonesia. World.title: Three times the rebate and way above inflation: the medical specialties with sky-high fees
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHealthcare Three times the rebate and way above inflation: the medical specialties with sky-high fees Brittany Busch November 8, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australians are paying 20 per cent more to see some specialists than they were a year ago as rising fees outpace inflation, reinforcing calls for the government to do more to rein in extravagant charges. New analysis from the Grattan Institute reveals some specialists are consistently charging patients much more than their colleagues. The most expensive 5 per cent of psychiatrists, for example, charged a median out-of-pocket fee of $669 for an initial consultation – more than double their peers. The most expensive paediatricians and cardiologists also charged three times more than their peers, setting median fees of $362 and $265 respectively for initial consults. Some specialists charge far more than their peers. Gabrielle Charotte The influential policy think tank is arguing that Labor should make specialists who charge the most extreme fees repay their Medicare rebates to the government.



Their intervention builds on momentum to overhaul specialist fees, an issue Minister for Health Mark Butler said would be a priority for Labor’s second term. He launched an inquiry into specialist affordability and accessibility in March, triggering a stoush with doctors who accused the senior frontbencher of blaming practitioners while neglecting real reform. More than 800,000 Australians skip or delay specialist care every year because of the cost, harming patient quality of life and further burdening under-pressure hospitals, the Grattan Institute said on Monday. Related Article Health Five graphs that show how the cost of seeing a doctor has skyrocketed The report into what it describes as a broken market builds on previous research that found specialist fees soared 73 per cent between 2010 and 2025 – three times faster than inflation, wages or other Medicare service fees. The latest report found specialist fees grew 4 per cent faster than inflation in the past year. The median fee for a first visit to a psychiatrist jumped 20 per cent, or $50 a year, while a dermatologist’s rose 7 per cent, and for most specialities, the highest fees grew the fastest.



“This policy failure is hurting patients and exacerbating the cost-of-living crisis,” Grattan Institute health program director and the report lead author Peter Breadon said. “Well over two million Australians now pay at least one extreme specialist fee a year – more than double the number in 2020.” Some specialties are more likely to charge “extreme fees”, which the think tank defines as more than triple the Medicare Benefits Schedule. This is the amount the government contributes to the cost. “More than 60 per cent of dermatologists would be classified as extreme-fee chargers, and more than a quarter of obstetricians and gynaecologists,” the report said. The think tank called for schedule fees to be reviewed to ensure doctors are fairly compensated, starting with those specialties. Fees vary both between and within specialties, and workforce shortages and swamped public care can exacerbate high costs and long wait times for patients.



Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Out of control’ specialist fees will be Labor’s next health priority The Australian Medical Association argued in its submission to the parliamentary inquiry that access and affordability issues were driven by government underfunding over many years, while private health insurance benefits were also failing to keep up. The peak body said Medicare had not matched rising costs of providing services after a freeze on rebates and subsequent slow indexation. “The growing shortfall must be absorbed by medical practices or passed on to patients,” the submission said. But the Grattan Institute said on Monday that specialists had on average recouped Medicare losses and then some, while rising costs also could not explain the highest fees. The median profitability of specialists grew more than that of GPs.



“The real problem is a market with almost nothing to restrain fees, which has been left on autopilot for far too long,” the report said. The institute said Labor’s moves to improve fee visibility and speed up the recognition of overseas qualifications were the simplest steps forward and called for the government to go further. “Rising fees and wait times won’t be reversed by cheap and easy reforms,” the report said. The Grattan Institute wants the government to require the “small minority” of specialists charging an average of three times more than the schedule fee to repay those Medicare rebates. Less than 6 per cent, or 2000 specialists, would be affected, and the annual assessment would avoid penalising genuine high fees needed for complex or lengthy consultations, the institute said. All GPs should also have easy access to specialist advice to avoid unnecessary referrals while a shortfall of 7000 specialists by 2033 had to be urgently addressed.



“No one is accountable for how many specialists are trained, in which specialties, or where,” the report said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.
