World.title: Candidate quality on the ballot paper
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Candidate quality on the ballot paper November 8, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tribute to Feng Jianming Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. ELECTIONS It’s been a real lift to the spirits to know that democratic institutions have held in the United States and extreme MAGA positions have been thoroughly repudiated in the recent elections.

Now Americans have intelligent, capable and diverse new senators, congressional representatives and governors who have been able to withstand the massive tide of big money advertising against them.

Nick McKenzie and his fellow investigative team members (″⁣Top One Nation official’s strip club links to bikie figure″⁣ 8/11) have revealed the chancers applying to be candidates for One Nation and the dubious figures behind them.

A longstanding fringe party has been backed with a great deal of money from ultra-wealthy donors with MAGA links and suddenly seems to in contention for seats in our state parliament. This feels like the fringe group who took over the Republicans two years ago.

Yet, there are 14 excellent independents standing for election who have been thoroughly vetted and selected by their own communities in seats from Ashwood to Shepparton. Two of these are standing in upper house seats.

If you want fresh voices, these candidates committed to integrity, the environment and their own communities rather than any parties are surely the better option. Fixed four-year terms in Victoria mean there’s no chance for a course correction in two years.

Helen Hook, Black Rock Choose candidate fit for purpose

In the natural world “fittest” does not mean strongest or most powerful. It actually refers to the idea of being “the best fit” for adapting to a changing environment. Applying this principle to the prospective frontbench members of the next Victorian government is a useful way of shaping one’s decisions when filling out the ballot paper. Who is better prepared and qualified – more “fit” – to govern?

Jim Spithill, Glen Waverley



Same as it ever was

With all the corruption and general bad behaviour in our governments nowadays, I yearn for the good old days of Joh Bjelke-Petersen, Robert Askin, Henry Bolte and Neville Wran.

John Rawson, Mernda Show us the detail

Perhaps it is time for the state governor, on behalf of the king, to dissolve parliament and appoint an administrator for Victoria. Elections should be deferred for 12 months to allow the three major contenders (devoid of any miscreants) to prepare a plausible management plan, so that Victorian voters can properly assess the offerings.

Richard McLoughlin, Dromana Faith is a matter of opinion

Columnist Barney Zwartz suggests that having ″⁣faith″⁣ in the Australian Electoral Commission, given that we cannot ″⁣verify all the facts″⁣ of how the AEC works, is the same as religious ″⁣faith″⁣ in a divine entity (Opinion, 8/11).

For Barney’s information, the AEC has offices throughout Australia, a phone hotline, a government-appointed commissioner and many hundreds of staff.

And it is staffed neither by angels, demons nor fairies at the bottom of the garden. It also does not require temples of professional intermediaries suggesting they speak on its behalf without the slightest knowledge of whether it actually exists.

Julian Guy, Mt Eliza One Nation credentials

The standard of candidates to represent One Nation continues to decline. Will some sort of criminal record soon be a prerequisite?

John Walsh, Watsonia THE FORUM



Bad influencers

It’s not often I agree with Neil Mitchell, but he is right to warn that social media is killing sensible political discourse (Victoria’s voters are going in blind, 11/3).

Not only has the election campaign become defined by edited 20-second video grabs that distort and misrepresent, voters are increasingly relying on the punditry of online influencers and culture warriors.

Traditional broadcast media may not be perfect, but at least it has trained journalists using credible sources, and regulators holding it to account. Unless we rein in social media, and teach the next generation to use it critically, our liberal democracy and our elections are under serious threat. The influencers shaping this election answer to no one, and that is precisely their appeal.

Tim Wright, Point Lonsdale Manipulation’s limits

Neil Mitchell (″⁣I interviewed Ben Carroll and Jess Wilson. One went viral, the other complained″⁣, 8/11) writes about how Jess Wilson and Ben Carroll are very guarded and evasive in their responses because in the social media age answers can be manipulated and distorted. If there is one thing we have learnt from the US midterm elections, it is that gross manipulation of public opinion has its limits.

Despite Musk’s saturation spending on pro-Republican propaganda, it had zero effect on the voters’ decisions.

David Fry, Windsor Trump-like stamp

Finally, we are seeing the writing on the wall. Populist parties like One Nation have been allowed to be racist and insulting because that’s their style (“Trump’s midterms shellacking is a gift in disguise”, 7/11) but according to a Stanford University political scientist, “populist parties aren’t good at governing”.

Hopefully, Australian voters will realise this when they cast their vote in the forthcoming Victorian elections. Pauline Hanson is not on the ballot card in Victoria, but her Trump-like stamp certainly is.

As voters we have the opportunity to put the values of a liberal democracy back on the table. Voting no for populist parties is a vote for moderate policies that puts our community first and that includes all Australians.

It’s time to put respect front and centre.

Marisa Di Giacomo, Beaumaris Take the Tulla

Build the airport rail down the middle of Tullamarine freeway, either raised or at ground level. No Sunshine station upgrade or other political agendas so that work can start now and finally get this project back on the rails.

Tony Danino, Wheelers Hill Biding time

In order to aid the reduction of state debt, the incoming state government should offer a 99 year lease on the land set aside for the proposed new rail lines. By that time, proper plans should be completed.

Elizabeth Meredith, Surrey Hills



Crippling awfulness

Your article by Nick McKenzie, Tony Ambrigetti and Paul Sakkal (″⁣Top One Nation official’s strip club links to bikie figure″⁣, 8/11) completely confirms my long-held opinion about the crippling awfulness of One Nation. Their xenophobia even extends to our First Nations. It also confirms my opinion that One Nation simply has ‘No Notion’.

Daniel Meszaros, Parkville Weekend stabbing

I read that the stabbing resulting in the death of a food delivery rider has sent ″⁣fears some of Melbourne’s China-born residents have for their safety into overdrive″⁣, 7/11).

Fear of crime is a daily reality of life in many parts of Victoria. The protest Sunday by Melbourne’s Chinese community and that in August by Sunshine’s Vietnamese community (about the death of shopkeeper Van Viet Truong) demonstrate that affected communities are angry, scared and frustrated about what happened.

Trang Vu, Eltham North Words on Chapel

Re Malcolm Knox’s tale of unneighbourly language (″⁣Some men can’t park their hatred of women″⁣, 7/11).

Passengers on a Chapel Street (7/11) had to endure a tirade of expletive language (every second word) from a male passenger, unhappy with the slow progress of said tram, every other topic on his mind, and oblivious to how his behaviour uncomfortably affected others. What did he expect? This was Chapel Street, not the driver’s fault. Cut the language mate, and your world might improve.

Christine Hinton, Glen Huntly Two-state questions

It’s not the first time that correspondents to this paper have referenced the historical fact that Palestinian authorities or spokesmen have rejected and resisted Israeli attempts towards a two-state solution in the past (Letters 7/11). Your correspondent reminds us that this was more than 20 years ago; does that mean that the option is off the table today?

Will it have helped that the Israeli government and IDF response to the October 7, 2023 atrocity committed by Hamas was to execute another atrocity in Gaza and embolden Israeli settlers in the West Bank to further persecute Palestinians there? Might a weakened Hamas make a two-state solution more achievable with the inclusion of the right negotiators and diplomats from across the Middle East deployed?

Will it have helped the hope for peace in the Middle East to have arguably produced in another generation some hundreds or thousands of children or youths who despise Israel for what it has done in Gaza?

Brendan O’Farrell, Brunswick Scrutinise Chalmers

Your Letters correspondent’s defence of Jim Chalmers (7/11) is a striking exercise in political apologetics, camouflaged as economic analysis.

Rather than objectively examining the treasurer’s performance, he selectively rewrites economic history, blames the failures of previous governments and paints Chalmers as a courageous reformer, now beset by forces beyond his control.

It ignores the negative consequence of Labor’s own (over) spending, taxation and productivity policies.

It is a remarkably generous assessment of the treasurer, who like all politicians, should be judged on his own record, not given “a free pass” through selective comparisons with his predecessors. Blaming Keating and Costello for today’s economic challenges defies the economic fundamentals.

Governments cannot control global shocks, but they certainly influence inflationary pressures and economic confidence. Additionally, independent RBA monetary policy is not some political inconvenience to be dismantled.

Certainly, debate negative gearing, CGT and trusts, but selective history, political spin and convenient blame shifting is not sound economic analysis.

Chalmers deserves the scrutiny on his own record, not immunity through comparisons with his predecessors.

Mark Tolson, Kew



No to recession

The lack of imagination the Reserve Bank demonstrates in its effort to manage inflation reflects poorly on the policy capability of the Board. As Governor Bullock admits, interest rate changes take time to have an effect.

Yet, their decisions make no concession that the measures they use are monthly, and based on past activity. They are imperfect reflections of inflation, with a miscellany of data that excludes important items such as mortgage costs. Maybe the RBA should find a more reliable measure of inflation. Or, to reduce demand, investigate ways that don’t target the less well-off. How about dropping calls for federal government to cut government spending and encouraging an increase in the tax paid by the better off?

What about ensuring that large corporate businesses pay their fair share of taxes? Or curtailing opportunities for the big banks to earn huge profits by passing on the full amount of the rate rise for loans? How about regulating the capacity of the large supermarkets or landlords to continually raise their prices without accountability? Without imagination, the RBA may well bring about the recession we don’t need to have.

Joy Mettam, Hawthorn East Gentle patient care

I am a retired obstetrician and gynaecologist and have a PhD in Spiritual Direction. As I have been diagnosed with Lewy Body Dementia, I am now living in one room at a supported accommodation facility in Carlton where I receive excellent care. I am fortunate that I have a diagnosis, a place which is now home, and supportive family and friends. I write today about my fear for the future for myself and all who develop neurodegenerative diseases if radical cuts to immigration are made.

We need gentle, patient care. All those who cared for me through an acute episode are people present in this country on temporary visas. Their ministrations meant that I was successfully diagnosed in my own bed, treated and nursed. I did not occupy a precious emergency bed. Simple treatment was given.

If immigration is curtailed in the way several political parties are demanding, this quality of care will no longer be available, and hospital emergency departments will be further overloaded.

Dr Janet Duke, Carlton A giant hug

A recent visit to the Alfred Centre for a day procedure made me count my blessings. Going into where the procedure took place was like walking into a mini United Nations. The professionalism, care and warmth shown made me tear up. It felt like a giant hug.

I know the health system has issues, but the people working in that system are gold.

Ann Maginness, Beaumaris AND ANOTHER THING Trump

The Democrats should welcome Stephen Miller’s appointment as White House chief of staff. As the saying goes, don’t interrupt your enemy when they’re making a mistake.

Stuart McArthur, Carlton North



Stephen Miller, Trump’s hard-line pick for chief of staff, says ″⁣Trump is the most transformative political leader in American history″⁣. Well, he sure got that right.

Merryn Boan, Brighton An aspect of the ″⁣American Dream’ is that any citizen, if their aspirations are high enough, has the potential to one day become the president. Unfortunately, an aspect of the ″⁣American Dream″⁣

is that any citizen, if their aspirations are high enough, has the potential to one day become the president.

Jae Sconce, Moonee Ponds Donald Trump wants to appoint UFC boss Dana White as his press secretary. Wasn’t King Kong available?

Ian Hetherington, Moama Victoria

The delay in delivering a major IT system to Victoria’s mental health system is no longer a delay; it’s a significant schedule slippage. Thank god for that.

Peter Randles, Pascoe Vale South I’m very impressed with Ben Carroll. So many completely new ideas and initiatives, you’d never realise he’s been in parliament for a decade.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill



Furthermore

The troubles of the Royal House of Windsor remind me of a quote from Tolstoy: “All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.” The Duchess of Sussex, Prince Harry and their children seem to be particularly unfortunate.

Sandra Torpey, Hawthorn Jimmy Saville, Russell Brand. It’s always the people you most expect.

Paul Custance, Highett First, it was Figgins Diorama to close, then Georges, now David Jones. Where to shop now?

Suzanne Palmer-Holton, Seaford The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Brisbane Lions close in on a successor to AFL coaching legend Fagan
World.content:
SportAFLBrisbane Lions Brisbane Lions close in on a successor to AFL coaching legend Fagan Peter Ryan November 8, 2026 — 7:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Brisbane Lions are expected to announce a replacement for three-time premiership coach Chris Fagan this week as they ponder whether to appoint internal candidate Cameron Bruce or take the club into a new era under external candidates Nathan Buckley, Hayden Skipworth or Adam Simpson. Despite Bruce being considered the favourite, the Lions have been adamant that they had not settled on a successor for Fagan who retired soon after leading the Lions to their third consecutive flag when they overcame Fremantle with a barnstorming finish in the final minutes of an epic grand final. The club is looking not just to 2027 – where they remain a strong premiership chance – but beyond into the next era. This group reached eight consecutive finals series and four straight grand finals under Fagan and have played in four finals in each of their past three premiership campaigns. Brisbane assistant coach Cameron Bruce is a candidate for the vacant Lions gig. Getty Industry sources with knowledge of the process and who wish to remain anonymous said the club need to be convinced an internal appointment is at least as capable as external candidates available.



They also want the new coach to meet the challenge of maintaining the momentum Fagan’s extraordinary record of success created for the club in Queensland and nationally with the position one of the most high profile in Australian sport. Alongside football manager Danny Daly, the club has created a well-led program which is, to a large extent, player driven. The Lions selection panel includes chair Andrew Wellington, CEO Sam Graham, Daly and coaching mentor Phil Smyth. Board member and four-time premiership coach Leigh Matthews is acting in an advisory capacity and Simon Black and Matti Clements are being consulted. Bruce has been involved in six premierships as a development and assistant coach at the Lions, Carlton and Hawthorn since 2013 and the players hold him in high regard. He played 224 matches for Melbourne and 10 games at Hawthorn before retiring in 2012. He joined the Brisbane Lions in 2022 and was responsible for midfield and centre bounces at the Lions in 2026. Chris Fagan left behind big shoes to fill after winning three flags as the Lions coach before retiring. AFL Photos via Getty Images Buckley and Simpson coached against each other in the 2018 premiership with the Eagles winning the flag with Simpson at the helm. Simpson finished at West Coast in 2024 with a 50 per cent winning record after 242 matches. He has worked in the media since finishing.



Buckley returned to coach as an assistant coach at Geelong in 2025 after finishing at the Magpies in 2021, having coached them to a 54 per cent winning record in 218 matches. He was a candidate for the Tasmania Devils job, having also met with Melbourne and North Melbourne when their coaching jobs were vacant. He played with the Brisbane Bears in 1993 before joining Collingwood, where he started his career under Matthews. He has also been Fox Footy’s On the Couch with Matthews this season. Skipworth is a well-credentialled assistant who started his stint at Collingwood in the coaches’ box with Buckley after coaching at Essendon, including stints coaching his own team in the VFL. He also played at the Crows and the Bombers and is considered a good communicator. It is rare for clubs to appoint a new coach following a premiership, with Allan Jeans returning to coach the Hawks in 1989 after Alan Joyce stepped in to coach the team to a flag in 1988 when Jeans took a break for health reasons. Peter Jones replaced Alex Jesaulenko as coach in 1980 after a board coup following the 1979 flag resulted in Jesaulenko leaving the job. Fagan announced last week he was joining Carlton as their director of coaching in 2027 after 243 matches with a winning percentage of 61.32.



Meanwhile, former Blue and Giants utility Zac Williams announced his retirement from the AFL on Sunday following a 183-match career. He played just 70 matches in an injury-riddled six seasons at Carlton and 113 matches at the Giants. His high point was a best on ground performance for the Giants in their 2019 preliminary final win over Collingwood. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Rugby League World Cup: Jillaroos hold off Fiji challenge to make final
World.content:
Australia held off a spirited Fiji Bulikula challenge to claim a 30-14 victory in their women's Rugby League World Cup semifinal in Sydney tonight.

The win means the Jillaroos will face New Zealand in the final in seven days.

The story truly belonged to the Fijian women, who were never a chance in their first semifinal appearance, against the world champions.

Even Australian captain Isabella Kelly paid tribute to the Bulikula team and said they now shift their focus to the final.

"It was great, the atmosphere was unreal for the Fijian girls to make it here in the semifinals and what they have been able to do for Fiji back home and paving the way for all those young girls," she said post-match.

"Incredible and I have so much respect for what they do."

Fijian captain Sereana Naitokatoka paid tribute to the fans and families for their support.

She said the players were proud and the scoreline did not reflect the effort they had put in.

"It was an amazing game and I am so proud of all my lewas (women)," she said.

"They put in the hard work right from the first minute of the game and to the very end and am very proud of them.

"Want to thank all our matavuvales (families) for coming to support the girls no matter what the scoreboard is I know they will continue to support us."

Fiji held their own in the first spell and led 8-0 with a converted try from Luisa Yaranamua, who also succeeded with a penalty kick.

The scoreline alone does not tell the story of how the Australians had to fight off the challenge from the islanders in front of close to 30,000 fans at the Allianz Stadium.

The Jillaroos scored six tries, with winger Abbi Church claiming four of her own.

Jocelyn Kelleher kicked three conversions for a personal tally of six points.

The other try-scorers for Australia were Tamika Upton and Jaime Chapman.

Fiji scored their second try through winger Maria Pasepa late in the second half.

The Bulikula played in their first world cup and created history by making it to the last four.

Fellow Pacific islanders Fetu Samoa also made the semifinals and lost to New Zealand on Saturday night.

Follow all the action in our live blog below:

World.title: Live: Australia v Samoa - Rugby League World Cup men's semifinal
World.content:
World champions Australia will face Samoa in a rematch of the 2021 World Cup finalists at Sydney's Allianz Stadium.

The Kangaroos narrowly edged New Zealand in the tournament opener and remained unbeaten in pool play, while the Samoans dropped a heartbreaker to rivals Tonga in their final preliminary outing.

The winners of this encounter will face the winners of New Zealand v Tonga in the final.

Kickoff is 10.05pm.

Follow all the action in our live blog below:

World.title: One dead after crash in South Waikato
World.content:
One person has died after a two-car crash on State Highway 5 in South Waikato on Sunday afternoon.

The crash happened around 1.30pm at Tapapa, near the intersection of Waiohotu Road, police said.

One person died at the scene.

Enquiries are ongoing into the circumstances of the crash.

Hato Hone St John sent three ambulances, a rapid response unit and one helicopter to the scene.

World.title: LIVE: Rugby League World Cup: Fiji Bulikula v Australian Jillaroos
World.content:
Australia held off a spirited Fiji Bulikula challenge to claim a 30-14 victory in their women's Rugby League World Cup semifinal in Sydney tonight.

The win means the Jillaroos will face New Zealand in the final in seven days.

The story truly belonged to the Fijian women, who were never a chance in their first semifinal appearance, against the world champions.

Even Australian captain Isabella Kelly paid tribute to the Bulikula team and said they now shift their focus to the final.

"It was great, the atmosphere was unreal for the Fijian girls to make it here in the semifinals and what they have been able to do for Fiji back home and paving the way for all those young girls," she said post-match.

"Incredible and I have so much respect for what they do."

Fijian captain Sereana Naitokatoka paid tribute to the fans and families for their support.

She said the players were proud and the scoreline did not reflect the effort they had put in.

"It was an amazing game and I am so proud of all my lewas (women)," she said.

"They put in the hard work right from the first minute of the game and to the very end and am very proud of them.

"Want to thank all our matavuvales (families) for coming to support the girls no matter what the scoreboard is I know they will continue to support us."

Fiji held their own in the first spell and led 8-0 with a converted try from Luisa Yaranamua, who also succeeded with a penalty kick.

The scoreline alone does not tell the story of how the Australians had to fight off the challenge from the islanders in front of close to 30,000 fans at the Allianz Stadium.

The Jillaroos scored six tries, with winger Abbi Church claiming four of her own.

Jocelyn Kelleher kicked three conversions for a personal tally of six points.

The other try-scorers for Australia were Tamika Upton and Jaime Chapman.

Fiji scored their second try through winger Maria Pasepa late in the second half.

The Bulikula played in their first world cup and created history by making it to the last four.

Fellow Pacific islanders Fetu Samoa also made the semifinals and lost to New Zealand on Saturday night.

Follow all the action in our live blog below:

World.title: Person critically injured after serious crash in Lower Hutt
World.content:
One person has been taken to hospital in a critical condition after a serious crash in Lower Hutt on Sunday afternoon.

Police were called to the scene near the intersection of High Street and Downer Road about 4.10pm.

Initial reports indicated that a vehicle had crashed into a parked ute, which then struck two pedestrians.

A second person has moderate injuries.

World.title: Tenancy Tribunal orders brother landlord to pay sibling tenant nearly $17,000
World.content:
After their mother died, one brother purchased the family home from her estate and rented it to the other.

For 17 years, neither treated the arrangement with any formality, allowing the home's condition to deteriorate, repairs to go undone and the rent to go unpaid.

The brothers, who have name suppression, ended up in the Tenancy Tribunal in October 2025, where the tenant brother was ordered to pay $19,548.57 in rent arrears and his tenancy was terminated.

That was not the end of their dispute.

A year later, the brothers returned to the tribunal, where the tenant sought exemplary damages for failures to maintain the premises and comply with Healthy Homes requirements, as well as reimbursement of fixed water charges paid during the tenancy.

This time, the tribunal sided with the tenant, ordering his brother to pay him $7000 in exemplary damages, $5000 in compensation for distress and loss of amenity, and $4966.74 to reimburse fixed water charges.

In the recently released decision, tribunal adjudicator Haamid Ben Fayed said he was satisfied there were significant failures to maintain the premises and comply with applicable Healthy Homes requirements.

"The respondent's evidence was essentially that, when his brother asked him to attend to something, he would come to the property and deal with it.

"Neither party appears to have treated the arrangement with the formality ordinarily expected of a residential tenancy."

The landlord told the tribunal this was how matters had operated between him and his brother for many years.

"That provides context," Ben Fayed said. "It does not provide a defence."

The tenant paid rent of $400 a week for a lengthy period, substantially below market rates, the decision stated.

Despite that, Ben Fayed said the breaches were significant and persisted for a substantial period, affecting the tenant's enjoyment of his home, and including matters relevant to health, safety and habitability.

The decision did not describe the home's issues.

He said there was insufficient evidence the applicant consistently notified the landlord of defects as they arose or gave him a reasonable opportunity to remedy them, which contributed to some of the issues continuing for longer than they otherwise might have.

Regarding the claim for re-imbursement of fixed water charges, the respondent's evidence was that the applicant paid the Watercare accounts directly.

Ben Fayed said responsibility for fixed water charges rested with the landlord, whose failure to meet that obligation resulted in the charges being passed on to the tenant.

The tenant also sought to revisit the earlier tribunal determinations concerning rent arrears and termination of the tenancy, but Ben Fayed declined.

The latest tribunal decision is unlikely to mark the end of the brothers' legal battles.

There is a High Court proceeding concerning ownership of the property and the circumstances in which the respondent acquired it from their mother's estate.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Starshield or nothing: NZDF moves closer to buying into Musk's satellite network for secrets
World.content:
New Zealand has moved closer to buying services from a satellite network set up by tech trillionaire Elon Musk for secret communications.

RNZ revealed in June that the NZ Defence Force (NZDF) was running a six-month trial of Starshield, the first confirmed case of a government other than America's trialling the two-year-old system that comprises hundreds if not thousands of satellites.

On Friday Defence told RNZ, "A Starshield trial has been completed and showed potential utility for the NZDF."

Starshield ran into controversy last month when Ukraine's access to it was reduced, jeopardising some combat and air defence missions, with critics warning this was the risk of relying on privately-owned systems in a war or crisis, as Time reported.

NZ Defence withheld details of the outcomes of its Starshield trial on the grounds releasing them might prejudice national security or defence or international relations.

"Any subsequent satellite communications acquisitions would follow normal capability management and acquisition processes," it said in a three-line statement.

The trial was purchased through the US government's Foreign Military Sales (FMS) system and required the defence minister here to sign an indemnity to shield the US from any damages claims, a routine requirement of the FMS.

Former Defence Minister Judith Collins. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Starshield or nothing

Judith Collins signed it last December after Defence made the case to her that it really needed Musk's system for "secure military grade" internet services and data transfer, documents and emails released under the Official Information Act (OIA) show.

Without Starshield "NZDF would have fewer satellite communications options to conduct operations", it told Collins.

"The NZDF cannot procure the deliverables from any other supplier" than the US government, it said.

The bonus was getting it at the same price and so benefiting from the US government's purchasing power, as well as from its management and technical support and "their unparalleled depth of knowledge" on a not-for-profit basis.

Any loss under the indemnity - which was unlikely - would be unlikely to exceed $10 million, Defence told her.

The NZDF already uses Starlink, Musk's network of 10,000-plus satellites used by millions of people to connect to the internet and relied on by Ukraine's military from the start of Russia's war in 2022.

Ukraine clash

Starshield's advent in 2024 gave customers an option with higher encryption and protection from the growing threat of "counterspace" attacks.

US Space Force said on Thursday it was "counting on partnerships with the commercial space industry to help it prevail against aggressive adversaries".

It rates Russia an "acute" threat and China the major (or "pacing" in Pentagon parlance) threat.

Reuters has reported the Pentagon is Starshield's largest customer and has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. The two clashed over the rising costs earlier this year.

"It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the [US spy agency] National Reconnaissance Office," reported Reuters.

Elon Musk became the world's first trillionaire after SpaceX went public on 12 June 2026. NurPhoto via AFP

Constrained from the start

New Zealand is almost entirely reliant on its Five Eyes partners for infrastructure in space but they in turn have been increasing their reliance on commercial partners.

A leading US Space Force-industry event late last month was titled 'Fielding the Arsenal of Freedom - Victory through Industrial Partnership'.

The constraints where New Zealand's space and military ambitions meet reality were evident from the start over Starshield, the OIA showed.

In an email in June 2024 headed "Expression of interest in Starshield - restricted", a capability manager asked an FMS manager at NZDF, "Is this something that you can assist us with from there?".

"I apologise for jumping around in subjects," they went on, "but when you are as hollow an organisation as we are, we have to wear many hats throughout the day."

Military bosses have repeatedly described the NZDF as "hollowed" out since the pandemic. The army at mid-2026 was still 700 personnel short "particularly in critical leadership" and instructors' ranks.

'Is there a fast track option?'

Another June 2024 email said Defence was "putting a plan together for future sustainment" and asked, "Is there a fast track option?" for Starshield.

It seemed not. "There are a few ducks we need to line up, especially as it is a service we are wanting access to; one that we have not seen any cost data on at all yet," the manager continued.

It took another 18 months for Collins to sign the indemnity in December 2025.

The Starshield trial that went ahead this year was to determine "what its uses are, if any", Defence told RNZ.

Friday's statement showed it had found some.

The government has talked about having a national mission to launch a sovereign satellite, and documents show this had come up in talks with NZ-founded, US-based Rocket Lab, but there have been few details.

Starshield has been linked to US President Donald Trump's Golden Dome. Reuters reported a $4 billion contract signed with SpaceX in May was to build a space data network "backbone" for superfast missile warning and tracking sensors. Similarly, the Dome would rely on a constellation of such satellites.

US President Donald Trump listens during the announcement about the Golden Dome missile defense shield, in the Oval Office of the White House in May 2025. AFP / JIM WATSON

'Fastest way'

Speed has been central to the directives and strategies coming out of both Washington and Wellington for buying new military tech - just on a massively different scale.

"The fastest way to get traction is to show how your idea accelerates warfighting outcomes across the architecture," the US Space Force told companies at its big open day last month.

"There are so many permutations of commercial integration across the ecosystem today that we weren't seeing even six months or a year ago."

The NZDF industrial strategy is to "deliver capability faster" including by buying or developing minimum viable products, using local small businesses or helping those businesses to partner with huge "primes" (big defence contractors, many of them American).

A big difference is the Pentagon has companies flocking to it, while NZ must go to them, as with SpaceX and Starshield. It also has to negotiate a way through US military export controls by using the FMS. AUKUS Pillar Two has removed some of those barriers between Australia, the UK and US but New Zealand has not joined Pillar Two. It has, however, signed on with several Pentagon space networks since 2020.

Spooked over US tech

RNZ is seeking from Defence any reports such as risk assessments or cost-benefit analysis arising from the Starshield trial, though the Official Information Act appears unlikely to be able to pierce the national security carapace.

In Europe last month, the disruption to Ukraine's access to Starshield spooked governments about relying on US technology.

Germany had begun evaluating 30 AI military tools but ruled out buying the US system used in the Iran war for targeting, called Maven Smart System, stating that letting a private, foreign contractor have access to national military databases was completely "out of the question" and "inconceivable".

The concerns last month prompted Maven's maker, Palantir, another tech company that has become central to Pentagon tactices, to reassure the Europeans that Maven had no "kill ‌switch" either it or the US government could use independent of NATO.

World.title: Luxon defends his leadership after 'huge loss' of senior MPs
World.content:
National Party leader Christopher Luxon is defending his leadership after the loss of multiple senior figures of his party in the election.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Luxon argued his party had done well, given global political trends that have resulted in major electoral upheaval.

"Ultimately, we've got the most seats in Parliament, and ultimately, we've been given a pathway to government," Luxon told reporters.

"When you think about global results and you look at incumbent governments, and particularly incumbent governments having to deal with a $3.60 fuel price, actually what we achieved, I think, is pretty good.

"I'd love 50.1 percent, but I'm proud of the result that we delivered last night."

Luxon said he took responsibility for the "huge loss" of four senior figures from his team.

Luxon hugs MP Paul Goldsmith on election night. Craig McCulloch.

Nicola Willis, Chris Bishop, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee are all gone, leaving a major hole in National's ranks, including some 20 ministerial portfolios and the Speakership.

"I'm going to miss them tremendously. These are friends of mine, personal friends of mine, and we have been through a lot together over the last five years," Luxon said.

"We've lost some huge talent.

"We have been in the trenches together."

Wait for results begins

Luxon said serious coalition negotiations would not begin until the final election results were released on 27 November.

He said he might speak informally with other party leaders in the meantime, but suggested politicians, journalists and the public could all do with a break after the six-week campaign.

"Everyone's over politics. Let's all just have a bit of a break for the next three weeks," he said.

After the 2023 election they hadn't started negotiations until the final results were in, and they would take the same course of action this time, Luxon said.

"Once you know where you are you can move through those things pretty quickly, and find the common ground and areas of disagreement."

Luxon says he's unlikely to need Opportunity to govern - but he intends to build a relationship with them. Phil Walter/Getty Images

Olive branch for Opportunity?

Media challenged Luxon over his previous pledge not to work with Opportunity on Sunday afternoon.

He said he intended to build a relationship with the party, despite repeatedly ruling out working with it during the election campaign.

He maintained it was "highly unlikely" National would need Opportunity's support to govern, with the preliminary results suggesting it could continue its coalition with ACT and New Zealand First.

But he said the election result showed a need for greater cooperation across Parliament.

"I think it's entirely appropriate to build a relationship with Qiulae [Wong] and Opportunity," Luxon said.

ACT leader David Seymour said his party was planning for two scenarios - one where the existing coalition can govern, and one where they need Opportunity.

"I think it would be prudent to understand what the possibilities were in either scenario so that we can form a government as rapidly as possible," he said.

"I know people will not be very patient with parties who appear to be slowing down the government formation process."

World.title: Swans, Hawks prevail in AFLW elimination finals
World.content:
AFLW superstar Chloe Molloy has once again lifted Sydney to victory, with the Swans defeating the Western Bulldogs by 29 points in an elimination final.

League-leading goalkicker Molloy pulled off a surprise cameo down back to help the Swans claim a 7.4 (46) to 2.5 (17) win at a wet and windy Henson Park on Sunday.

Sydney will next play Geelong in an away semi-final. The Bulldogs' season is over.

Molloy's leadership in a wet-weather scrap proved the difference for the Swans, with the former Swans co-skipper finishing with one goal, 12 intercepts, and 14 contested possessions.

Tanya Kennedy was just as crucial for the Swans, locking down Bulldogs co-captain and gun midfielder Isabelle Pritchard.

Pritchard, on return from a knee injury, was kept to just 14 disposals and three clearances as Kennedy laid 17 tackles.

Fellow Bulldogs midfielder Ellie Blackburn, also returning after being rested in last week's loss to the Cats, led the visitors with 29 touches and a goal.

Swans captain Lucy McEvoy needed just 20 seconds to score the opener with a long bomb from outside the 50-metre arc thanks to the strong breeze.

A rushed behind gave the Bulldogs their sole score of the first quarter, as the hosts made the most of conditions to fire off their four unanswered goals and build a 24-point lead.

The Bulldogs could only manage one point with the breeze in the second, with Molloy helping limit the damage with five contested possessions and four intercepts as a defender.

Molloy's stint in defence forced Bulldogs coach Tam Hyett to bring defender Vaomua Laloifi into the forward line, and the pair's battle continued well into the second half.

Sunday's final turned into a slog after torrential rain came in the third quarter, with the Swans doing just enough to maintain a 25-point lead en route to victory in front of 4,325 dedicated fans.

Hawks break through for finals win over Suns

Hawthorn has broken through for their its AFLW finals victory in an 18-point defeat of Gold Coast.

A commanding third quarter paved the path for the Hawks to prevail 8.9 (57) to 6.3 (39) at People First Stadium on Sunday.

Hawthorn, who bombed out of the finals in straight sets in 2024 and 2025, will face Carlton in the first semi-final next Saturday night at Princes Park.

Eliza West (29 disposals, one goal) and Laura Stone (21, two) were outstanding for the Hawks, while Casey Sherriff, Hayley McLaughlin and Jasmine Fleming all picked up 20 touches.

Jenna Richardson was a wall in defence, with a game-high 11 marks while completely blanketing Suns forward Dekota Brown.

The Davies sisters — Darcie and Georja — impressed for Gold Coast, who were also chasing their maiden AFLW final success.

Charlie Rowbottom battled hard for her 20 disposals (18 of them handballs), a figure matched by Niamh McLoughlin and Daisy D'Arcy.

Adding injury to insult for the Suns, young gun Ava Usher suffered a serious-looking injury to her right knee in a heavy collision with teammate Maddy Brancatisano in the dying stages.

Hawthorn kicked two goals in the last 77 seconds of a high-octane opening term — through Poppy Stockwell and Jacqueline Dupuy — to lead by six points.

The Suns responded to take a three-point half-time lead, but Hawthorn raised its pressure in the third quarter and Gold Coast couldn't go with it.

The Hawks' backline repelled 11 consecutive entries from the Suns, while their midfield trampled Gold Coast at clearance and on the outside.

Hawthorn had 33 more disposals for the term, 13 more tackles and pulled ahead by 15 points at three-quarter time.

Mikayla Nurse goaled early in the fourth quarter to give Gold Coast a sniff, but the Hawks continued to pile on the pressure and exorcise their own demons.

AAP

World.title: Meet the surgeon saving the careers of cricket's best fast bowlers
World.content:
Fast, fearsome, and fragile were words often associated with former New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond, whose promising cricket career was drastically curtailed by injury.

He debuted as a 26-year-old against Australia in Hobart in 2001, but it was in his next series, against Bangladesh, where he truly announced himself.

He took 11 wickets in two Tests at an average of 13, and it looked like the beginning of a long and lucrative career.

But Bond's back had other ideas. A stress fracture kept him out the game for almost two years from 2003.

Shane Bond is considered "patient zero" after his successful back surgery allowed him to continue his international career. (Phil Walter: Getty Images)

A meeting with back surgeon Grahame Inglis offered him hope he could overcome his injury by undergoing a little-known surgery that is now commonplace in the fast bowling fraternity.

"If I can't fix this, then the career is potentially over," Bond said of his decision to undergo pars stabilisation surgery in 2004.

"He [Inglis] talked about a procedure that he had done, one on a New Zealand high jumper and one other athlete.

" He thought that the chances I came back and bowled fast were slim, but ... I was prepared to give it a go. "

While other injuries limited Bond to just 14 more Tests before he retired in 2009, his back didn't trouble him again.

Last surgeon standing

Renowned New Zealand spinal surgeon Rowan Schouten was working with Dr Inglis at the time and said Bond was "patient zero in this whole story."

Bond took 147 ODI wickets, including a stunning hat-trick against Australia at Bellerive Oval in 2007. (AAP Image/Andrew Cornaga)

The success of that surgery laid the groundwork for a procedure that Schouten and his team have now performed on around 30 professional cricketers.

When surgeons in the UK stopped performing the procedure and Dr Inglis retired, Dr Schouten became the world's leading authority on repairing spinal stress fractures in fast bowlers.

Rowan Schouten says pars stabilisation surgery isn't a new procedure, but has recently become popular with cricketers. (Supplied: rowanschouten.co.nz)

"We were kind of left as the last man standing with experience on international fast bowlers and since then it's taken off essentially," he said.

"We're dealing with calls and connections from all around the world, from the UK, India, South Africa, Europe, Bangladesh, everywhere."

Bond still helps fast bowlers who have struggled with back issues and is often approached for advice.

He's coached Jofra Archer, Jason Behrendorff and James Pattinson, who all had the surgery and returned to play at the top level.

What is pars stabilisation surgery?

When a fast bowler is considering spinal surgery, like Australia's Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris did in 2025, it sounds like a drastic step.

Loading Instagram content

But Dr Schouten said the surgery was straightforward and "not that extreme".

It involves grafting the spine to stimulate repair, before putting screws and wires around the injured portion to provide stability.

WA quick Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris hopes to be even faster after surgery After years of back issues, Lance Morris is finally fit and firing, and the West Australian is keen to put his name in the frame for a Test call up once again.

"We've got a few little added components to it that we believe are important ... but it's a pretty standard technique," he said.

The injury, often referred to as a stress fracture, is common across sport and very prevalent in cricket.

Dr Schouten stressed the surgery is not a fusion, and most stress fractures do not need it.

"You need to preserve all that spinal motion that these guys need to be able to bowl full pace," he said.

Cameron Green opted for surgery in 2024, following several stress fractures during his career. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

If a player did opt to go under the knife, the recovery involves a six-to-nine month rehab program.

"Some stress fractures in some players become a recurring theme," Dr Schouten said.

"And then if you do that, if you have that two or three times in a row over multiple seasons, it can really disrupt a career."

World.title: Khawaja says he has thrown nobody 'under the bus'
World.content:
Usman Khawaja insists he has not thrown anyone under the bus with his bombshell ball-tampering revelations that have rocked Australian cricket.

One day on from admitting sandpaper had been used in the Test prior to Cape Town 2018 and the entire team was responsible, Khawaja defended the timing of his claims.

In a five-minute long Instagram explanation, Khawaja revealed he had planned to go public with the details days after the incident before the suspended Steve Smith talked him out of it.

Loading Instagram content

He also detailed how he made another attempt to ensure the entire team took the blame for it in 2021, before a public statement from the bowlers denied any knowledge.

But Khawaja said he had made a promise with his childhood friend David Warner to spill the details of the saga post-retirement in his book, believing Warner, Smith and Cameron Bancroft had taken the fall for the entire team.

"I haven't thrown anyone under the bus," Khawaja said.

"The guys that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we're not the victims.

"These three guys took the blame for all of us. They're the victims … people telling them that they're cheats, getting nailed by the crowd. Public humiliation."

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith were both put through the ringer. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

Extracts from Khawaja's memoir Sabr, which will be released on Tuesday, detail how an Australian player applied sandpaper to a ball in the change room in the second Test against South Africa at St George's Park in 2018.

When teammates saw how scuffed up one side became, they realised how much it would swing and Khawaja claims Bancroft volunteered to use the substance.

While Khawaja says that was initially only done at the start of sessions when entering the field, the tactic then expanded to on field in the next Test in Cape Town.

Khawaja also alleges in the book that a member of Australia's coaching staff had encouraged Bancroft to ramp up whatever he was doing with the ball, before the West Australian was caught by cameras and eventually umpires.

In the post on Sunday, Khawaja said he would "not deny" that everyone knew, and revealed how he wanted to go public in 2018 once Smith, Warner and Bancroft were suspended.

"I told Smudge [Smith] that I was going to come clean to the media," Khawaja said.

Usman Khawaja says Steve Smith talked him down from going public earlier. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

"I couldn't believe the penalties he got. But Smudge being the man and leader he was, he talked me out of it.

"He wanted to take the blame. I argued with him, but he was having none of it. That's the first time I try to come out."

Khawaja claimed he spoke extensively with then-coach Justin Langer and Todd Greenberg in 2021 about the team taking collective responsibility, with Greenberg then CEO of the players' union before becoming boss of Cricket Australia.

Lehmann claims 'everyone' was ball tampering Darren Lehmann rejects Usman Khawaja's claims the entire Australian camp knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot, but says "everyone around the world" was ball tampering up until that day.

The 39-year-old then said he never felt comfortable talking about it while back in the Australian team from 2022.

But he argued the fact he had held back the book until after Australia's Test return to South Africa last month was proof this was not a money-making venture.

"Call me a chicken or whatever you want. I didn't know how to do it because I was still in the team," Khawaja said.

"I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I'm not in that team anymore. What I say now isn't a reflection of them anymore.

"I stuck up for all cricketers in the past with the ACA [players' union] fighting for what I thought was right. This is no different.

"These three guys deserve justice and I haven't pointed fingers at anyone."

Khawaja has also been critical of Cricket Australia (CA) over its handling of the investigation into Cape Town, and that he was not interviewed.

CA has maintained it is "comfortable" with its findings from 2018 that only Warner, Smith and Bancroft knew of the idea.

Other players including bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon distanced themselves from the incident, insisting they had no knowledge "of a foreign substance" being taken on the field.

AAP

World.title: Extraordinary scenes as fog descends on 'farcical' FA Cup tie
World.content:
Does a defeat count if nobody saw it?

Altrincham fans may well be wondering that this weekend, after fog descended upon its FA Cup first round tie against Notts County at Moss Lane in Manchester.

League One side Notts County, featuring Australian former Sydney FC striker Luka Smyth, had taken a first half lead before Manchester-based Altrincham, of the fifth-tier National League, hit the front.

A late equaliser for Nottingham-based County, who won the FA Cup back in the 1893/94 season, forced extra time.

However, by that stage a heavy fog had enveloped the entire stadium, meaning extra time and penalties were played in scarcely believable conditions.

It made one slightly pity the commentators.

"I don't want to worry anyone — we can't see those dugouts at the moment because of the mist," Steve Bower said on the BBC in the closing stages of normal time, before fatefully adding that "it's getting heavier".

"We will try our best to let you know who has got the ball."

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard said on the BBC Radio Nottingham call that "We're looking around … no-one knows where the ball is."

"We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

At least he was only supposed to be summarising.

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," his play-by-play caller Adam Hassell said.

The scenes were reminiscent of another famous foggy incident involving legendary Charlton goalkeeper Sam Bartram.

On Christmas Day, 1937, a London pea souper rolled into Stamford Bridge and completely covered the field.

In his autobiography, Bartram recalled seeing "fewer and fewer figures as we attacked steadily" over the course of the match, right up until a policeman appeared on the edge of his penalty area.

"'What on earth are you doing here?' he gasped. 'The game was stopped a quarter of an hour ago. The field's completely empty,'" Bartram wrote.

"When I groped my way to the dressing-room, the rest of the Charlton team, already out of the bath and in their civvies, were convulsed with laughter."

Fortunately, nothing like that happened in Altrincham, with the game eventually going to penalties, which took place in front of the Altrincham fans.

The Notts County fans, 100 or so metres up the other end of the ground, were left to guess what was happening based on the reactions they could hear through the gloom.

The Notts County fans didn't have the greatest view of the shootout … (Supplied)

They weren't the only ones.

"He's put it wide, I think," commentator Adam Summerton said on TNT Sports as Max Sanders stepped up for Notts County.

"It's hard to tell, I'm sorry, but it's so hard to see up here.

"No, it's in. I'm really sorry, it's so hard for us to see up here," he added as the replay was shown on his monitor.

At least Altrincham fans could see if the ball had gone in or not. (Supplied: TNT Sports)

Meanwhile, Notts County's fans started celebrating after a pause of a couple of seconds, presumably because the Altrincham fans were not.

That pattern continued all the way through the shootout, right up until the final spot kick was taken, by "I think it's [Rosaire] Longelo," Summerton said.

He scored, and Notts County was through to the second round.

At least, I suppose, nobody could see the Altrincham players' disappointment.

Don't worry Eddy Jones, I think most people couldn't see your penalty miss. (Getty Images: Jess Hornby)

World.title: Socceroos wary of Jordan friendly due to security threats
World.content:
Football Australia will continue to assess security ahead of the Socceroos' planned friendly against Jordan, with an under-strength squad named amid player concerns over safety.

Tony Popovic's squad was revealed at 10:30pm on Saturday night for upcoming friendlies against Qatar in Doha on November 13 (November 14 AEDT) and Jordan in Amman three days later.

The friendlies were initially meant to serve as preparation for the Asian Cup which has since been pushed back from January to December 2027 due to security concerns in host country Saudi Arabia.

Professional Footballers Australia (the PFA) on Friday said players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

Captain Maty Ryan and fellow veterans Jackson Irvine and Milos Degenek, plus midfielder Aiden O'Neill, are the most prominent omissions from coach Tony Popovic's squad, which includes seven uncapped players.

It is unclear whether those players made themselves unavailable for safety reasons.

As yet, there has been no movement on the Amman fixture, despite Indonesia recently cancelling their own planned friendly in Jordan.

"For the match against Jordan, we will continue to assess the security environment and provide players and staff with timely, comprehensive updates, including relevant safety advice and risk assessments," FA chief executive Martin Kugeler said.

"The safety and wellbeing of our players and staff remains our highest priority."

There are eight changes to the squad from September's friendlies against Brazil in Australia.

Diesel Herrington is one of seven new faces in the Socceroos squad. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

New call-ups are Central Coast defender Diesel Herrington, older brother of Hull City ace Lucas Herrington, Portsmouth striker Thomas Waddingham and FC St. Pauli midfielder Sam Klein.

Attacker Daniel Arzani returns after finding form at Ferencvaros, along with defender Gianni Stensness (Viking FK), who scored against Bayern Munich in the Champions League.

Stunning free kick shows Irankunda's star is aligning for Socceroos Nestory Irankunda's incredible free kick against Brazil in Townsville shows that the Socceroos have stars to rival some of the biggest and best in the world.

Striker Kusini Yengi joins brother Tete, while goalkeepers Joe Gauci (Lincoln City) and Tom Glover (RB Omiya Ardija) have been recalled.

"While the Asian Cup has been rescheduled, that does not take away from the importance of this window," Popovic said in a statement.

"We have limited opportunities to be together as a group, so every camp and every game is important.

"We will have an eye on continuing to evolve the squad for the future, with our World Cup 2030 qualifying campaign and the Asian Cup both now in the second half of 2027.

"This camp gives us another chance to work with new players and see how they fit into what we are building."

Socceroos Squad

Goalkeepers: Patrick Beach, Joe Gauci, Tom Glover*

Defenders: Kealey Adamson*, Aziz Behich, Kasey Bos*, Alessandro Circati, Jason Geria, Diesel Herrington*, Lucas Herrington, Jacob Italiano, Harry Souttar

Midfielders: Sam Klein*, Riley McGree, Connor Metcalfe, Paul Okon-Engstler, Gianni Stensness, Patrick Yazbek

Forwards: Eli Adams*, Daniel Arzani, Nestory Irankunda, Thomas Waddingham*, Kusini Yengi, Tete Yengi, Marcus Younis

(* denotes uncapped player)

World.title: Moesha Johnson's Open Water World Cup winning streak continues
World.content:
The Cancún leg of the Open Water Swimming World Cup may have been the start of a new season.

But for dominant Australian Moesha Johnson, absolutely nothing changed.

Following a stunning 2025/26 season in which Johnson won every single open water event she entered, the 29-year-old started the 2026/27 campaign with yet another double gold medal-winning weekend in Mexico, underlining a dominance rarely seen in top level international sport.

In Friday's 10km race, Johnson set out her stall early by claiming the $US1,000 ($1,455) bonus for winning the sprint lap, before easing up.

"After the sprint lap the goal was just to drop back and relax," Johnson told World Aquatics.

"I haven't got the big endurance work behind me for this season so far, so my endurance strength isn't quite there.

"I really wanted to practice my open water skills, get in the pack, just play around a little bit."

After recovering amidst the melee of the main group, Johnson made her way back to the front and powered to victory, finishing in a time of 2 hours, 3 minutes and 31 seconds, 13 seconds ahead of Japan’s Airi Ebina and Italy’s Ginevra Taddeucci.

St Peter's Western swimmer and World Cup debutant, 22-year-old Jacqueline Davison-McGovern, finished in seventh place.

After her success in the 10km, Johnson backed up to win a second gold medal in the 3km elimination race.

Johnson won the 1,500m heat, the 1,000m semifinal and the 500m final dash to make it two-from-two to start the year.

"For me this was a bit more of a closure to 2026 rather than a start to the new season," Johnson said after the 10km.

"We haven't had our normal preparation so I didn't know where I was at, but today I gave myself every opportunity to finish 2026 as my year on top.

"I know people might have come to expect [winning] from me, but it's not that easy to be on top every single race.

"It's really stressful and it takes a lot of work, and it's something that I'm really proud of now.

"Hopefully, the increasing standard keeps lifting the professionalism of our sport and the girls around us and it's just as entertaining as ever."

World.title: Wet-weather chaos in qualifying for Brazilian Grand Prix
World.content:
Oscar Piastri will start the F1 São Paulo Grand Prix from 10th place on the grid after a chaotic wet-weather qualifying session at Interlagos.

The Australian only jumped into the top 10 due to grid place penalties meted out to his rivals, however, in a wet and wild session that was twice red-flagged, and delayed by 80 minutes as torrential rain teemed down on the circuit.

Piastri was only 12th fastest in the tricky conditions, missing out on Q3.

"Today's qualifying was a very tough session," Piastri said.

"The car felt reasonable in the wet, and we've been more competitive and comfortable in the dry this weekend, so it's disappointing not to have made more of the session.

"We'll review what happened and see what the weather and final grid order bring tomorrow.

"If it's dry, we look strong; if it's wet, we're still decent, but we'll need to work hard overnight and into the race to make progress up the field."

The entire grid dealt with atrocious conditions. (Getty Images: Clive Mason)

For the third year in a row, Piastri's McLaren teammate Lando Norris will start on pole.

"It's been a long day," Norris said.

"To be on pole here two years in a row… Different conditions to last year, but I am very happy.

"It was about getting two laps in, not making any mistakes and yeah, it has been a very good day.

"This was my first time driving the car in the wet, but I think I figured it out."

George Russell, who fumed at his team for telling him to back off during a flying lap, qualified second, but will start seventh after taking a five-place grid place penalty for a power unit change.

That puts world champion Kimi Antonelli on the front row of the grid after he qualified third.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was fourth fastest but has a 10-place grid drop, promoting Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson to third, with Audi's Nico Hulkenberg fourth.

Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, Oliver Bearman, Fernando Alonso and Alex Albon all made up the rest of the top 10 on track.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start from the back row of the grid after both veterans took grid-place penalties.

However, with wet weather forecast for race day, both men will back themselves to make their way through the firled to the front places.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the F1 São Paulo Grand Prix on Monday morning, with lights out at 4am AEDT.

What happened to Oscar Piastri?

Piastri was struggling on the wet-weather tyres and was delayed in changing to intermediates as the track dried during a brief window in the weather.

Then, once he changed to the correct tyres, a crash to debutant Rafael Camara meant that Q2 was brought to a premature end.

That left the Australian in 12th place and unable to participate in the final phase of qualifying.

"The track was incredibly slippery [at the beginning]," Piastri said.

"It became a little easier towards the end, but the call on tyres was always going to be difficult because I was a long way up the road and there was always a risk that an earlier red flag could change things.

"But we paid the price by missing out on Q3."

World.title: Wilson backs Wallabies to overpower mutinous England
World.content:
Harry Wilson believes the Wallabies are ready to test England's reported lack of unity at Twickenham while looking to unleash a key 'X-factor' strike weapon from their bench.

The build-up to Sunday's Nations Championship Test has been dominated by stories about unrest within the England camp at their Pennyhill Park base, leaving Australia's captain Wilson to suggest his team will be out to discover whether there's any truth in the supposed disunity.

Asked on the eve of the match whether any unrest in the opposition camp might galvanise or disrupt the hosts, Wilson said: "It could go one or two ways for them, and I guess it's on us to put them under pressure to see how close they are as a team."

But the skipper was also keen to make the point of just what a united outfit his own team has become.

"We know how close we are, how much we care for each other, and how much we love playing for our coach and coaching staff," Wilson said.

"So I'm really only worried about us, and I just want us to keep keep caring for this jersey, keep caring for every person in our group."

A report had claimed England players wanted showdown talks with coach Steve Borthwick during the July tour because of a toxic environment.

But leading England players responded with indignation this week, with Jamie George declaring they would demonstrate their loyalty to Borthwick with a stirring performance.

Yet Wilson believes his men are primed for "an epic battle in the forwards" as they seek to make amends for being outplayed at Twickenham last year.

The Queenslander is particularly enthused by the new impact role for one of their best, usual back-row starter Rob Valetini.

Last November, Australia suffered when the England second-half reinforcements came on — but now, led by Valetini, he's backing the likes of Taniela Tupou and Carlo Tizzano to fight fire with fire against the so-called 'Pom Squad'.

"It's different for Bobby, and it's just a genuine X factor coming off the bench," Wilson said.

"It's rugby now, a lot of teams have some really strong players coming off the bench, and we've got one of the best players in his position in the world coming off the bench. So he can be some genuine X factor if it's close when he comes on.

"Having a player like him coming on gives the boys a lot of confidence, and that's what England did to us last year. Hopefully, Bobby can really spark us on the bench again this year."

Harry Wilson led Australia to a famous victory at Twickenham two years ago. (Getty Images: CameraSport/Andrew Kearns)

The Wallabies' last-gasp win at Twickenham in 2024 was a breakthrough moment for Wilson himself in the early days of his captaincy, as he scored a try and had an inspirational game.

Now "comfortable" in the leadership role, he's overseeing a team which has "a lot to be excited about" and is ready to rebound from the two recent chastening defeats by a rampant New Zealand.

"We definitely want to be us. We want to play our own game," said Wilson.

"We've seen this year when we do play our style of footy how much we can hurt teams.

"In the South Africa win, when we really backed our skills and kept attacking, we really played some really good footy, and we learned some valuable lessons in those New Zealand games. We really need to take them forward."

AAP

Tech.title: There’s no slowing down media’s pivot-to-video 2.0
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the pressures of creating content for the internet, follow Mia Sato. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Almost exactly a decade ago, the media industry was in the middle of a video revolution — or so it thought. In the mid-2010s, publications poured money into burgeoning social media video efforts, chasing the promise of reaching larger audiences and opening new lines of revenue. Print publications and digital news outlets alike hired teams, pumped out content, and entrusted platforms like Facebook with their reach and distribution.

That pivot-to-video slowly revealed itself to be a lot of smoke and mirrors when it became clear that Facebook had inflated video views. Newsrooms cut writers and editors in a move to video — and then cut those video teams when they realized the pivot had not paid off. For many in the media industry, social video brings to mind layoffs and instability rather than the promised abundance.

A “pivot” feels inadequate to describe the current emphasis on social video, not just in newsrooms but in society writ large. Social media companies have reorganized their feeds to emphasize video, spurred by the massive growth of TikTok during the pandemic. But the media industry is still playing catch-up, and in some cases it seems to have been slow to jump in (perhaps cautious given past experience). It took years for some publishers to start incorporating vertical video on their websites, apps, and stories, for example, and it takes coordination and intention to get individual reporters in front of a camera to talk about their work. In the meantime, YouTube has become the most popular streamer, commanding nearly 16 percent of TV viewing, according to Nielsen. Twenty percent of Americans regularly get news from TikTok, and that number jumps to 39 percent for people 18 to 29 years old, Pew found.

Viewers favor the stripped-down selfie-style video dispatches from personalities they trust, even if those creators are not themselves reporting and writing the news. Compared with a decade ago, the barrier to entry and cost of making video content has plummeted: Anyone with a smartphone can become a video creator, no fancy equipment or editing needed. Social video is fast, personality-driven, casual, and, at times, unfiltered — the exact opposite from what news outlets are used to. A second pivot-to-video is underway, and the media industry once again wants in.

How it’s going

Video is unavoidable on social media, if not an expected part of how people and institutions show up online. TikTok’s influence is felt everywhere: on competitor platforms like Meta’s Reels and YouTube Shorts, of course, but also in unexpected places, like LinkedIn. There are no signs of it slowing down, either: The time spent watching Reels on Facebook was at an all-time high in Q3. Early tests in other countries suggest Meta is toying with the idea of dropping users directly into full-screen video upon opening the Instagram and Facebook apps. The appetite for video seems insatiable, and if news organizations won’t lean in, armies of content creators will be happy to scoop up the audiences.

Some news outlets were relatively early to the short-form social video boom. The Washington Post, for example, found notable success on TikTok before many peers had even created dedicated accounts on the platform. (Dave Jorgenson, the face of the Post’s social video effort, left the paper last year. He now makes short and longform videos under Local News International — perhaps a testament to the trust that viewers place in individual creators.)

Beyond having a short-form video presence, some traditional news outlets are leaning into formats and styles popularized in the vertical video era. CNN partnered with Jubilee, the popular channel that produces debate-me-style videos on hot-button political topics. The CNN town hall with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico was conducted in the Jubilee style. The New York Times, which for years has produced polished documentary-style videos, recently introduced the vertical video series “The Call.” Unlike the Times’ more buttoned-up videos, the point of “The Call” is to create a sense of intimacy, like you’re getting updates from a friend: The show’s host ostensibly makes a video call to a journalist reporting on the ground to ask them about what they’re witnessing.

News outlets are also directly hiring or working with content creators. Some outlets like The Washington Post have spun up so-called creator networks, where they partner with influencers to produce content independent from the newsroom. A new program supported by Poynter and Microsoft pairs content creators with a handful of news outlets so they can create content tailored for social media.

And then, of course, there are the clips. Podcasts became videos, which became bite-sized clips of podcasts formatted for vertical feeds. TV shows became web shows, which gave rise to microdramas. News articles — even major investigations — are now adapted for vertical video audiences. Individual reporters (myself included) make talking-head clips explaining our reporting. Earlier this year, I called this phenomenon “the clippening”: the reformatting of all media to be legible in a vertical video feed, even if the original work is neither vertical nor video. It’s hard to fault the people and institutions putting resources into social video — audiences are consuming it — but it’s also feeling a lot like the past.

One of the misguided beliefs of pivot-to-video 1.0 was that traction, views, or engagement on social media platforms would be enough to offset (and ideally surpass) the cost of making the content. For many, that ended up not being true, with flawed metrics, of course, being part of the reason: Virality feels nice, but monetizing that attention isn’t always straightforward. These days, social media companies have largely coalesced around the “views” measurement meaning the number of times a post was served up on somebody’s feed, whether they watched the whole thing or swiped away immediately. How many people who watch a clip of a podcast go on to listen to the full episode? Are the people watching my TikToks about my stories actually going to The Verge to read it, or buying a subscription to support my work? You can’t eat views.

The hope is that we will find new audiences where they’re already spending time. There are millions of people discussing news that journalists are uncovering — it’s important that we reach them, build trust, and be part of the conversation. What’s certain is that if reporters and news outlets don’t, a whole slew of creators will be there to take their place.

What happens next

Just as we’re getting used to short form, the ground is once again shifting under our feet. Not content simply being social media, platforms are looking to be a destination for longer form, higher production quality entertainment. Tech companies know that people watch videos on their phones, but they would also really like users to watch on their televisions, too.

This spring, YouTube’s pitch to content creators (and advertisers) was to make exclusive shows for the platform. YouTube is dominating the TV streaming wars, but other platforms like Instagram are pushing in that direction, too: Its recently announced “Features” effort allows for 90-minute horizontal video uploads, and it seems to be specifically angling for television viewing. (Unsurprisingly, there are a lot of questions from creators about what they get in return for posting longer content.) Some news outlets are already thinking ahead and eyeing longform. The BBC struck a deal with YouTube in early 2026 to create special programming specifically for the platform, then followed it up by announcing a 24/7 YouTube livestream in an effort to reach young people.

Short form isn’t going anywhere, at least right now. But these efforts to move into longer, more resource-intensive video content could be a harbinger of what’s to come — and what could soon be asked of news publishers and influencers alike. News media have had a complicated relationship with tech platforms. On one hand, it’s where audiences are, and platforms allow publishers to reach those people. On the other hand, tech companies signal to outlets (and creators) what kind of content they should prioritize, and everyone has to scramble to meet the new demand. Just as soon as journalists start getting comfortable with front-facing selfie videos, we may be facing a whole new beast: videos that are horizontal and longer, with a higher production value and higher barrier to entry that we typically associate with TV and streaming.

By the way

Instagram is already starting to place horizontal videos in discovery feeds — I recently saw the format bumped to the top of my Explore tab, mixed in with photos and vertical Reels.

Even platforms like X that are traditionally associated with text-based content are trying to sweeten the deal to get users to post more videos. The company has an invite-only bonus program that pays creators who post videos regularly. Screenshots shared by X staff indicate that creators can make thousands of dollars for posting vertical videos under 3 minutes.

If you feel like you’ve been seeing a lot more New York Times Cooking videos, it’s not your imagination: It’s a deliberate strategy to make video content from non-news verticals at the company.

Read (or watch) this

It would only be appropriate to include a video here, given the topic this week. Here’s Instagram head Adam Mosseri trying to explain the about-face the platform is doing around longform video. The comments on YouTube hammer home a big question: Instagram benefits from more content like this, but what’s in it for creators (and, by extension, news outlets)?

Short-form audiences were recently described as “rented attention” in the Link In Bio newsletter. Could longer-form content create more durable, lasting relationships between creator (or news org) and audience? Longer formats could put pressure on creators to deliver higher-quality, more in-depth material that is harder to fake than in a quick-hit 60-second clip.

News publishers are in a constant push and pull with the platforms that make their work discoverable — and not just with social media. Consider Google’s AMP page format , for example, which promised to make the mobile web a better experience for readers.
